synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Raiden Lin plays the cheerful, slightly useless Lin son so well that the Syndicate and the police both ignore him. In fact he draws the family's safe rooms, and knows the weak point of every building in the city. One night he's kneeling in the middle of an illegal race on the old shipyard road, drawing a warehouse, and a motorbike stops two metres from him.

Jinx gets off it to beat some sense into him. He looks up, smiles, and tells her that her intake manifold is beautiful. The next morning he's at her garage near the Docks with three coffees. She drinks all three.

She grew up in a chop shop under the flyover and swore she'd never be owned by anyone again, least of all the Lins. He'd like to marry her. He asks on a napkin, drawn to scale. She says not yet. He keeps asking.

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Raiden is the Lin who talks. In every other book he's in the background, cheerful, drawing something, being an idiot on purpose. I wanted to know what he was like when he stopped pretending, and who would be the first person he did it for. It had to be someone who'd see through him at a hundred and ninety kilometres an hour.

This is the lightest book in the series so far, and the most kissing. They get together in chapter three and never really stop. The trouble isn't whether they'll fall in love. It's her father's shop, his father's name, and two people who were each hidden as children learning to stop hiding each other.

He's rich, and he spoils her: a building, a dyno, a lathe, a hill. She's paying half. She insisted.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This is a warm, funny romance, but it has some hard moments:

• A man hit by a van, with injuries and a night in hospital (Raiden Gets Hit by a Car)

• A child hidden in a freezer for eleven hours, and a ten-year-old crossing a border alone (Memes at 2 A.M., Ten, Walking Home Alone)

• A threat against a loved one, a knife and an armed crew (Her Father Calls After Five Years, The Men Who Own Her Father, She Builds Her Way Out, Raiden Stops Playing Dumb)

• A remembered attempted assault on a teenage girl, which she fought off; not shown on the page (Her Father Says Sorry, She Lets Him In)

• A friend coming back injured, and grief and fear (The Masterpiece He Could Never Draw)

• A workshop fire and smoke inhalation (The Fire at the Shop)

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
The black door — Jinx's first garage, near the Iron Docks, under an old sign that says TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS.
The shipyard road — Two kilometres of cracked concrete between the dead shipyard and the cranes. Illegal races at one in the morning.
Mrs. Tong's — The noodle place on the corner that only serves men off the container ships. The table by the fridge, back to the wall.
The Meridian — Raiden's glass tower in the Symmetrical Ward. Thirty-one floors. The desk man calls the pale green bike “the tram”.
The pale green bike — The one Jinx built him. Twenty kilometres an hour, lights like a train, a drawing board on the tank, a bell.
The steel room — Behind her tool wall. A light that comes on by itself, air, a line out, a warm lamp she added, and a tin of peaches.
The napkins — Thirty-one proposals, each drawn to scale, kept in his wallet where other people keep photographs.
Under the flyover — The Slums of the Industry, where the sun never gets in. Her father's shop, CAO MOTOR REPAIR.
The gap — Behind the scrap heap, between the wall and the pillar. On the archive drawings from 1974.
The triple — A 1973 two-stroke, three cylinders, a widowmaker. Seized for seven years. Ran at 5:40 a.m.
Oh-three-one-one — The day she left. The code to everything she owns.
JINX — The shop in the old chandler's warehouse three doors down, with a long low window anyone can see into. The sign she cut herself.
The stair — Behind the third shelf on the mezzanine. Two hours of fire board. Used once.
The driveway — One point two kilometres on the hill above the reservoir road. It is a racetrack.
The monkey — The passenger in a racing sidecar, who hangs off the side. Raiden says navigator.
Dyno — A rolling road that measures a bike's power at the back wheel.
Intake manifold — The pipes that carry air and fuel into the engine. Hers are all the same length, by hand.

chapters.title: Sketching in the Middle of a Race Track
chapters.desc: May 2021. Jinx is testing a new intake on the old shipyard road when a man kneels down in front of her to draw a warehouse. She stops in time. Then she nearly kills him anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “I didn’t hit him. Write that down. I want it on record that I didn’t hit him.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
Jinx didn’t race. She tested.

Men in leather jackets never got the difference, so she’d stopped explaining. A race was when you wanted to beat somebody. A test was when you wanted to know something. Tonight she wanted to know if the new intake would hold past nine thousand revs.

She’d made it on Tuesday. Four runners, each the same length to the millimetre, curving down into the head like fingers. She’d matched every port by hand with a file and a lamp. Plus a lot of swearing. One runner a hair too long, and that cylinder breathed wrong. The whole engine felt it. A stone in a shoe.

It idled clean. Big deal. Everything idled clean.

The only straight in the city long enough to find out was the old shipyard road, two kilometres of cracked concrete between the dead yard and the cranes. Nobody ran it until the last security van had gone past the Iron Docks gates and not come back. So she sat at the back of the line under the last working streetlight, visor up, and listened.

“JINX!” Big Fok had a voice like a ship’s horn. “You racing or knitting?”

“Testing.”

“Same thing!”

“It isn’t.”

“You want to go or not?”

“Last.”

“Why last?”

“Clean road.”

“Princess,” Big Fok told the boy beside her, and went back up the line to wave his flag at somebody else.

The bike under her was black and low and long. The frame was hers. The swingarm was hers. The tank came from a breaker’s yard, dented, and she’d beaten it smooth over a week of evenings. On it, in orange and white, a carp swam up toward a spark plug. Same carp as the one up the inside of her left forearm. She’d had the arm done first.

The boy beside her had a stolen-looking sports bike with a fairing that didn’t match the frame. He revved it at her.

“Nice tractor, auntie.”

“Your fairing’s from a different bike.”

“So?”

“So’s your frame.”

“How do you—”

“Your bolts are crying.”

He looked down at his bolts. She put her visor down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twelve bikes tonight. Eight cars earlier, which she hadn’t watched. Cars were bikes for cowards. A few hundred people hung on the fences with beer and phones, and nobody was looking at the road behind them.

The world went small inside the helmet. Her breathing. The engine. Two kilometres of orange light, and the cranes at the far end like giraffes.

Big Fok dropped his arm.

The bike went. Nought to a hundred in the time it took to think the number. The front lifted a hand’s width and came down. She tucked in flat and wound it on. Six. Seven. Eight. The note hardened. No flat spot. Nine thousand. Nine and a half.

It was holding. It was HOLDING. She was going to have to buy herself a drink.

Then there was a man in the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was kneeling.

That was the bit she kept coming back to later, staring at her ceiling in the dark. Not standing. Not running. Kneeling, on the concrete, just past the last shipyard gate, back half to her. Sketchbook on his knee.

Drawing.

At a hundred and ninety you see things all at once. White shirt. Black hair in his eyes. A pencil. His face tipped up at the big warehouse with the arched roof, like nothing else on earth existed.

She didn’t think. Thinking would have killed him.

Her hands did it. Both brakes, harder than she’d ever squeezed them. The front tyre screamed. The back came round and wanted to go. Forks diving. Road coming up at her face. She held it. How? No idea. The bike bucked. Slid. Slowed. He got bigger in her visor, and he still didn’t move—

She stopped.

Next day she measured it with a tape. Two metres eleven, from the black stripe of her tyre to the scuff where his knee had been. She wrote it on the wall by her bench in marker. 2.11. In case she ever forgot how close.

He looked round. At her. At the smoking bike. At her front wheel, more or less in his lap. And he smiled, big and easy and delighted, like she’d turned up early for lunch.

“Oh, hello.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got off the bike. She didn’t put the side stand down. She found that out a second later, when the bike fell over behind her and scraped her brand new exhaust. She would never forgive him for that either.

She ripped her helmet off and threw it at the road. Then she grabbed his white shirt in both fists and hauled his face down to hers.

“Are you trying to DIE?”

It was meant to be a shout. It came out low and shaking. Worse.

“No.” He seemed to give it real thought. “I don’t think so. Not tonight.”

“You’re kneeling in a race.”

“Is it a race? I thought it was more of a…” He waved the pencil at the fences. The fireworks. The beer. “A gathering.”

“There are twelve bikes on this road!”

“Eleven now.” He looked past her. “Oh no. Is it all right? I’m so sorry. I’ll pay for it.”

She shook him. He was taller than her, just, and thinner, and he let her do it. That was the worst part.

“You suicidal idiot. I could’ve put you through that fence!”

“You didn’t, though.”

“I’d have gone through after you!”

“That would have been bad.”

“They’d be scraping us off the concrete with a SHOVEL. What is wrong with you?”

He held the sketchbook up between their faces. Politely. A waiter with a menu.

She looked. She couldn’t not.

It was the warehouse. Five minutes of pencil, and it was beautiful. The long curve of the roof. The iron ribs. Over it, faint, a spiral, tiny in one corner, opening out until it met the edge of the roof exactly.

“The golden ratio,” he said. “The whole building. Somebody built it like that on purpose, in 1931, and then everybody forgot.”

“So?”

“So look, the windows too. I’ve been trying to see it from the front for a year. There’s always a lorry parked there. Tonight the road was empty.”

“The road was empty because there’s a RACE on it.”

He looked at her then. Properly. His eyes went over her face, then past her shoulder to the bike on the ground, and the polite smile went. What came instead was greedy. She knew that look. She got it herself when she opened an engine and found the fault.

“Oh. Oh, that’s beautiful.”

“What?”

“Your intake manifold.”

“What about it?”

He stepped round her with her fists still in his shirt, so she had to turn with him. Some stupid dance.

“They’re all the same length. All four. Same curves. You made that. Didn’t you? Nobody sells one like that.”

“…Yes.”

“It looks like a hand. Like someone holding on to something they don’t want to drop.”

Jinx had nothing.

Behind them the bikes had stopped coming. The fences had gone quiet, waiting for the fight, and there was going to be one. Her right hand had been ready since the brakes. She’d grown up in a chop shop under the flyover. Men there settled things with their hands.

Except he’d looked at her bike and seen a hand holding on. Her father never looked at anything she made like that. The collectors talked horsepower and resale. Who’d ever seen what she was trying to do? Nobody.

She let go of his shirt.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Get off the road.”

“Yes. Of course. Sorry.” He didn’t move. “I’m Raiden.”

“Don’t care.”

“What’s your name?”

She picked up her helmet. New scrape down one side. She looked at that instead of him.

“Jinx.”

“That’s not a name. That’s a warning.”

“Yes.”

He laughed. Loud, surprised, like it had got out without asking. The corner of her mouth moved. She pressed it flat and went to pick up the bike. He came to help.

“Don’t touch it.”

“Sorry! Sorry.”

He stopped with both hands in the air like she’d pulled a gun on him. He watched her lift two hundred kilos off the concrete on her own, and his eyebrows went up and stayed there.

Exhaust scraped. Left mirror gone. Intake fine. She checked it twice anyway, crouched with her phone torch, thumb along every runner.

He crouched beside her. He’d picked up her helmet and was wiping the grit off the visor with his shirt cuff, slowly, ruining the shirt. She snatched it back.

“Can I see you again?”

“What?”

“Not like this. Not in a road. Somewhere with chairs.”

“No.”

“I want to see the rest of it.” He nodded at the bike. “I want to draw it properly. And I want to buy you dinner. For the mirror. And because I’d like to.” He thought about it. “Mostly because I’d like to.”

She put the helmet on.

“Get. Off. The road.”

She rode back to the start in second gear with the whole crowd watching. Nobody said a word. Not even Big Fok. At the line she looked back.

He was off the road. He was sitting on the fence by the shipyard gates with the sketchbook on his knee.

Drawing. Obviously.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden drew her bike lying on its side.

He did it fast, before the picture in his head could go. The front wheel still turning. The carp. The intake, every runner right, because he’d stared at it the whole time she was busy wanting to kill him. Her boots. Her hand, hanging by her side, fingers still curled from his shirt.

He tried her face. He got the line of her jaw and stopped. Tried again. Rubbed it out. Odd. He could draw anything.

Big Fok came down the fence and stood over him with his arms folded.

“You know who that is?”

“No. Who?”

“Bad luck, that’s who.” Big Fok spat over the fence. “She’ll kill you, boy.”

“She stopped, though. Did you see? Two metres. Maybe less.”

“Heh.”

“Where does she work?”

“Ha!”

“Is that a yes?”

Big Fok laughed all the way back up the fence and didn’t answer. That was fine. Raiden had a whole night, and a city full of people who wanted him dead or amused. One of them would tell him.

Under the drawing, in small neat capitals, he wrote: J’s bike, as it really is. R. 2021.

By ten the next morning he was at her door with three coffees.

chapters.title: “Nice Intake Manifold” Is Not a Pick-Up Line
chapters.desc: The man from the road turns up at her garage the next morning with a drawing and three coffees. She drinks all three, tells him no all day, and somehow ends up saying Thursday.
chapters.epigraph: “I brought three because I didn’t know how you took it. Now I know. You take all three.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Nobody found the black door by accident.

That was the point of it. Her garage sat near the Iron Docks, in a street of ship chandlers and rope shops. Marine paint on one side. Anchors on the other. Over the roll-up door it still said TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS in faded white letters. She’d never painted it out. It put people off.

Two rooms upstairs. A hot plate. A shower that worked if you hit the pipe. Downstairs, the only part that mattered. The workshop. Long, high, cool. Bikes on stands, bikes on the floor, bikes hanging from the ceiling on chains.

Sunday morning. She was on her creeper under a little red bike. A pair of clean brown shoes stopped beside her boots.

“Good morning!”

She lay very still under the bike.

“I’ve brought coffee. Three. I didn’t know how you took it. So there’s black, and there’s one with milk, and there’s one with condensed milk from the man on the corner. He says nobody under sixty drinks it, but you might.”

Jinx rolled out on the creeper and looked up.

He was in the doorway with the sun behind him, a cardboard tray in one hand and a sketchbook under his arm. A different white shirt. Grey trousers that had cost more than her lathe. A pencil behind his ear. He looked about twenty-three, very pleased with himself, and wrong for the street in every possible way.

“How did you find me?”

“I asked the man with the flag.”

“Big Fok doesn’t tell people where I live.”

“He didn’t. He told me you’d kill me if I came.” He seemed cheerful about it. “Then I asked the boy with the wrong fairing. He told me the street, because he wanted me dead. Then I asked the lady who sells anchors. She looked at me for ages and said the black door.” He held out the tray. “Coffee?”

✦ ✦ ✦

She drank the black one standing up, in four swallows. She’d been up since six and her head hurt.

She drank the milk one slower, sitting on an oil drum. He walked round the workshop with his hands behind his back like it was a museum. He didn’t touch a thing.

Then she looked at the third cup.

“Have it,” he said, without turning round. “I don’t drink coffee. It makes my hands shake. I’d be no use to anyone.”

“Then why buy three?”

“I didn’t know how you took it.” He’d stopped in front of the lathe. “Now I know. You take all three.”

She drank the condensed milk one. Sweet and strong and thick. Her father used to drink it at five in the morning under the flyover. She hadn’t had one in three years. She wasn’t going to tell him that.

“This is a Weiler.”

“Yes.”

“It’s older than me.”

“It’s older than both of us.”

“It’s beautiful. Everything in here is.” He looked up at the bikes on their chains. “The light comes in at the door and goes right to the back. Somebody built it like that for the rope makers, so they could see the twist in the line. And you’ve put your bench exactly where the light’s best in the morning.”

“I put it there because that’s where the plug is.”

“Then the plug’s in the right place.”

He said it completely seriously. Then he sat on an upturned crate across from her and opened his sketchbook.

“I brought you something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the drawing.

He held it out across the gap between the crate and the oil drum. She wiped her hands on her overalls, twice, and took it.

Her bike, on its side, on the concrete. He’d had a minute, maybe. It was all there anyway. The wheel. The scrape on the exhaust. The carp. Every runner of the intake. Even the little lip on the third one, where she’d filed the mouth by hand because the casting was rough.

Her boots. Her hand.

J’s bike, as it really is. R. 2021.

“Is it wrong?” He leaned in. “I only had a minute. I did the intake from memory afterwards, so if I’ve got the—”

“It’s not wrong.”

“Oh.” He sat back. “Good.”

She didn’t give it back. She got up and went to the back wall, where a string hung between two nails with clothes pegs on it. Her own bad drawings hung off it, biro on the backs of invoices, parts she was working out. She took one down and pegged his up in its place.

When she turned round he had his chin on his hand. The big grin was gone. He looked like somebody had handed him a present.

“Have dinner with me.”

“No.”

She went back to Xiao Pan’s bike and lay down and pushed herself under it.

“That’s fine,” came his voice from above. “I’ll wait.”

“For what?”

“For you to say yes.”

“I’m not going to say yes.”

“Then I’ll wait a long time.” The crate creaked. “It’s all right. I’m brilliant at waiting. I’ve got nothing on today. I’ll draw your workshop. You won’t even know I’m here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She knew he was there.

She knew all morning. He hardly talked, which surprised her. He drew. Every so often the pencil stopped. She knew he was looking at her, and then it started again. Once he got up and walked round to see Xiao Pan’s bike from the other side and stood there for ages. She nearly told him to go away. She didn’t.

Then a cup of tea appeared by her elbow.

She hadn’t heard the kettle. He’d found it on the back shelf, found the tea, found the cups, and found the tin of biscuits she kept for customers. Two biscuits on the saucer.

“I didn’t say you could use the kettle.”

“No,” he agreed, and went back to his crate.

She drank the tea. It was exactly how she liked it. How? She hadn’t said a word about tea.

Around eleven the anchor woman put her head in at the door. She was seventy and built like a bollard. She looked at Raiden on his crate. She looked at Jinx under the bike.

“Still here, then.”

“Still here!” Raiden waved his pencil at her. “Thank you for the directions.”

“Hah. Didn’t think you’d last an hour.”

“Neither did I,” muttered Jinx, from under the bike.

The anchor woman went back to her anchors. Jinx heard her laughing in her shop for a good while after.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve Xiao Pan came for his bike.

He was young and thin. Burn scars on both hands, shiny and pink. A delivery bag from a flower shop on his shoulder. He came every month for a service she didn’t charge him for. In the winter he’d stood at her door and said Zhao Zhendong’s name, the way he’d been told to. She’d owed Zhao Zhendong a favour. So she’d built the boy a bike his hands could manage: a thumb throttle, light controls, a clutch that pulled like a feather.

He stopped dead in the doorway when he saw the man on the crate.

Raiden looked up from his sketchbook. “Oh! Hello.”

Xiao Pan looked at Jinx with huge eyes. Then he grabbed the red bike, wheeled it into the street without a word, and rode off faster than she’d ever seen him go.

Jinx watched him vanish round the corner.

“Do you know him?”

“No. Never seen him in my life.”

She looked at him. He looked back, pleasant and blank.

Lying. She could always hear it when an engine lied to her. A fine sound with something wrong under it. This was the same. But what was he lying about? She had no idea. Her headache had gone and it was Sunday. She let it go.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three he went out without saying anything and came back with two paper bags from Mrs. Tong’s on the corner.

Mrs. Tong’s served men off the container ships. As a rule, it did not serve men in grey trousers.

“Mrs. Tong says you have the beef. With extra greens. And you take the greens out and leave them on the side, and she doesn’t know why you order them.”

“She talks too much.”

“She does. I loved her.”

He put a carton down on the bench beside her on a clean rag. Lid off. Chopsticks split and laid across it. The little packet of chilli oil already torn open. Neat and quick, no fuss, like he’d done it a thousand times.

“She asked if I was your boyfriend.”

Jinx had the noodles halfway to her mouth. “What did you say?”

“I said not yet. She gave me extra beef.”

“You can’t say that.”

“Why not? It’s true. Not yet is completely true. I checked.”

“Give me the beef.”

“Say please.”

“Give me the BEEF.”

“That’s close enough.”

He gave her the beef. Then, without looking, he picked her greens out of her carton with his own chopsticks and ate them.

“Those are mine.”

“You don’t eat them.”

“They’re still mine.”

“Then I’m keeping them safe for you.” He chewed. “In me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By six she’d done two brake jobs and a carb rebuild. Then a collector rang who wanted his bike painted gold.

“No.”

The collector said something.

“Because it’s ugly.”

The collector said something longer.

“Then buy a gold one!” She hung up.

Across the workshop, Raiden made a noise into his sleeve.

“Are you laughing?”

“No! No. I’m coughing. It’s the dust.” He wasn’t coughing. “Do you talk to all your customers like that?”

“Only the stupid ones.”

“Is it most of them?”

“Yes.”

He’d filled half his sketchbook. He sat in the long low light from the door with his sleeves rolled up, drawing the bikes on their chains. Pencil all over his fingers. The big smile from the road was gone. He looked calm. Somebody doing the thing he was good at, in a place he liked.

He wasn’t going to leave, she thought. And she didn’t want him to, which was much worse.

“Why are you still here?”

He looked up.

“I’m waiting for you to say yes. And you’re really interesting to watch. You talk to nobody, you never stop moving, and everything you do, you do properly.”

He turned the sketchbook round.

It was her, from behind. Bent over the carb, shoulders up, the light on the back of her neck. Not her face.

“I’ve been trying all day. I can’t get you. It’s driving me mad.”

“You don’t know anything about me.”

“Don’t I? Let’s see.” He counted on his fingers. “You nearly died last night so you wouldn’t kill a stranger. You held that bike at a hundred and ninety. Then you got off and checked your intake before you checked your own hands.”

“That’s not—”

“You build bikes for boys with burnt hands and don’t charge them. You won’t paint a bike gold because it’s ugly. And you take your coffee all three ways.” He shut the sketchbook. “I want to know the rest. I’ll go when you tell me to. Then I’ll come back tomorrow and ask again.”

“Every day?”

“Every day. So you might as well say yes now and save us both the bus fare.”

Outside, a container ship sounded its horn in the basin. Next door the rope man pulled his shutter down with a crash.

“Thursday.”

He went completely still on his crate.

“Really?”

“I’m busy till Thursday.”

“Thursday’s perfect. Thursday’s the best day of the week. Thursday’s—” He stopped himself. He stood up. He collected the empty coffee cups off the floor and put them in the bin by the door. Then he stood in the doorway in the evening light like there was something else he wanted to say, and he’d decided not to.

“I’ll pick you up at seven. There’s a thing I have to go to. A party. It’ll be terrible. You can watch me be an idiot in public. Then I’ll take you somewhere good to eat, and you can tell me what was wrong with everybody there.”

“I don’t go to parties.”

“You don’t have to talk to anyone. You can stand behind me and frighten them.”

That was so exactly what she’d have done that she nearly laughed.

“Give me your number,” he said.

“No.”

“Then have mine.”

He took the pen from behind her ear, where she hadn’t known she’d stuck it, and took her left hand by the wrist. Gently. Before she could pull away he’d written eight digits across the back of it in neat capitals, above the carp’s tail.

“Wash it off if you want.” He put the pen back behind her ear. “Seven, Thursday.”

“Seven.”

He gave her the big grin. The one from the road.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard him walk away up the street. She heard him stop at Mrs. Tong’s. She heard Mrs. Tong say something, and then she heard him laugh, loud and happy, the whole length of the street.

Jinx stood in the middle of her workshop with grease to her elbows and looked at the back of her hand.

She didn’t wash it off. She’d wash it off after she copied it. Obviously.

At eleven that night, sitting on her mattress, she typed it in.

Jinx: this is jinx

The reply took nine seconds.

Raiden: I know. Nobody else has this number who’d text me at eleven at night with no capital letters.

Jinx: dont be late thursday

Raiden: I’m never late. I’m early for everything. I was early for you.

Raiden: That’s not true, I was on the road first. You were early for me.

Raiden: Goodnight, Jinx.

She put the phone face down on the floor.

Then she picked it up again and saved him as IDIOT, in capitals, and lay there in the dark.

From the corner, through her open window, came Mrs. Tong’s voice, shouting at somebody in the kitchen.

“THURSDAY! She said THURSDAY!”

Jinx put the pillow over her head.

chapters.title: The Socialite Everyone Ignores
chapters.desc: Their first date is a gallery opening forty-one floors up, where he plays the fool so well the whole room believes him. On the back stairs he tells her his surname, and she goes home to choose a spanner.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody shoots the boy who can’t find his own coat.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
On Thursday afternoon a courier came to the black door holding a box at arm’s length, like it might go off.

“Sign here, miss.”

“What is it?”

“Don’t know, miss. Heavy, though. Sign here.”

Jinx signed with a greasy thumb. She stared at the box while she finished a wheel bearing. Then she washed her hands, twice, and opened it.

Black tissue paper. Inside it, a leather jacket.

It was nothing like hers. Hers was fifteen years old and had belonged to a man at her father’s shop who’d died. Cigarette burn on the left cuff. A zip that only went up if you held your breath. This one was soft and heavy, high collar, silver zips. She held it up against herself in the lathe guard. It fitted across the shoulders.

Nothing fitted across her shoulders. She bought men’s jackets, and then the sleeves hung over her hands. These stopped at her wrists. Who had he asked? Under the jacket were black boots in her size and a card in small neat capitals.

You don’t have to wear these. I just wanted you to have something that fits. You’ll look better than everyone there in your own anyway. R.

Nobody had ever bought her anything to wear. She stood there holding it until her arms ached. Then she put on her own jacket, the old one with the burn, and the new boots.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at seven in a taxi. She was waiting on the step. He got out and stopped on the pavement and looked at her, boots first, all the way up, slowly. Dark grey suit. A silver waistcoat with a pattern like the inside of a watch.

“You wore the boots.”

“They fit.”

“I know. I asked the anchor lady your size.”

“She doesn’t know my size.”

“She guessed. She’s very good. She says you’ve got shoulders like her husband had, and he worked the cranes for thirty years.”

“Not the jacket, though.”

“No. Not the jacket.” He didn’t seem upset. “Your jacket’s better. Mine doesn’t have a burn on it.”

“It’s not a burn. It’s history.”

“It’s a burn, Jinx.”

“It’s HISTORY!”

He opened the taxi door for her. “You look wonderful. You look like you might hit someone.”

“I might.”

“Please do. There’s a man there called Deputy Director Hsu. Start with him.”

He waited on the kerb until her door was shut. Then he walked round and got in on the traffic side.

✦ ✦ ✦

The gallery was forty-one floors up in a new tower in the Coastal High-Rise. It smelled of money and lilies. White walls, white floor, big red paintings. Waiters with trays. Women in dresses worth more than her bike, men in suits who all seemed to be the same man. A string quartet nobody was listening to. And one long window with the whole city underneath it in lights.

Every head turned when she walked in. Every head turned away.

A woman in pearls drifted up to her. “Are you with the caterers, dear?”

“No.”

“The band?”

“No.”

“Oh.” The woman looked at her tattoos. “How lovely,” she said, and drifted off again.

Raiden had taken a glass of champagne off a tray. He didn’t drink it.

“Watch.”

Then he went into the room.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d been watching men all her life. At the chop shop you learned it before you learned to read. Who was in charge. Who was frightened. Who was carrying. Who’d hit you, and who’d only shout. Give her five minutes in a corner and she’d tell you which man in the room was dangerous.

In five minutes, every person in that gallery had decided Raiden was the least dangerous man they’d ever met. He was wonderful at it. He was awful.

“Auntie! That painting is about your divorce. Clearly. Look at the red.”

“I’m not divorced.”

“Not YET!”

“Raiden, really…”

“Uncle! Uncle. Have you seen the columns in the lobby? They’re fighting the river. You can feel it in your knees. Can’t you feel it? I can feel it.”

“My knees are fine, young man.”

“For now.”

He got the owner’s name wrong twice. He laughed at things that weren’t jokes. He knocked a canapé off a tray and apologised to the waiter until the waiter was laughing too. Everyone smiled at him like you’d smile at a nice dog. Then they turned back to each other and forgot him.

Except once.

A man in a grey suit by the window had watched her come in. He leaned over to the woman beside him. Whatever he said, she laughed at it, and looked at Jinx’s jacket. Jinx had heard men say worse. She didn’t turn her head.

Ten minutes later Raiden drifted past the window with his full glass. He stopped by the grey suit and murmured something in his ear, smiling, like he was telling a friend his flies were undone.

The man’s face went the colour of putty. He put his glass on the sill, found his coat, and left without saying goodbye to anyone. The woman hurried after him. Raiden was already telling an old lady her earrings were wonderful.

The back of Jinx’s neck went cold.

He wasn’t drinking. Forty minutes, and the glass was full to the same line. Every time he moved, he touched something. A wall. A column. A door frame. Just his fingertips in passing, the way she ran her thumb over a weld. When somebody new came in, he knew, without looking round. He just shifted a little so he could see them.

When he’d done the whole room he came back and leaned on the wall beside her.

“Three ways out.”

“What?”

“The door we came in. The service corridor behind the bar, to the kitchen and the goods lift. And the fire stairs past the toilets, which the caterers have propped open so they can smoke.” He looked at the long window. “That glass isn’t holding anything up, by the way. The whole floor sits on six columns and the core. Two of the columns are wrong.”

“Wrong how?”

“Not feng shui wrong. Actually wrong. Somebody saved money on them in 2018.”

“Is it going to fall down?”

“Not tonight.” He finally sipped his champagne. “It’ll stand for a hundred years. Probably. Shall we eat?”

He still had the silly smile on. His eyes weren’t silly at all.

“What did you say to the man by the window?”

“I gave him the floor number of his other flat. And the name of who pays the rent on it.” He watched a waiter go by. “His wife was standing right there. So he left before I could say it louder.”

“Why?”

“He laughed at your jacket.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her out through the service corridor. Past the bar. Past two waiters smoking by the goods lift, who straightened up, saw it was him, and slouched again. Through a steel door onto the back stairs. Bare concrete, cigarettes and bleach, a little window on every landing looking out at the dark side of the city.

He sat on a step and pulled his tie off.

“Sorry. That’s always the worst part. The first hour.”

“Why the first hour?”

“After that they’ve made up their minds about you. Then you can do what you like.” He stuffed the tie in his pocket. “Mrs. Tong’s is still open.”

“Fine.”

“Or there’s a place on the eleventh floor that does the best duck in the city.”

“Fine.”

“There’ll be a man in the lift who wants to talk to me about columns.”

“Then Mrs. Tong’s.”

“She’ll want to know how the date went.”

“It’s not a date.”

“I bought you boots, Jinx.”

“You bought me boots. That’s not a date. That’s a delivery.”

Jinx didn’t sit. She stood two steps below him so their faces were level and folded her arms.

He looked at her for a moment. Then he reached out and caught the zip of her old jacket between two fingers. The one that only went up if you held your breath. He tugged. She came up a step. Her knees bumped his. His face was right there in the ugly light.

“I’ve wanted to do this since the third coffee.”

He leaned in. She didn’t move. His mouth was a breath from hers and her heart was going hard enough to hurt. Then he stopped.

“No. Not yet.” He let go of the zip. “There’s something you need to hear first. You’d hate me if I did this before you heard it.”

She stepped back down. Her face was hot.

“You’re not stupid.”

The smile didn’t move. It just stopped being a smile.

“No. I’m not.”

“So why do you do it?”

He looked down at his hands on his knees.

“My name’s Raiden Lin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d seen a Lin once.

When she was nine a black car came down the lane under the flyover and stopped outside her father’s shop. Every man in the shop stood up. Her father first. A big quiet man in a dark coat went into the office. Ten minutes later he came out and the car drove away. Afterwards her father sat at his desk with his hands flat on it for an hour.

Who was that, Ba?

Lin. From the Walled City. Don’t ever go there.

She never had.

“Lin Jian.”

“He’s my father.”

She took a step back. Her boot heel hit the edge of the stair below.

“I’m the son. The only one. Four girls and me.”

“So?”

“So lots of people would like to have Lin Jian’s only son. To use. To hurt him with. Or just to have.” He turned his hands over. “I worked that out when I was ten.”

“And?”

“And I decided to be the son nobody would want. Pretty. Loud. Silly. Useless. The one who draws. The one who can’t find his own coat.” He shrugged. “Nobody worries about a boy like that. And nobody shoots the boy nobody’s worried about.”

“What do you really do?”

“I draw. That part’s true. Buildings, for a firm in the south.” He paused. “And sometimes for my family. Walls that look like walls. Floors that look like floors.”

“Meaning?”

“I make places safe. I’m good at it. And nobody knows, because nobody looks at me.”

His fingertips on the gallery walls. Xiao Pan’s face in her doorway, and the lie under the nice sound. Xiao Pan delivered for a flower shop in the old town, and everyone in the Docks knew whose wife owned that shop.

“Your sister’s married to Zhao Zhendong.”

“Elowen. Yes.”

“You knew who Xiao Pan was.”

“Yes.”

“You knew Zhao sent him to me.”

“Yes.”

“Did Zhao send YOU?”

He looked genuinely shocked. Then he laughed, short and surprised, the first real one since the stairs.

“No! God, no. Zhao only notices me when I’m standing on his foot. I didn’t know who you were till the boy walked in. I just saw your intake.” The laugh went. “I’m sorry I didn’t tell you on Sunday. I should have. I wanted one day where you didn’t know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood on the stair and didn’t say anything.

Her father’s hands flat on the desk. The men standing up. Twelve, fourteen, seventeen, in a chop shop that broke stolen bikes for the Syndicate’s buyers. Twenty-two and out, with a van and a lathe. And the promise she’d made in the van, driving away. Nobody owns you again. Not the buyers. Not the crews. Not the families in the Walled City who sat on top of the whole heap.

And here was the top of the heap, on a concrete stair, with his tie in his pocket.

“I’m going home.”

He stood up but didn’t come after her. He let her go down past him, then followed a flight behind, all the way, not saying a word. They came out of a fire door into a lane full of bins. She walked to the main road. A taxi stopped. She opened the door.

“Jinx.”

She looked back. He was standing under a security light in his silver waistcoat with his hands in his pockets.

“I liked you before you got off the bike.”

“Don’t.”

“You stopped two metres from me and you held it. I looked round. That was it. Before the intake, even.” He took a breath. “I’m coming to the garage tomorrow. Ten o’clock. With coffee.”

“Don’t!”

“If you want me gone, throw a spanner at me. I’ll go.”

“I will.”

“Then I won’t come back. I won’t send anyone. You’ll never hear the name Lin from me again. That’s a promise.” He smiled, a bit crooked. “I keep those.”

“Are you getting in or not?” the driver demanded.

She got in. She didn’t look back. But the taxi stopped at the lights, and in the wing mirror she could see him still standing in the lane under the light.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t sleep. She lay on her mattress with the window open and the Docks coming in. Cranes. Trucks. A horn. The black car. Three coffees.

Spanners.

In the black hours before morning she went downstairs in her vest and shorts and put the workshop lights on. Her spanners hung on the tool wall in order of size. Tiny carb ones at one end. At the other, a big one as long as her forearm.

What was she doing? No idea. She stood there anyway, barefoot on the cold concrete, until her toes hurt.

She took down the thirteen. The one she used most, worn smooth at the grip from her own hand. She weighed it in her palm. She put it on the bench by the door, where she’d be able to reach it at ten.

Then she went back to bed and slept like a dropped stone.

chapters.title: The First Kiss Smells Like Oil
chapters.desc: She throws the spanner and misses on purpose. Under her bike, on two creepers, he makes a rule about her real name and begs his way right up to the edge of it.
chapters.epigraph: “I said I’d go if you threw a spanner. I didn’t say what happens if you miss.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
She woke at nine to three texts.

IDIOT: Coffee in an hour.

IDIOT: Get your spanner ready.

IDIOT: That was a joke. Please don’t actually. Unless you want to. Then aim for the left arm, I need the right one for drawing.

She didn’t answer. She looked at the thirteen on the bench by the door for a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at ten.

She heard the taxi stop at the top of the street, because taxis never came down it. Then the clean brown shoes on the cobbles. She was standing at the bench with her back to the door when he stopped in the doorway with three coffees.

She picked up the thirteen and threw it.

She’d been throwing spanners since she was seven. This one went hard and flat, spinning, a metre left of his head. It hit the brick with a crack like a gunshot. It dropped. It skidded under a bike.

He didn’t flinch. He looked at the wall. At the spanner. At her.

“You missed.”

“I never miss.”

“No.” He said it slowly. “No, I don’t suppose you do.”

Then he smiled, and it was a new one. It started in his eyes and took its time getting to his mouth, and when it got there it stayed. He walked in and set the coffees on the bench beside her.

“Good morning!”

Like nothing had happened. Like she hadn’t just thrown a spanner at his head.

She drank the black one. Her hands were shaking. She didn’t let him see.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t sit on the crate today. He walked round the bikes and asked her things. Real things.

“What does the lathe turn?”

“Anything under a metre.”

“Why carbs on the old bikes and injection on the new ones?”

“Carbs are simpler.”

“Simpler how?”

“Fuel goes in. Air goes past. Air pulls fuel through a jet.” She didn’t look up from the gearbox she was stripping. “Change the jet, change the mixture. You can hear it. You can fix it on the side of a road with a screwdriver.”

“And injection?”

“A computer guessing. It guesses well.” She shrugged. “Still guessing.”

“And your bike? The black one?”

“Carbs. Four. I tuned them on a dyno at a shop up north. Took two days.”

“What’s a dyno?”

She looked up at him.

He waited. Pencil ready. Was he serious? He was serious.

“Rolling road. You strap the bike down with the back wheel on a drum. You run it. The drum measures power at the wheel. A sensor in the exhaust tells you if it’s rich or lean.” She went back to the gearbox. “Then you change the jets and run it again. And again. Till the line on the screen’s smooth all the way up.”

“And was it?”

“After two days.”

“Then you rode it in a race, and a man knelt in the road, and nothing came loose.” He shook his head. “I’d love to see that. The line on the screen.”

“There isn’t one here. They cost a fortune.”

He wrote something in the sketchbook. She leaned over to look.

DYNO. Fortune. Find out how big a fortune.

“That’s none of your business.”

“I know! It’s just a note.”

“How did you get the tank so smooth?”

“Hammer.”

“Just a hammer?”

“A hammer, a sandbag, and a week.” She held up her left hand. There was a dent in the side of her thumb that had never quite gone. “And this.”

He took her hand and looked at the dent. He didn’t let go straight away. He turned her hand to the light from the door like it was something he might want to draw later.

“Does it hurt?”

“No.”

“Did it?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” he said, and gave her hand back. “I mean, not good. I mean I’m glad it’s a real story. I’d hate it to be a sandbag accident.”

“It was a sandbag accident.”

“Oh.”

After an hour she realised she’d said more to him than to anyone else in a month.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twelve she lay on the creeper and pushed herself under the black bike. The scraped exhaust had been bothering her all week. Was the bracket bent? She wanted to see.

It was dark under there. Just the work light hooked on the frame, the smell of oil and hot metal, and cool concrete under her shoulders. She liked it. It was the only place in the world nobody could stand over her.

She heard him move.

Then she heard the second creeper. She kept it by the bench for jobs that needed both sides at once. Its little wheels rattled across the floor. A pause. A lot of creaking. One swear word she pretended not to hear.

Raiden lay down on it and pushed himself under the bike beside her.

His shoulder was against hers. His head was right by hers, under the sump.

“I’ve never been under a bike before.”

“Get out.”

“It’s lovely. It’s like a little house.” He looked up at the underside of the engine, orange in the work light. “Oh, look. You can see everything. What’s that?”

“The oil filter.”

“It’s beautiful. Don’t laugh. It is.”

She wasn’t laughing. She went back to the bracket. He lay there and watched her hands.

It was quiet. The street outside slept in the noon heat. A fly went round the work light. She could hear him breathing and feel his shoulder, warm through his shirt. She undid one bolt and did it up again. Why? No idea.

“Can I tell you something?”

“No.”

“I’ve made a rule.”

She stopped with the spanner on the bolt.

“I made it last night. In the lane, after your taxi.” His voice was low in the dark little space. “I thought, if she misses with the spanner, I’ll want to kiss her. So much I won’t be able to think straight. And I’m not going to.”

“Good.”

“Not until you tell me your name.”

“You know my name.”

“I know what they call you. Jinx is a thing men called you. I want the one you were given.” He turned his head on the creeper. “And I’m not kissing you till you tell me what it is.”

“That’s a stupid rule.”

“It’s a terrible rule. I’ve been regretting it since about five past ten.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did the bolt up. She undid it again.

“I could ask nicely. Look, I’m asking. Jinx. What’s your name?”

“No.”

“I could beg. I’m a good beggar. I’m a Lin, we’re brought up to it.” He sounded serious. “Please. I’m begging. I’m lying on a concrete floor under a motorbike, begging. Nobody’s ever made me do that.”

She pressed her mouth flat.

“I could guess. Mei? Lan? Xiu? Fen? Ah Lam?” He waited. “Little Cabbage?”

“No.”

“Was it Little Cabbage?”

“NO!”

“Then it’s something better.”

His hand moved. She saw it at the edge of the light, pencil on the side of his finger, coming across the gap between the creepers. It stopped just above hers, where hers lay on the concrete by her hip. Not touching. She could feel the warmth of it.

“Can I?”

She didn’t answer. He waited.

“Please.”

She didn’t know how he’d got that close. She turned her hand over on the concrete, palm up, under his. He put his hand down on it.

That was all. His hand on hers, on the cold floor. His thumb went once across her palm, over the calluses and the old burn. She felt it all the way up her arm. Ridiculous. It was a hand. She’d had men’s hands on her before, and none of them had felt like this. Like a key going into a lock that had rusted shut.

“That’s not fair.”

“No. I’m a very unfair man. I’ve got loads of rules and I cheat at all of them except the important ones.” His thumb went across her palm again. “Tell me your name, Jinx.”

She turned her head.

He was right there in the orange light. Grease on his cheek where he’d touched the frame. Eyes dark. Not one bit of silly in his face anywhere.

“Cao Jia.”

He shut his eyes, like it had hurt. Then he opened them.

“Jia.” Properly, this time. A word he’d been practising in another language and had finally got right.

“Well?”

“Can I kiss you now?”

“You made the rule. Not me.”

“Is that a yes?”

“It’s—”

He kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was awkward. It was under a bike. Her elbow hit the sump and his head hit the frame.

“Ow!”

He said it against her mouth. She laughed. Out loud, actually laughed. He laughed too and kissed her through it. Then nobody was laughing.

His hand left hers and went to her jaw. The back of her neck. He kissed her slowly, the way he drew, like he wanted every line right. Then not slowly at all. She grabbed his shirt in both fists and dragged him across the gap between the creepers. One of them rolled. They both slid. She ended up half on top of him, one knee on the concrete. Her hair fell in his face. His hands went into it.

“Your bike. We’re going to knock your bike over.”

“It’s on the stand.”

“I’ll buy you a new mirror.”

“I don’t want a new mirror.”

“What do you want?”

She stopped. Her mouth on his. Her hands in his shirt. Her heart banging on his chest.

“You talk too much.”

“I always talk. It’s the worst thing about me. You’ll have to stop me.”

So she did.

✦ ✦ ✦

They came out from under the bike because a creeper wheel had run over his sleeve and pinned him. He couldn’t get up. She had to roll him out by the shoulders.

He lay on his back on the concrete in the light from the door. Oil on his face. Shirt half undone. Hair everywhere. Laughing.

She sat beside him with her back against the bench and her heart still going. She wiped her mouth with the back of her hand. It came away black.

“You’ve got oil on your face.”

“So have you. All over. I did that.” He sat up and looked at her, very pleased with himself. “Hold still.”

He put his thumb on the corner of her mouth and wiped. Then, without thinking, he licked his thumb.

His face crumpled.

“Oh, that’s horrible. That’s engine oil.”

“Yes.”

“Why does anyone kiss mechanics?”

“Nobody asked you to.”

“No. No, I’d do it again.” He wiped his tongue on his sleeve. “I’m going to do it again. Give me a minute.”

She snorted. She couldn’t help it.

He stopped laughing then. He looked at her across the concrete.

“Cao Jia. Thank you for telling me.”

She didn’t say anything. She’d never told anyone. The men at the shop stopped using it when she was twelve and started calling her Jinx. Every bike she touched got away clean, so she was bad luck for the police. Her father called her girl. Collectors called her Miss Jinx, or nothing. She’d almost forgotten she had another name, till he lay on a cold floor under a bike and begged for it.

“Don’t tell anyone.”

“I won’t. I’ll only use it when it’s important.” He tipped his head. “Can I still call you Jinx the rest of the time? It suits you. It’s a good name for a woman who throws spanners.”

“I missed.”

“You missed on purpose. I’m going to remember that for the rest of my life.”

He reached under the bike and picked up the thirteen from where it had skidded. He turned it over in his hands. He looked at the worn place on the grip, where her hand had been for years.

Then he got up and hung it back on the tool wall. Between the twelve and the fourteen. Exactly where it lived.

“How did you know where it goes?”

“I looked. On Sunday.” He wiped his hands on his very expensive trousers. “I look at everything, Jia.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At three they went to Mrs. Tong’s, because she was starving and he’d forgotten lunch existed. They hadn’t washed. Not even their faces.

Mrs. Tong looked up from her ladle. She looked at Jinx’s mouth. She looked at Raiden’s mouth. Both black. She put the ladle down.

“Hah!”

“Afternoon, Mrs. Tong!”

“Grey trousers.” She pointed the ladle at him. “Sunday you said not yet.”

“I did.”

“And now?”

Raiden beamed at her with oil all over his chin. “Now it’s yet.”

“Don’t,” Jinx growled.

Mrs. Tong turned to the kitchen hatch and shouted something in her coast dialect. The cook shouted something back. Two big men off the container ships at the counter put their bowls down and started clapping, slowly, very seriously.

“Stop it.”

They didn’t stop. Raiden bowed to them. Then he pulled out her chair at the table by the fridge, the one with its back to the wall. He sat down across from her looking like he’d won a prize.

Mrs. Tong brought two bowls of beef. Hers had the greens on the side, the way she liked. His had a mountain of beef on top, nearly falling off.

“Why does he get more?”

“Because he’s thin. And because you’re smiling, and in three years I’ve never seen it.”

“I’m not smiling.”

“Eat, then. Before it goes cold.”

She ate. Across the table he was trying very hard not to look delighted, and failing completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

At six he stood on her step, still oily, with his jacket over his shoulder.

She heard herself say it before she could stop.

“Tomorrow. Ten.”

“With coffee?”

“Four.”

He stared at her. “Four? Who’s the fourth one for?”

“Me.”

chapters.title: Raiden Gets Hit by a Car
chapters.desc: June 2021. She’s forty minutes late to pick him up, and a van finds him first. She sits up all night at City Hospital, and at dawn he begs her to leave by the back before his family arrives. She goes.
chapters.epigraph: “I was on the pavement. I promise. I was on the pavement.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
For two weeks he came every day. Ten o’clock. Four coffees. She drank all four. He sat on the crate and drew. At one he went out and came back with Mrs. Tong’s beef, greens on the side. In the evenings he took her to places she’d never been, where the waiters knew him. He ordered for both of them without looking at the menu and was always right. It was infuriating.

And every night on the step of the black door, he kissed her goodnight. Hands on her face. Cranes lit up over the roofs. Every night she nearly asked him in. Every night he stepped back first.

“Tomorrow.”

Then he’d walk off up the street, and she’d stand in the doorway listening to him go, thinking idiot. She didn’t know which of them she meant.

On the second Thursday she said it.

“Why do you always leave?”

“What?”

“You always leave.”

He was already on the bottom step. He turned round.

“Because if I come up those stairs, I’m not leaving till you throw me out.”

“So?”

“So I want you to be sure you won’t.” He looked at her in the light from the door. “I’m not in a hurry, Jia. I want all of it. I want it to take years.”

He stepped back. She caught him by the collar before he reached the pavement. She dragged him back up the step and kissed him first, hard, against the door frame. Would the rule hold? She wanted to see.

For a second it didn’t. His hands went into her hair. His whole weight came against her. He made a noise in his throat like a man losing an argument with himself. Then he took his mouth away. An inch.

“Tomorrow.”

“That didn’t count.” She let go of his collar.

“It counted a bit.”

“It didn’t count AT ALL.”

He went up the street laughing. She shut the door and leaned on it with her eyes closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday he wanted to draw the cranes. The big ones at the end of the Docks road. They worked all night under floodlights, stacking containers like blocks.

“Most beautiful machines in the city,” he announced. “And nobody ever looks at them.”

“I’ll pick you up. Eleven. On the bike.”

“Lovely.”

“Don’t stand in the road.”

“I never stand in the road!”

“You knelt in the road.”

“That’s different. That was for art.” He kissed her in the doorway at four in the afternoon with a customer watching. “Eleven. I’ll be on the pavement like a good boy. You can check.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was late. A man turned up with a big touring bike he’d dropped on the expressway. Fairing smashed. Clutch lever gone. He’d ridden it across the city in first gear because nobody else would open that late, and he was shaking.

“I’ve got a job at six. My wife’s going to kill me.”

“Sit down.”

“Can you—”

“Sit DOWN.”

He sat. She did the lever, taped the fairing, and checked the forks. It took forty minutes. She didn’t think about the time until she was wiping her hands and looked up at the clock over the door.

“Oh no.”

“What? What’s wrong with it?”

“Not your bike. Go home.”

She rang him. It rang and rang. She rang again from the bike at the top of the street, helmet off. It rang and rang.

Jinx: coming. stay on the pavement

No answer. She put her helmet on and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was an ambulance on the Docks road. She saw the lights a kilometre off, blue, going round and round against a stack of containers. Her body knew before she did. Her hands went cold on the bars.

A white delivery van sat across the road at an angle with its wing caved in. The driver was on the kerb with a policeman, holding his head.

“I didn’t see him! I didn’t see him, he was just there—”

“Sit still, sir.”

Glass everywhere, glittering blue. On the pavement by the railings, a stretcher. Two paramedics. A white shirt. And a sketchbook in the road.

A paramedic with short grey hair put an arm out. “Miss. Miss, stay back—”

“Move.”

“Do you know him?”

“MOVE.”

His face. Blood all down one side from a cut over his eye. The eye already swelling shut. Left arm in a splint across his chest. Shirt cut open. Skin white under the floodlights.

His other eye was open.

“Oh. You came.”

“I was late.”

“You came.” His voice was thick and slow. “I was on the pavement. I promise. I was on the pavement. He came round the corner too fast. He was on his phone. He didn’t see me. It wasn’t…”

He stopped. Breathed in. Something hurt him badly. She watched it cross his face.

“It wasn’t you, Jia. It wasn’t you.”

She took his good hand. It was cold.

“Don’t talk.”

“I always talk,” he mumbled, and shut his eye.

✦ ✦ ✦

They took him to City Hospital. She followed the ambulance through every red light and left the bike on the pavement outside the emergency doors with the key in it. She went in after the stretcher with her helmet still on.

“Miss, you can’t—”

“I can.”

“Please sit down.”

She stood outside the room where they cut off the rest of his shirt and put a line in his arm. Outside X-ray. Outside the CT scanner, by a window with the blind half down, while a machine looked inside his head.

A doctor came out with a clipboard. “Family?”

“I’m his.”

The doctor looked at the helmet. The grease. Her face.

“His what?”

“His.”

The doctor looked a moment longer. Then she sighed and told her.

“Three ribs cracked on the left. That’s where the wing caught him. Broken left wrist, the end of the big bone. We’ve set it. Plaster in the morning, when the swelling’s down.”

“And his head?”

“Seven stitches over the eyebrow. A concussion. The scan’s clear. No bleeding.” The doctor tapped the clipboard. “Half a step further out, and this is a different conversation.”

“Is he staying?”

“Two nights, for the head. Tonight somebody has to wake him every couple of hours. Check he knows his name.”

“I’ll do it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They put him in a room of his own on the sixth floor. He was a Lin, and somebody had looked at his wallet. She sat on a plastic chair by the bed in her helmet until a nurse made her take it off. He was asleep, or nearly. Arm strapped up. Face swollen. Black stitches over his eye. A machine beside him drew a green line that went up and down.

She watched the line. Was it supposed to do that? It kept doing it. She decided that was good. In the middle of the night she woke him the way the nurse had shown her.

“Raiden.”

His good eye opened.

“What’s your name?”

“Raiden Lin. I’m twenty-three. It’s Friday.” He frowned. “No. Saturday. You’re Cao Jia, and you’re beautiful, and you came.” The eye drifted shut. “Is that enough?”

“That’s enough.”

“Hold my hand. Please. I won’t tell anyone.”

She held it. The nurse came in and wrote on the chart at the foot of the bed. Jinx held out her hand.

“Give me that.”

“I’m sorry?”

“The pen. I’ll do the next one.”

“Visitors don’t write on the chart.”

“I’m not a visitor.”

The nurse looked at her. Then she shrugged and handed the pen over. Jinx wrote on the line beside the tidy writing. Big blocky biro, like a workshop manual. woke him, knew name and day.

Two hours later she did it again.

“What’s your name?”

“Raiden Lin. Still. Saturday.” His eye opened a crack. “I dropped my sketchbook.”

“I’ve got it.”

She’d picked it up off the road. It was in her jacket. The cover was wet. A tyre had gone across the back. On the last page there was the crane, half drawn. The long arm reaching out over a ship. The floodlights. The line of the cable going down and stopping halfway, where he’d been when the van came.

“Is it ruined?”

“No.”

“Good.” He slept.

She wrote it on the chart. woke him, knew name and day.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry. The room got warm, so she took off her jacket and hung it on the back of the chair. She put the sketchbook on the seat beside her. She’d stopped crying at the shop when she was eight. There was no point. Crying didn’t fix anything. You found what was broken and you fixed it, or you couldn’t. Either way, you didn’t stand there with your face wet.

So she sat in the plastic chair and held his hand. The window over the Symmetrical Ward went from black to grey to dirty pink.

He was on the pavement. I was forty minutes late.

The cable on the page, going down and stopping. Something in her chest did up tight and stayed tight. A bolt turned past where it was meant to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

When the window went pink, his phone rang. It was in a plastic bag on the cupboard with his wallet and his keys and his watch, all of them bloody. It rang and rang. Elowen. It stopped. It started again. Baba.

He woke up. Properly this time. His good eye went to the ceiling. Then to the phone. Then to her. The bit of his face that wasn’t swollen went white.

“The hospital rang them. They saw the name.” He tried to sit up. The ribs stopped him. He lay back, breathing badly. “Jia. They’re coming. My father’s people. My sisters. They’ll be here any minute.”

“Good. Somebody should be.”

“No.” He had her hand hard now with his good one. Harder than she’d have thought he could. “No. Listen. Listen to me. They can’t see you.”

She went cold.

“You have to go. Now. Before they come. There’s a door by the linen room, end of the corridor. Stairs down to the service entrance. Take your bike and go home, and I’ll ring you tonight. I promise. But you have to go before they see you.”

She looked at his hand on hers. At his white swollen face and the black stitches. She thought: he’s ashamed of me. It was so clear it was like hearing it out loud. A girl from a chop shop under the flyover. A dead man’s jacket. Grease under her nails. Sitting by the bed of Lin Jian’s only son. Of course they couldn’t see her. Of course he’d want her out the back, by the linen room, with the rubbish.

She took her hand away.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Jia.”

She stood up. She picked her helmet off the floor. The jacket stayed on the chair. Her head was empty.

“Jia, please. It isn’t… you don’t understand. It’s not—”

“I understand.”

She did. She always had. That was the trouble. For two weeks she’d let herself not understand, because of coffee and a drawing and the way he looked at her intake. Because of tomorrow on her step. She’d let herself forget who he was and who she was. Now it was morning, and his family was coming, and she remembered.

“Your sketchbook’s on the chair.”

“Jia—”

She went out. Past the nurses’ station. Past the linen room. She pushed the door at the end and took the stairs two at a time, helmet in one hand. On the turn a tall man in scrubs stepped back against the rail to let her by. She didn’t look at him.

Above her, faint, Raiden was shouting her name.

“JIA! Jia, wait—”

“Mr. Lin! Lie still!”

Then nothing. Just her boots on the concrete, all the way down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden lay and stared at the door. It opened once. His heart went. It wasn’t her. It was a tall doctor in glasses with a face like an unpaid bill.

“Surgical. About your ribs. Can I look?”

“I’m fine.” He used the silly voice. It came out thin. “Totally fine. Look all you like. I’m a picture.”

The doctor pressed under his ribs on the left. Raiden made a face and turned it into a joke. The doctor didn’t laugh. He read the chart. He stopped at the blocky biro and read it twice. Then he looked at the plastic chair, pulled right up to the bed, with a tyre-marked sketchbook on the seat. He didn’t touch it.

“You’re fine. Your spleen’s fine. It’s not a surgical problem. They’ll keep you two nights for your head.”

“Told you.”

He shut his eye. He opened it again when the corridor filled up.

Feet. A lot of them. His father’s low voice. He knew who’d come before they came round the corner. Baba, enormous and grey, with two men who stopped at the end of the corridor and stayed there. Evangeline in pale blue, silent, looking at everything. Eliana with her laptop. Elara, talking at top speed about spleens to a nurse who hadn’t asked.

Elara’s voice came first. “…and the spleen sits right under the left ribs, so if nobody’s checked—”

“Somebody’s checked, Elara,” his father rumbled.

“How do you KNOW?”

Elowen got to the door first. Green dress. Her husband a step behind her.

“RAIDEN.”

“Hello, Elowen. I’m fine. It’s nothing. I was drawing a crane.”

She sat on the edge of the bed and took his face in both hands, very gently, and didn’t say anything at all. Her thumbs were shaking. He let her hold on.

Zhao Zhendong didn’t come in. He stood in the doorway in his black coat with his hands in his pockets and looked at the room. The machine. The bloody bag on the cupboard. The sketchbook with the tyre mark across its back.

The plastic chair. Over the back of it hung an old black leather jacket. Far too big across the shoulders for most women. A cigarette burn on the left cuff. Grease ground into the collar.

Zhao looked at it for four seconds. Then at Raiden. Over his sister’s shoulder, with his one good eye, Raiden gave the smallest shake of his head.

“Hm.”

Zhao lifted the jacket off the chair. He folded it once over his arm. He walked out with it before Elowen could turn round and see.

chapters.title: A Bike That Goes Twenty Kilometres an Hour
chapters.desc: She ignores him for three weeks, and Zhao Zhendong turns up at her door with her jacket. Then she builds a pale green bike that can’t go faster than twenty, rides it into his tower, and finds out what he was really afraid of.
chapters.epigraph: “If you’re going to draw in roads, you do it on this.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
He rang that night. She didn’t answer.

He rang the next morning. And the next night. She turned the phone face down on the bench and let it buzz itself across the wood until it fell off the edge.

IDIOT: Jia, please.

IDIOT: Please pick up.

IDIOT: I know what you think. It isn’t that.

IDIOT: I’m not allowed out till Sunday. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.

Forty-one unread by the second night. She didn’t open one of them. She read them all on the lock screen instead, which was completely different.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third day Zhao Zhendong came to the garage.

She heard the car stop. Not a taxi. Something heavy that idled like a cat. Then nothing. When she looked up from the bench he was in the doorway. Black coat, in June. Her old jacket folded over his arm.

She’d seen him twice before. Once at a race years ago, standing at the back with his arms folded while the whole crowd made a space round him without noticing. And once in November 2018, the night she first opened the black door. Three of her father’s buyers had come down the street to drag her back. His men came out of the dark and stopped them. Afterwards he stood in the street and looked at her and said four words.

You owe me one.

She’d paid it in the winter, with Xiao Pan’s bike. They were even.

He walked in and put the jacket on the bench beside her.

“Did he send you?”

“No.”

“Then why are you here?”

He looked at her for four seconds.

“He hid you.”

“He put me out the back. By the linen room.”

“Hm.” Zhao looked at the drawing of her bike, pegged on the string. “He was hidden. Ten years. A farm in the borderland. So nobody could use him.”

“What’s that got to do with me?”

“He thinks hiding is how you keep someone.”

He turned round and walked out. The car door shut. The engine went away up the street, slow. Mrs. Tong came out of her shop with her hands in her apron and watched it go.

Jinx stood at the bench with her hand flat on the jacket for a long time.

Ten years. A farm. How old was he when they sent him? A baby? What kind of father does that?

What kind of father lets a buyer’s man… no. Not that. Not now.

She picked up her phone off the floor.

Jinx: zhao came

The reply took four seconds.

IDIOT: Oh no. Is he still there? Did he say anything?

Jinx: 28 words

IDIOT: That’s a speech. For him that’s a speech. What did he say?

She didn’t answer. But she didn’t turn the phone over either.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth morning, at ten, he started sending drawings.

No words. Just a photo. The first was her lathe, from memory. The second was Mrs. Tong’s window with Mrs. Tong in it, glaring. The third was the black bike. The fourth was the thirteen, lying on the floor where it had skidded, with a little arrow pointing at the wall a metre away. MISSED.

He was drawing right-handed. At the edge of the fourth photo she could see the plaster on his left arm. White. Something drawn on it she couldn’t make out.

She looked at every one. She answered none of them.

That night she started building the bike.

She didn’t decide to. She just found herself at the back of the workshop, pulling down an old step-through frame that had hung on its hook for a year. Cheap commuter thing, light and low, bought for parts. She stood it on the floor and walked round it the way she walked round every bike, until she could see what it wanted to be.

Then she started.

She did it at night for two weeks, after the customers had gone. Stripped it. Straightened it. Painted it pale green, the colour of the old trams in the Walled City, because she thought he’d like that. Fat tyres. Wide bars. The softest springs she had.

She took the engine out and put in a quieter one. Lowest gearing she could cut. Then she put a stop on the throttle and a limiter in the wiring, so it would never do more than twenty kilometres an hour. Not downhill. Not with the wind behind it. Not if he begged.

Big lights. One on the front like a train, two at the back. Reflective tape down the forks and the frame. Anything coming round a corner at night would see it from half a kilometre off.

Over the tank, on a steel arm that swung out and locked, she put a board. Sketchbook-sized, covered in cork, with a clip at the top and a little tray underneath for pencils. Wherever he stopped, he could swing it out and sit sideways on the wide seat and draw. Up on the pavement. Lights on.

The anchor woman stood in the doorway on the tenth night and looked at it.

“That’s a tram.”

“It’s a bike.”

“Hah. It’s a tram.” She went back to her shop.

She put a bell on it too. For safety, she told herself.

On the last night she sat on it in the middle of the workshop with every light on and rang the bell, once. It made a silly cheerful little ding in the empty building.

She put her face in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

The tower in the Symmetrical Ward was called the Meridian. It was all glass. The man on the desk in the lobby looked at her pale green bike as if she’d ridden in on a horse.

“Lin. Thirty-one.”

“Is Mr. Lin expecting you?”

“No.”

He looked at her old jacket. The new boots. The bike. He picked up the phone.

“Good afternoon, sir. There’s a lady here with a bicycle. Well. A sort of bicycle.”

She heard Raiden’s voice through the phone from across the lobby. She couldn’t make out the words. She could make out the volume. The desk man held the phone a little away from his ear and looked at it.

“Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Immediately, sir.” He put it down. “He says to send you up immediately. He says if the lift’s too small for the bicycle, I’m to carry it.”

“It’s not a bicycle.”

“No, madam. I can see that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The goods lift was big enough. She rode it up thirty-one floors with her hand on the seat and her heart going like a bad idle.

He was already there when the doors opened.

T-shirt. Old trousers. Bare feet. Left arm in plaster to the elbow. The stitches gone from his eyebrow and a thin pink line in their place. He was thinner. His hair needed cutting. He looked like he hadn’t slept since the hospital.

On the plaster, in purple marker, somebody had drawn a lumpy bean with a face and written SPLEEN: CHECKED. Love, E.

He looked at her. Then he looked at the bike.

He didn’t say anything. Raiden. Not talking. Was he ill? He came forward slowly in his bare feet and put his good hand on the handlebar. He looked at the lights. The tape. The wide soft seat. The board, folded down over the tank. He found the catch and swung it out. It clicked into place. He stood looking at the cork, the clip, the little tray for pencils.

He rang the bell. Ding.

“It does twenty. It won’t do more. Not downhill. Not anything.” Her voice wasn’t working right. “If you’re going to draw in roads, you do it on this. On the pavement. Lights on.”

“Jia…”

“Or I break your other arm.”

His eyes were wet.

“I’m sorry. At the hospital. I’m so sorry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His flat was enormous and nearly empty. White walls. Grey floor. A whole wall of glass looking out over the Symmetrical Ward to the harbour. A long table with nothing on it. A tilted drawing table by the window with drawings all round it, on the floor, in piles, pinned up. A kitchen somebody had actually cooked in.

She stood in the middle of it. The tram waited by the door like a pale green pony.

“I wasn’t ashamed of you.”

He was by the window. He hadn’t sat down. He kept starting to move his good hand and stopping it.

“I know what it looked like. The back door. I saw your face.” He took a breath. It hurt him. She saw it. “I’ve seen it every night for three weeks.”

“Then why?”

“I was frightened.”

“Of what?”

“Of them seeing you.”

“That’s the same thing.”

“It’s the opposite thing!” He winced and held his ribs. “Sorry. Sorry. It’s the opposite. Listen.”

He told her. In bits. With her interrupting.

“You know about the farm. Zhao told you. I could tell from the twenty-eight words.”

“Ten years.”

“Nearly. From when I was a baby. Uncle and Auntie and a water tower.” He looked out at the harbour. “My father loves us. All of us. He’d kill for us. He has. And everybody knows it.”

“So?”

“So anyone he loves is something somebody else can take. That’s why they sent me. I was the son. The son’s the one they’d take first.” He turned round. “When that phone said Baba I didn’t think, oh good, my family. I thought, in an hour the whole Walled City knows Raiden Lin has a girl. What she looks like. Where she works. That she sat by his bed all night.”

“And then?”

“And then you’re something somebody can take.”

She didn’t say anything.

“It’s been a bad month,” he said. “My sister’s shop window came in. Elowen. She’s fine. The floor I built her held.” His mouth went crooked. “I’ve been at my father’s every night since. Everybody’s watching everybody. And I lay there thinking about you on the stairs.”

“You could have rung.”

“I rang eleven times.”

“Before I left. You could have said it before I left.”

“I know.” He looked at the floor. “I was a coward by the linen room. I’m sorry. I’ll never do it again. If anybody ever comes through a door when you’re with me, I’ll stand in front of you. I won’t send you anywhere.”

She folded her arms.

“I’m not going to the Walled City.”

“All right.”

“I don’t want your father. Or his business. I grew up with my father’s buyers in and out of the shop. I got out. Nobody owns me again.” She glared at him. “I’m not going out with a Lin. I’m going out with you.”

“Yes. Yes. Good. That’s… yes.”

“So we keep it separate. Your side. My side. Your people don’t come to the garage.”

“Fine.”

“And you never put me out of a room again. Somebody comes, I stay. I can stand in front of myself.”

“I know you can. I’ll stand in front of you anyway. You can stand in front of me. We’ll take turns.”

Her mouth moved. She pressed it flat. He saw.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came across the room, slowly, in bare feet, and stopped right in front of her. He didn’t touch her. He looked at her face the way he looked at buildings, learning where everything went.

“I made a rule, too. While you weren’t answering.”

“You’ve got a lot of rules.”

“This one’s new. Not till the plaster’s off.” He held up the arm. “I wanted two hands. The first time. I wanted to do it properly.”

“Fine.”

“It’s a stupid rule.”

“You make stupid rules.”

“I know.” He lifted his good hand and put two fingers under her chin. “Here’s the problem. On your step I had another rule. If I came up your stairs, I wasn’t leaving. So I wouldn’t come up till you were sure.”

“I remember.”

“Well. These are my stairs.” His thumb moved along her jaw. “And you came up them. On a pale green bike. With a bell.”

“That’s not the same.”

“It’s exactly the same. It’s better.” He swallowed. “So I’m breaking the plaster one. I’m sorry. I’m completely breaking it. I’m in plaster, three ribs are held together with hope, and I’m going to be absolutely useless.”

“Raiden.”

“And I don’t care. I’d have crawled to the Docks on my knees if I’d thought you’d open the door.” He took a breath. “Jia. Will you stay? Tonight. Please.”

She looked at the pink line through his eyebrow. His mouth. His fingers under her chin, not quite steady.

“Yes.”

He made a sound like something in him had come loose. Then he kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was a disaster. It was the best disaster of her life.

He kissed her against the glass wall with the whole harbour behind her, one-handed. His plaster knocked on the window like someone at a door. She laughed into his mouth. She pulled his T-shirt up over his head.

“Ribs! Ribs, ribs, RIBS—”

She froze, horrified. He laughed so hard he had to sit down on the floor.

Then she was on the floor with him, on the grey boards in the sun, and he was kissing her neck. Her shoulder. The carp on her arm, all the way up, slowly, the whole length of it, like he was reading it.

“I can’t do anything,” he said into her collarbone. “I’ve got one hand. I’ve thought about this for six weeks and I’ve got ONE HAND.”

“Then lie still.”

“I don’t want to lie still.”

“Raiden.”

“I’m begging. Look. I’m on the floor. I’m begging again. That’s twice in a month. Nobody’s ever—”

She put her hand over his mouth.

He looked up at her over it with his hair everywhere and his whole face shining. He turned his head and kissed the inside of her wrist. Just there. Where the skin was thin.

She took her hand away and kissed him instead. She pushed him down flat on the floor, minding the ribs. He let her for about one breath. Then he didn’t. He pulled her down with his good arm and rolled them both, swore at his ribs, kept going. After that nobody was careful about anything. His plaster was cold on her back. His mouth was hot everywhere else. He kept talking, of course he did, her name, please, there, oh God, Jia, until she stopped being able to tell him to shut up.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ended up in the bed eventually. Huge. White. Only one side creased. He’d never slept in the middle of it, she could tell.

She lay in the middle of it now with the sheet round her waist. The light on the glass went gold, then pink, then blue. He lay on his good side with the plaster across her stomach and his face in her neck. His heart was still going fast against her arm.

“I’ve got a new rule.”

“No.”

“It’s a good one. You don’t ever have to leave. You can. Whenever you want. You don’t have to.”

She thought about her two rooms over the garage. The mattress on the floor. The shower you had to hit. Her jacket folded on the bench, and Zhao in her doorway, and a sketchbook in the road.

She turned her face and put her mouth against his hair.

“Idiot.”

It came out softer than she meant. He laughed. She felt it all down her side.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, when it was dark, he got up and found his sketchbook. He sat on the edge of the bed by the lamp and tried to draw her.

She let him. She watched his face while he did it. He frowned. Rubbed things out. Turned the page. Started again. Drew fast, then slowly, then not at all, and sat there with the pencil in his hand looking from her to the paper and back.

He tore out three pages and folded them up small.

“I can’t do it.”

“So don’t.”
