“No, you don’t understand. I can draw ANYTHING. I can do a building from across the harbour and get the windows right. I did your bike in the dark in a minute.” He stared at her over the lamp like she’d played a trick on him. “And I can’t get your face. I’ve tried for a month.”

“Then don’t.”

“I have to. One day.” He put the pencil down and lay back and pulled her against him with his good arm. “If it takes me my whole life.”

In the morning he went down thirty-one floors in the goods lift, barefoot, in plaster. Then he rode the tram round the car park at twenty kilometres an hour. Ringing the bell. Every lap.

The desk man came out to watch with his coffee.

“Good morning, madam.”

“Morning.”

“Is it always going to be like this?”

Jinx watched Raiden take the corner by the bins at full speed. Twenty. Ding.

“Yes.”

chapters.title: Her Father’s Chop Shop
chapters.desc: August 2021. She takes him to a roof across the lane from her father’s chop shop under the flyover and tells him some of it. She won’t go down. He goes home and maps every way out.
chapters.epigraph: “First word I ever read was torque.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
The plaster came off in July.

He came to the garage the same afternoon and held his arm out across the bench like a man showing off a new bike. It was thin and pale and strange. Something that had been kept in a drawer.

“Look! Two hands.”

She took it. She turned it over. She ran her thumb along the inside of his wrist where the bone had gone, feeling for it, like she’d feel a frame for a crack.

“Does it hurt?”

“Only when you’re not holding it.”

She dropped it.

He laughed and picked her up off the floor with both arms. His ribs must still have been sore, because he said “ow” in her ear. He didn’t put her down.

“You’ll break them again.”

“Worth it.”

“Put me DOWN.”

“Make me.”

She bit his shoulder. He put her down.

✦ ✦ ✦

By August he knew everything about her workshop and almost nothing about her.

She noticed one Sunday, lying on the floor of his flat with her head on his stomach and his fingers in her hair. He was telling her about the borderland. Not the bad bits. The farm.

“There was a water tower. White. I climbed it every day. Auntie used to stand at the bottom and shout.”

“What did she shout?”

“’Come down, you’ll break your head, and then what will I tell…’” He stopped. “Then what will I tell people. She never said who. Nobody ever said my surname out loud. Not once.”

“What else?”

“A kiln. Uncle made bricks. That’s where I learned about arches.” His hand moved in her hair. “Every brick in an arch is pushing against the one next to it. That’s what holds it up. Take one out and the whole thing comes down.”

“And goats?”

“So many goats. I could milk a goat before I could tie my shoes.”

“Show me.”

“I’m not milking you, Jia.”

She snorted into his shirt.

“And then I came home, at ten,” he said. And went straight on to Ah Sim, his father’s cook, and how she thought he was too thin. He always did that. He always stopped at the same place, with the same words, and jumped.

She noticed it. She didn’t ask. He’d tell her when he told her.

But he asked her things too. Between goats.

“Where did you grow up?”

“Under the flyover.”

“Doing what?”

“Bikes.”

Then he’d wait. She wouldn’t say anything else. So he’d go back to goats.

He never pushed. He asked once and let it go. It was starting to drive her mad.

“Ask me.”

His hand stopped in her hair. “Ask you what?”

“The thing you want to ask. About the shop. You keep not asking.”

He was quiet for a bit.

“I don’t want you to tell me because I asked. I want you to tell me because you want to.”

She looked at the ceiling.

“I’ll show you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He’d never been on the back of a motorbike. She found that out in the Meridian car park, when she handed him the spare helmet and he put it on backwards.

“Is this right?”

“No.”

“It feels right.”

“You’re looking at the inside of it.”

She turned it round. She did the strap up under his chin herself and tugged it to check. He stood very still while she did it, looking down at her.

“Feet there. Hold on to me, not the bike. Lean when I lean. Don’t fight it.”

“What if I do something stupid?”

“I’ll leave you on the expressway.”

“Can I hold on tight?”

“Yes.”

“How tight?”

“Raiden.”

He held on tight.

She took the expressway north. Over the river. Past the Iron Docks. On the first long straight she opened it, once, just to feel him. The black bike went from a hundred to a hundred and sixty like something let off a chain. His arms locked round her waist. His whole body pressed into her back.

Over the wind she heard him inside his helmet.

Laughing.

Not scared at all. He laughed like a little boy the whole length of the straight. She slowed down. She didn’t want to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Slums of the Industry weren’t on any map. On the map they were the old industrial zone, built in the sixties and seventies and left behind when the factories went north. Grey streets under three flyovers stacked on top of each other, so the streets underneath never saw the sun. Scrapyards. Workshops. Rooms over them for people with nowhere better.

At the end of a lane under the lowest flyover was her father’s shop. The concrete pillars went into the ground there like the legs of something huge.

She didn’t take him down the lane.

She stopped two streets away by a noodle factory that had closed when she was fifteen. Round the back. Up a fire escape she’d climbed a thousand times. Six flights of rusty iron to a flat roof covered in pigeon mess and broken tiles. The flyover went over their heads so close you could feel the traffic in your teeth.

“Oh.” Raiden was staring up at the underside of the road. “Oh, that’s horrible. Who designed that? Those joints are—”

“Raiden.”

“Sorry. Sorry. Not now.”

From the edge of the roof you could see straight down the lane.

A long low building of grey block. Corrugated roof. Three roll-up doors, all up. Over the middle one, hand-painted and older than her: CAO MOTOR REPAIR. Bikes on the pavement. Bikes in heaps in the side yard, stripped. A man with an angle grinder cutting a frame, the sparks going up orange in the shadow under the road.

“It’s a chop shop.”

“I know.”

“Do you? Do you know what that means?”

“Stolen bikes come in. Parts go out.” He had his hands in his pockets. “Frames get cut, so nobody can trace the numbers. Engines get new numbers. Some go out whole with new papers, to buyers who don’t ask.”

“Who told you that?”

“My father’s people used to buy from places like this. Not this one. Places like it.”

“They bought from this one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat on the edge of the roof with her boots over the drop. He sat down beside her very carefully, like a man who wasn’t used to heights without walls.

“My mother left when I was four.”

“Where to?”

“South. With a man who sold fridges.” She shrugged. “I don’t remember her face. I remember a red dress. And the door.”

“And your father?”

“Kept me in the shop. Nowhere else to put me. I slept in the office on a camp bed.” She nodded down at the little square window in the side wall. “That one.”

“How old were you when you started on bikes?”

“Five. First thing I took apart was a carb. Put it back. It ran.” The corner of her mouth went. “He laughed and showed everyone.”

“And school?”

“No.”

“No school?”

“Nobody thought of it. I couldn’t read till I was nine.”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“So I taught myself. From the workshop manuals. The big greasy ones with the diagrams.” She looked at the shop, not at him. “First word I ever read was torque. Then clearance. Then do not overtighten.”

He made a noise that wasn’t quite a laugh.

“By twelve I could strip any engine that came through the door. Faster than any of the men. And every bike I touched got out clean. Police never caught one.” She rubbed her thumb over the burn on her palm. “So they started calling me Jinx. Bad luck for the police.”

“And you liked it.”

“I was proud of it. Best thing anyone ever called me.”

“How old?”

“Twelve.”

He didn’t say anything to that.

“And then?”

She watched the sparks go up from the yard.

“Then something happened when I was seventeen. I’m not telling you that one.”

“All right.”

“I mean it. Not today.”

“I said all right. I meant it. Whenever you want. Or never.” He looked down at the shop. “Is he there? Your father?”

The little window with wire in the glass had a light on in it. A desk lamp, yellow. A big grey-haired man in a vest bent over a book, writing slowly, like every number cost him money.

“That’s him.”

“When did you last talk to him?”

“The night I left.”

“Do you want to go down?”

A truck went over the flyover with a noise like the end of the world. Her father didn’t look up. He never did.

“No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew it.

He didn’t ask. He took the sketchbook out of his jacket and drew it right there on the edge of the roof, fast, in the grey light under the road. The lane. The pillars. The three doors and the sign and the bikes. The sparks. And the little square window with the lamp, and the man at the desk, small and bent over his book.

It took him twenty minutes. She watched him the whole time.

He tore it out and held it out to her.

“No.”

“All right.” He didn’t put it away. He held it a bit longer. Then he folded it in half, very carefully, and put it inside his jacket against his chest. “I’ll keep it. In case you ever want it.”

“I won’t.”

“Then I’ll keep it anyway. It’s the best thing I’ve done all summer.”

His face had gone still and flat. Was he angry? She’d never seen him angry. She didn’t know what it looked like on him.

“He let you sleep in an office in a chop shop. He never taught you to read. He let a load of men call you a name for being useful to them.” He stopped. “And he was proud of you for it.”

“Raiden.”

“And something happened when you were seventeen, and I can see from here he didn’t stop it.” He shut his eyes. “Sorry. I said whenever you want. I’m not asking. I just… I can see it from here.”

She didn’t answer.

She put her hand out on the filthy roof between them, among the pigeon mess, palm up. He looked at it. He put his hand in it. He held on hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed till it got dark.

The orange lights came on along the pillars. The grinder stopped. Her father turned off the lamp and came out and pulled the three doors down, one after another, three crashes, same as every night of her life. Then he walked off down the lane with his hands in his pockets, a big grey man, slow. He didn’t look up.

Raiden got up and knelt behind her. He put both arms round her and his chin on her shoulder and held on. She felt him breathing against her back, slow and even.

She leaned back into him.

“I’m never going to be owned again. By him. By his buyers. By anyone.”

“I know.”

“That means you too.”

“I know.” He said it into her ear. “I don’t want to own you. I want you to let me stay. That’s the opposite.”

She sat in his arms on the roof of the dead noodle factory with the traffic going over until her legs went numb.

Then she twisted round on her knees and kissed him. Hard. Both hands in his hair. He made a surprised noise and kissed her back. They tipped. His foot went over the edge of the roof.

“SHIT—”

So he did know swear words. She laughed so hard she had to hold on to the rusty old water tank.

“It’s not FUNNY, I nearly died!”

“You nearly died last time.”

“That was YOUR fault!”

“Get away from the edge.”

“I’m not touching the edge again. I’m never touching an edge again in my life. I’m going to live in a bunker.” He crawled toward the middle of the roof on his hands and knees, still swearing. “Come here. Come here and do that again, away from the edge, like a normal person.”

She did it again. Away from the edge.

✦ ✦ ✦

He held on round her waist all the way home without a word. She stayed in the slow lane the whole way.

At the black door he went straight upstairs. He sat at her kitchen table under the bare bulb and started drawing. The shop. The lane. The roof they’d sat on. Then the next street. And the next. Every street under the flyover they’d ridden through. Every corner and alley and fire escape.

“What are you doing?”

“Making a map.”

“Of what?”

“Every way out.”

“Which way did the buyers come in?”

“What?”

“The buyers. When they came to the shop. Which end of the lane?”

“The top. Always the top. Cars can’t turn at the bottom.”

“And the police?”

“They didn’t come.”

“Never?”

“Not once. Bad luck for the police, remember?” She sat up. “Why are you asking?”

He’d already drawn an arrow at the top of the lane. He drew a little cross at the bottom, where the cars couldn’t turn. He didn’t answer. Did he even hear her? He was off somewhere, inside the paper, counting.

“Raiden. Why?”

He looked up then.

“Because I’m a Lin, and I make places safe. And that’s the most dangerous place I’ve ever seen you look at.” He went back to the paper. “And one day you might want to go down that lane. If you do, I want to know every way you could come back.”

She lay on the mattress and watched him.

“Go to sleep.”

“Nearly done.”

He wasn’t nearly done. At some point in the night she woke up and he was drawing the drains.

chapters.title: He Asks Her to Marry Him on a Napkin Drawing
chapters.desc: September 2021. At Mrs. Tong’s he slides a napkin across the table with their whole life drawn on it to scale. She says yes, on conditions, and they sign the terms in chilli oil. Then she has thirteen days to break every rule he makes.
chapters.epigraph: “Yes. A registry. Not your father’s house.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
By September he lived in two places and so did she, and they’d stopped pretending otherwise.

Some nights it was the thirty-first floor. She’d wake up to the whole harbour going gold. He’d be at the drawing table already, in his shorts, pencil behind his ear, humming. Some nights it was her mattress over the garage, with the cranes going and the shower you had to hit. He’d wake with his feet hanging off the end.

“Best sleep of my life.”

“You say that every time.”

“It’s true every time!”

He’d won a prize in August. A library he’d drawn for the firm in the south, with a roof like an open book. There’d been a dinner and a speech and a heavy glass thing with his name on it. He brought the glass thing to the garage and put it on the shelf over her bench. Between the tin of washers and the jar of brake fluid.

“Why there?”

“That’s where the important things go.”

He rode the tram everywhere at twenty kilometres an hour with the lights on in broad daylight and the bell going. He stopped strangers to tell them his girlfriend had built it. The desk man at the Meridian had started calling it the tram to its face.

And every morning at ten there were four coffees.

✦ ✦ ✦

“After dark you ring me.” She pointed her chopsticks at him. “Wherever you are. I’ll come and get you.”

It was Friday, the middle of September, and still hot. Mrs. Tong’s was full of men off the container ships, big men in vests who ate fast and didn’t talk. Mrs. Tong was behind the counter shouting at the kitchen. They had the table in the corner by the fridge, the only one with its back to the wall.

“I’ve got the tram.”

“The tram does twenty. Vans do sixty.”

“I nearly got killed by a man on his phone.”

“Yes.”

“And you’d have to come across the city at midnight because I wanted to draw a bridge.”

“Yes.”

He looked at her for a moment. “All right. But I’m not getting in a car. Cars are for cowards.”

“Cars are bikes for cowards.”

“Exactly. So you’ll come on the bike, and I’ll hold on very tight.”

She snorted and ate her noodles. She pushed the greens to the side. He reached over without looking and took them, the way he did every time now, and ate them himself.

He was drawing on his napkin.

He did that everywhere. Napkins. Receipts. Menus. The margins of her invoices, which drove her up the wall. Most of the time she didn’t look. It was just what his hands did, like hers turning a bolt over in her pocket.

But tonight he’d got out the little ruler he kept in his jacket and never used on napkins. Every so often he looked up at her. Then back down. He hadn’t said a word in ten minutes. In a noodle shop. Was he ill?

“What are you drawing?”

“Nearly done.”

One more line. He looked at it. He wrote something tiny at the bottom. Then he put the pencil down, turned the napkin round, and slid it across the table to her. Past the chilli oil. Past the soy. Past the little dish of her greens he hadn’t finished.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the garage.

Not as it was. As it could be. A plan, from above, walls in thick black lines and doors as little arcs. Her workshop downstairs with every bench and the lathe where they really were. The stairs. And upstairs, not two rooms any more. One long one, with windows down the street side. A kitchen at one end with a long table. A big bed at the other end. A bathroom with a bath, a real one, with taps drawn in. A drafting table by one window. A bench with a vice by another. And a shelf over the bench with the glass prize and the tin of washers and the brake fluid on it, tiny.

At the long table, two little circles side by side. Beside them, in his small neat capitals: J. R.

In the corner, a scale bar. 1:50.

Under that, so small she had to bring it up to her nose:

Will you marry me?

She couldn’t breathe.

The shop went on round them. Mrs. Tong shouted. A man scraped his bowl. The fridge hummed and shuddered. She sat there holding a paper napkin with their whole life on it, drawn to scale. Her heart took off worse than in any race.

She looked up. He wasn’t smiling. He was pale. His hands were flat on the table either side of his bowl, holding it down.

“I measured. Everything. I went round with a tape when you were at the dyno shop up north.” It came out fast. “The walls are right. I checked the beams. The wall between your two rooms with the crack in it isn’t holding anything up. Somebody put it in in the eighties.”

“Raiden.”

“The bath fits if we put the water tank on the roof. I’ve drawn the tank. It’s on the back.” He turned the napkin over for her. It was. “I didn’t want you to think it was just a drawing. It’s a plan. It’ll stand up.”

“Raiden—”

“I know it’s four months. I KNOW it’s four months. I don’t care. I knew on the shipyard road. You grabbed my shirt and I thought, oh, it’s her. I’m not going to know it any better in a year.” He swallowed. “Jia. I love you. Marry me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The man at the next table had stopped eating. Mrs. Tong had stopped shouting. The whole shop had gone quiet behind her, pretending not to listen.

She looked at the two little circles. J. R. The bath. The glass prize between the washers and the brake fluid.

She wanted to say yes so much her hands shook.

And she thought of her father’s hands flat on the desk. The black car in the lane. Lin. From the Walled City. Don’t ever go there. What would it mean, marrying the only son of the man in the dark coat? Not Raiden. Him. The Walled City. The family. The whole heap she’d climbed out from under with a van and a lathe.

She put the napkin down flat between them.

“Yes.”

He didn’t move. Had he even heard? Then his mouth opened.

“…Yes?”

“On conditions.”

“Anything. Anything. What conditions?”

She held up one finger. “A registry.”

“Yes.”

Two. “Not your father’s house.”

“Yes.”

Three. “Nobody from the Walled City. Nobody, Raiden. Not your father. Not your sisters. Not a cousin.”

“Yes.”

“Not till I can walk in there on my own feet.”

He was already pulling a second napkin out of the holder. He wrote across the top in capitals. TERMS. Then underneath, numbered, every one of hers. She watched him do it. His hand was shaking so badly the three looked like a five.

Then he wrote a fourth.

“What’s that?”

“Mine. I’m allowed one.” He turned it round. 4. R. may ask again. For the other one. With his family.

“The other what?”

“The other wedding. The big one. My father’s house. My sisters crying. Ah Sim shouting at the caterers.” He looked straight at her. “I’ll do the registry. I’ll do it tomorrow. But one day I want the one they come to. So I’m going to ask for it.”

“Ask, then.”

“Will you marry me again? In front of all of them?”

“Not yet.” She heard her own voice go rough. “Ask me when I can say yes without walking into your father’s house.”

“Every month.”

“You’ll get not yet.”

“I’ll take not yet. I’ll take a thousand of them.” He held out the pencil. “Sign.”

She signed. Cao Jia. In capitals. He signed under her. He drew a tiny bike next to his name.

“WITNESS!”

Mrs. Tong was standing at their table with her ladle. Nobody had seen her come round the counter.

“Mrs. Tong, you don’t have to—”

“Give it.” She took the pencil and wrote her name under theirs in enormous characters. Then she tapped the napkin. “Registry. Good. Which day?”

“We haven’t—”

“Thursday.” Raiden didn’t even look up from the napkin.

Jinx looked at him.

“Thursday’s the best day of the week. Remember?”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was red to the ears. He folded the proposal in half, and in half again, along the scale bar so it didn’t crease the bath. He folded the terms with it. He opened his soft old brown wallet with the worn corners and put them both behind his cards, where other people kept photos. He put the wallet back in his jacket. Against his chest.

Then he cleared his throat.

“I’ve made a rule.”

“Of course you have.”

“No kissing till the registry. I want that one to count.”

“That’s thirteen days.”

“Thirteen days. I can do thirteen days. I’m extremely disciplined. Ask anyone.”

She got up. She came round the table past the fridge, in front of every man in the shop and Mrs. Tong with her ladle. She sat down on his knee and kissed him. Hard. He still had his chopsticks in his hand.

When she let go he was pink to the collar.

“That… you can’t… that was a rule. That was a whole rule.”

“It didn’t count.”

“It ABSOLUTELY counted.”

“Engaged people don’t count.”

“That’s not a thing! You’ve made that up!”

She sat back down and ate her noodles.

Mrs. Tong brought a plate of extra beef and banged it down between them. The men off the container ships went back to their bowls. One of them was grinning into his soup.

Under the table, all through the rest of dinner, his foot stayed pressed against hers, the whole length of it. Like he was making sure she didn’t go anywhere.

She didn’t want to.

✦ ✦ ✦

He booked it on Monday. The registry office in the old town. Thursday the thirtieth. Ten in the morning.

He kept the rule.

She broke it.

She broke it on Monday at the bench, by grabbing his belt when he walked past with the coffees. She broke it on Tuesday morning in her doorway, with the anchor woman watching from next door. She broke it at the drawing table on the thirty-first floor, by sitting on his drawing.

“That’s a hospital!”

“Mm.”

“You’re sitting on a hospital, Jia, they need that by Friday—”

She kissed him. He made a noise of real anguish and kissed her back for a good while before he remembered.

“No! No. Rule.” He held her off by the shoulders, breathing hard. “That’s four.”

“It didn’t count.”

He’d started keeping a tally. On the back of a receipt in his wallet. Every one she broke got a line. Under the lines, in capitals: SHE SAYS IT DIDN’T COUNT.

“Why do you even want a rule?”

“So the registry one’s special.”

“They’re all special.”

“Don’t.” He put his face in his hands. “Don’t say things like that, I’ve got nine days left.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mid-Autumn was on the Tuesday.

Mrs. Tong gave them two mooncakes in a paper bag and told them not to share them with the anchor woman. They took them up onto the flat roof of the garage. They sat with their backs to the water tank and watched the moon come up fat and orange over the cranes.

He’d gone quiet.

“What?”

“I’ve never missed one. Since I came home. Not once.”

“Then go.”

“No.”

“Go, idiot. It’s an hour.”

“I’m busy.”

“With what?”

“With you.” He got his phone out. He looked at it for a long time. Then he rang.

She heard it pick up. She heard a woman’s voice, old and loud and furious before he’d even said anything. Through the phone, across the roof, every word.

“WHERE ARE YOU?”

“Ah Sim! Hello! Happy Mid-Autumn!”

“Don’t happy me. Your father’s sitting at the table. Your sister’s done the lanterns. Where ARE you?”

“I’m busy. Tell Baba I’m sorry. I’m busy and I’ll come at the weekend.”

“Busy with WHAT?”

“Work. Lots of work. Sunday. I promise. Save me a mooncake!”

He hung up before she could shout again. He sat there holding the phone in his lap.

Jinx broke her mooncake in half and gave him the bigger half.

“You’ll have to lie to them.”

“I lie to them every day.”

“About this, too.”

“About this, too.” He turned the mooncake over in his fingers. “Ah Sim’s going to kill me. She does the lotus seed herself. She’ll know I’m not working. She always knows.”

“Then tell them.”

“You said nobody.”

“I said nobody comes.” She looked at the moon. “I didn’t say you had to lie.”

“If I tell them, they come. You don’t know my family. Elowen would be here in an hour with a cake and a lawyer.” He laughed, but it was thin. “No. It’s yours. Your terms. I signed. You get your registry with nobody from the Walled City.”

“And you?”

“I get you.”

He leaned his head on her shoulder. She let him. After a while she took his hand in her lap and held it. He ate his half mooncake one-handed. He got lotus paste all over her jacket and didn’t notice.

✦ ✦ ✦

He went to the Walled City on Sunday.

She worked all day with the radio on and didn’t think about it. At ten that night she took the tin of washers down off the shelf.

She tipped it out on the bench. Steel. Every size. She picked through them with one finger until she found two she liked. A thick one. A thin one.

The thick one she put on the lathe. She took the hole out to the size of her own ring finger, and then a hair more, because her knuckles swelled when she’d been working. She took the outside down, smooth. She rounded the edges so they wouldn’t catch. She polished it on the wheel until it shone like water.

The thin one was harder. She didn’t know his size.

She did, though. She’d held his hand on a cold floor under a bike. In a hospital. On a roof. She closed her eyes and felt for it. Then she opened them and cut.

She was polishing the second one when the taxi stopped at the top of the street. Feet on the cobbles. The key in the black door.

He came in slowly. His good shirt. His face tired. He looked like Sunday lunch had been long.

“How was it?”

“Elowen asked why I’m so happy.”

“What did you say?”

“The tram.” He sat down on the bottom stair. “Eliana looked at me over her laptop for the entire lunch. She didn’t say anything. She never says anything. That’s what frightens me.”

Then he saw the bench. The two little steel bands on a clean rag, under the lamp.

He went completely still.

“Jia. Are those…”

“Washers.”

“They’re RINGS.”

“They’re washers with ideas.”

He got up off the stair. He came over and stood at the bench. He didn’t touch them. He put his hands behind his back like he was in a museum again.

“Can I try mine?”

“Thursday.”

“Just to see if it fits—”

“Thursday.”

“What if it doesn’t fit? What if my finger’s—”

“It fits.”

“How do you know?”

She put the polishing rag down and looked at him.

“I know your hands.”

He made a noise like she’d hit him. Then he grabbed her by the front of her overalls, pulled her in, and kissed her. Hard. Right there at the bench. No asking. No rule.

When he let go, they were both breathing like they’d run up the stairs.

“Four days.”

“Shut up.”

“You broke it.”

“It didn’t count,” said the man who’d made the rule.

chapters.title: The Trophy Husband Has Dinner Ready
chapters.desc: They marry at the old-town registry with two washers for rings and Mrs. Tong crying louder than anyone. Then her husband moves into her two rooms with a wok, saves her in his phone as Tyres, and loses an argument about dumplings.
chapters.epigraph: “Somebody has to cook. You’d put soup in a gearbox if I let you.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
He’d been up since five. She could tell because the kettle was cold again and there were four abandoned cups of tea on her windowsill.

“I can’t do it.”

He was standing in the middle of her two rooms in his silver waistcoat with the buttons wrong. All of them. One off, all the way down.

“Come here.”

“I’ve done it four times. My hands won’t work. I’m a draughtsman, my hands ALWAYS work—”

“Come here.”

He came. She undid every button and did them up again, bottom to top, while he stood there breathing through his nose like a horse. Then she took his tie in her fist and yanked it straight. Hard. His head went forward with it.

“Ow.”

“Better.”

“You’re very calm.”

“Somebody has to be.”

He looked down at her. She was wearing the jacket. The one from the black box, soft and heavy, silver zips, sleeves the right length. First time she’d had it on. Under it a clean white vest and black trousers and the boots. Round her neck, a thin steel chain with nothing on it yet.

“You’re wearing it.”

“It fits.”

“Jia…”

“Don’t cry. You’ll do it at the registry anyway.”

“I’m not going to cry at the registry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong had shut the shop. There was a sign on the door in red marker: CLOSED. WEDDING. She’d never shut it on a weekday in twenty years except for her husband’s funeral. She told everyone that, all morning, including the taxi driver.

The anchor woman came out in a good grey coat with a brass anchor brooch on it. She looked at Raiden’s waistcoat.

“Hah.”

“Is that a good hah?”

“It’s a hah.”

Raiden put both old ladies in a taxi and paid the driver about three times too much. Then he got on the back of the black bike in his silver waistcoat. He held on to his wife-to-be very tight, all the way to the old town.

The registry office was up a flight of stone steps, between a bank and a shop that sold wedding cakes nobody looked at. Inside it smelled of floor polish. The clerk was a thin older man with a cold. He sniffed between every sentence.

“Papers.”

They gave him their papers. He sniffed. He read. He stopped.

He looked at the card in his hand. LIN RAIDEN. He looked up at Raiden. He looked at the card again.

“Any relation…?”

“To who?” Raiden gave him the biggest, silliest smile in the whole city. “There are millions of us. I’m the useless one. Ask anyone.”

The clerk looked at him for a long moment. Then he looked at Jinx. Tattoos. Shaved head on one side. Black nails. Jaw set.

“Right, right.” Sniff. “Sign here. Both of you. Full names.”

She took the pen. She hadn’t written it on paper in years. Not since the shop. She wrote it in big blocky capitals, like a workshop manual. CAO JIA. The pen dug into the paper. Her hand didn’t shake. Much.

Raiden signed under her. Then he started drawing a little bike next to his name.

“No drawing on the register.”

“It’s a very small bike.”

“No.”

“It’s barely a bike—”

“No, sir.”

Raiden put the pen down with enormous dignity. Mrs. Tong signed as a witness in characters so big they went over the line. The anchor woman signed neatly with her own fountain pen, which she took out of her coat and put back after.

The clerk read them a paragraph. Sniffing. Then he looked at Raiden.

“Do you consent?”

“Yes. Yes! Absolutely yes.”

“Do you consent?”

“Yes.”

“Rings?”

She put her hand in her jacket pocket and took out the two steel bands on the clean rag.

The clerk leaned forward. “Are those… washers?”

“Rings.”

“They’re RINGS!” Mrs. Tong had a voice for kitchens.

Raiden picked up the thick one. His fingers were shaking again. He took her left hand and slid it on. Over the knuckle. It went exactly where it was meant to go and stopped.

She took the thin one and put it on his finger. It fitted. Of course it fitted.

He stared at it. He held his hand up to the window like he was checking a weld.

“It fits.”

“Course it fits.”

“You never even MEASURED me, Jia.”

“You may—” the clerk began.

“Can I?” Raiden turned to her. “I mean, I had a rule. Thirteen days. I want to do this properly—”

She grabbed him by the waistcoat and kissed him.

The clerk sneezed into his sleeve. Mrs. Tong burst into tears so loudly that someone in the corridor opened the door to look. The anchor woman said “Hah,” and then, after a bit, “Hah,” again, a lot softer.

Raiden kissed her back like he’d been waiting thirteen days, which he had. When he finally let go his face was wet.

“You cried.”

“I did NOT.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong took the photo on the steps outside with her old phone.

“Closer! You’re married. Stand closer. Hold her hand. Not like that! Like a husband!”

“How does a husband hold a hand?”

“Like he owns it!”

“Don’t.”

Raiden held her hand like he was carrying a full cup of tea up a staircase. Mrs. Tong took eleven photos. Every one was crooked. She’d put the best one on the wall behind her counter by Sunday, next to her late husband, and never take it down.

On the bottom step he stopped and turned her round to face him.

“Jia.”

“What?”

“I love you.”

She looked at him. The silver waistcoat. The washer on his finger. His face, wet and blotchy and so happy it was stupid.

“I know.”

He laughed. Out loud, on the registry steps, with pigeons going up off the railings.

“That’s it? I know?”

“Yes.”

“That’s the best thing anyone’s ever said to me.”

Then she took her ring off and threaded it onto the chain round her neck.

“What are you doing? We’ve been married four minutes!”

“Rings catch in engines.”

“Four MINUTES—”

“I’ve got a clutch at two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding lunch was at Mrs. Tong’s, with the sign still on the door and the shop full anyway. Word had got round. Every man off the container ships who knew the black door had come in and was eating beef in total silence.

Mrs. Tong stood on a chair.

“She married him!”

The men put their bowls down. One by one they stood up, big men in vests and work boots, and held up their tea.

“Congratulations, Bad Luck,” said the biggest one.

Jinx went red to the ears. Raiden was so happy he couldn’t sit still. He shook every hand in the shop. He tried to pay for everybody’s lunch. Mrs. Tong hit him with a ladle.

Then his phone buzzed on the table.

Baba.

He looked at it. All the happy went out of his face in one go. He turned it face down. Did he think she hadn’t seen?

“Answer it.”

“It’s my wedding.”

“Answer it, Raiden.”

He picked it up and walked to the door. She watched him through the glass. He was doing the voice. The silly one. Hands waving. Fine! Busy. Lots of work. Sunday, Baba, I promise. His left hand was in his pocket the whole time.

When he came back he didn’t sit down straight away.

“What did he want?”

“Dinner. Tonight. At the house.” He sat. He took his hand out of his pocket. The ring was still on. “I said work.”

“You’ll have to say it a lot.”

“I know.” He picked up his chopsticks and took the greens out of her bowl. “Eat your lunch, wife.”

“Don’t call me that.”

“Wife.”

“I’ll put you through the window.”

“Wife.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He wanted to carry her over the threshold.

“That’s the rule. I carry you over. Every husband in history.”

“The door’s a roll-up door.”

“I’ll manage.”

He tried. He got one arm under her knees, then realised he needed both hands for the door. He put her down. He hauled the door up a metre. It came straight back down on its springs and nearly took his head off.

“Right. Right. Hold the door.”

“No.”

She bent, got her shoulder into his stomach, and lifted him. Fireman’s carry. His silver waistcoat over her shoulder and his legs kicking.

“JIA. That’s not… you can’t… I’M supposed to—”

She shoved the door up with her free hand and walked under it. Then she carried him up the stairs.

He laughed upside down the whole way. He was still laughing when she dropped him on the mattress. Then she climbed on after him and he stopped.

“Wife,” he said, against her mouth.

“Stop saying that.”

“I’m never stopping. I’m going to say it till I’m ninety.”

His hands were in her jacket, pushing it off her shoulders. He got her vest half over her head and got stuck, and she was laughing inside it, blind. He kissed her stomach through the cotton until she wasn’t. The ring on its chain lay cold between them. His was warm on her back.

“Slow,” she managed.

“I can do slow.”

“Liar.”

“Watch me.” He kissed down her arm, the carp, the inside of her elbow, taking his time about it like a man reading the small print. “See? Slow. I’m extremely—”

She hooked her heel round the back of his knee and pulled.

“Oh,” he breathed. “Oh, that’s not fair.”

He couldn’t do slow after that. He lasted about a minute and gave up and swore into her shoulder. She pulled him back by the hair and kissed him. The mattress slid half off its frame. His feet went off the end, as usual. Her name. Again. Jia. Over and over, like he was learning it all over.

“Look at me.”

“I am.”

“Keep looking. Please. Don’t shut your eyes, I want…”

He never finished. She held his face and looked at him the whole way. Then she couldn’t look at anything. She held on to his back instead and stopped thinking.

Afterwards he lay with his face on her stomach and his arm across her hips.

“Mrs.…”

“Don’t.”

“Cao Jia, beloved wife of—”

“I’ll throw you down the stairs.”

“You’d have to carry me first,” he mumbled. “You’re good at that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He moved in properly on the Saturday. Two suitcases, a drawing table in four pieces, and a wok.

He swept the floor. He washed the window that didn’t close, so the street lights came in clean for the first time in three years. He found a blue tablecloth from somewhere and put it on her little table.

That night she came up the stairs black to the elbows. The clutch job had gone wrong three times. She stopped in the doorway. The room smelled of ginger. He was at the hot plate in an apron printed TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS. Where had he even found that? The box under the stairs, probably.

“Sit down. Don’t touch anything. Wash your hands first. Twice. The orange soap, not the other one. The other one smells of petrol.”

“What is that?”

“Fish soup. Ginger, tofu, and the greens you don’t eat, so I can eat them.” He turned round. “You’ve burned your thumb.”

“It’s nothing.”

“Let me see.”

He took her wrist and held her hand under the cold tap for a full minute. He didn’t let go once. She stood there dripping oil on his clean floor and didn’t argue.

“Who taught you to cook?”

“Auntie, at the farm. Then Ah Sim, when I came home at ten. Nobody else ever went in her kitchen. I sat on the step and drew her, and she made me chop things.” He put a bowl in front of her. “Eat. You’d put soup in a gearbox if I let you.”

She ate two bowls. She didn’t say anything. He watched her the whole time with his chin on his hand.

Later, while he was in the shower, she picked up his phone to check the time. Her own text from an hour ago was still on the screen.

Tyres: where r u

She stared at it.

When he came out in a towel she was holding his phone up at him like evidence.

“TYRES?”

“Ah.”

“I’m TYRES?”

“In case Baba sees my phone. Or Eliana. Eliana sees everything.” He dripped on the floor. “Nobody looks twice at Tyres. Everybody needs tyres.”

“I’m your WIFE.”

“Shh!”

“Who are you shushing? There’s nobody here!”

“Habit!” He took the phone off her very carefully. “What am I in yours?”

“IDIOT.”

“Still?”

“Capitals.”

“I was always capitals.”

“Exactly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong asked in November why Jinx hadn’t been in for dinner in three weeks.

“He cooks.”

“Every night?”

“Yes.”

“And cleans?”

“Washes my overalls.”

Mrs. Tong put her ladle down.

“In thirty-one years my husband washed one bowl. Once. In 1997. I remember the day.” She jabbed the ladle at Jinx. “Keep him. If you don’t want him, I’ll have him.”

The men at the counter laughed so hard one of them choked on his tea.

He’d done the October napkin right there, at the table by the fridge. A lighthouse on a rock. A workshop at the bottom for her bikes. A bed at the top under the lamp. Every stair drawn in. Will you marry me again? With everyone? (The view is good.)

“Not yet.”

“I’ll take that.”

Number two went in the wallet behind number one. In November it was a houseboat. Number three.

She had a cold that week. He’d offered in October to get a man in for the window and the wet wall behind the bed. She’d said no.

“It’s my window.”

“It’s our window.”

“It’s the cousins’ window. I pay the rent.”

“We pay the rent.”

“I PAY THE RENT.”

He shut up. He put more ginger in the soup. She coughed under every bike for a week, and they didn’t talk about it again, and the window still didn’t close.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third Wednesday in November he made dumplings.

He had flour on the table. Flour on the floor. A long white streak of it down one cheek where he’d pushed his hair back. She came up the stairs after four hours under a bike, black from her hair to her boots.

“Don’t touch anything!”

She looked at him. The flour. The sleeves rolled up. The bare bulb over his head. Something in her chest went loose all at once, like a stuck bolt when the heat finally gets in.

She walked across the room. She didn’t wash her hands.

“Jia. Jia. Your hands. I’ve got forty dumplings. They’re perfect. Ah Sim would weep. Don’t you dare—”

She put both hands on his face. Two big black handprints, over the flour.

“You did that on purpose.”

“Yes.”

“I’ll have oil in my eyebrows for a week.”

“Yes.”

He dropped the dumpling. He put his floury hands on her waist and lifted her onto the cracked wooden counter by the sink in one go. She wrapped her boots round the backs of his legs.

“They’ll go soggy,” she said into his mouth.

“They’ll be fine.”

“You said on Monday. If you leave them out they stick.”

“Are we arguing about dumplings? Right now?”

“You started it.”

“I was making DUMPLINGS. You came in and put your hands on my face.” He was undoing the knot of her overall sleeves at her waist. “Deal. They go soggy, I make you eighty tomorrow. And you stop talking about them.”

“That’s not a deal. That’s you getting what you want.”

“Those are the best deals,” he said, and got the knot undone.

Her elbow went into the bag of flour. A white cloud went up round both of them. They stopped and looked at each other through it, coughing, black and white and ridiculous. She started laughing and couldn’t stop. He kissed her through it until she did.

The dumplings went soggy. All forty. Nobody cared.

They ate the ones that could be saved at midnight, lumpy and torn and stuck together in pairs. He gave her the last one without asking. She ate seven.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke in the night, cold. The window that didn’t close had let the whole of November in.

He was already up. In his shorts, with a roll of tape, taping cardboard over the gap. Shivering. The hot plate glowing red for warmth.

She lay still and watched him. He put a hand on the outside wall, on the long damp stain behind the bed. He looked up at the cracked ceiling. He looked at the shower you had to hit.

He didn’t know she was awake. There was nothing silly in his face at all.

“No,” he muttered. “No. That’s not good enough for my wife.”

She shut her eyes before he turned round.

She found out in December what he meant.

chapters.title: The Roof That Will Never Fall
chapters.desc: Winter 2021 to spring 2022. A letter says her building has been sold, and it has, to her. Her husband spends New Year at his father’s table with his ring on a string, then spends three months building the napkin, with steel in every wall.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s in your name. Only yours. I’m sorry. I know I promised I’d only use it when it was important.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
The letter came on the second Monday in December.

It was from lawyers for the Tai Hing Rope & Canvas Company. The company had stopped making rope in 1994. Now it was three old cousins in three different countries who owned the building and fought about it by email. She’d paid them rent for three years, in cash, on the first of the month, to a man on a scooter.

Dear Tenant. We write to inform you that the property at the above address has been sold. The new owner’s representatives will be in contact regarding your tenancy.

She read it standing at the black door with grease on her hands. She read it again.

Then she went cold all over. The lathe weighed a tonne and a half. It had taken four men and a crane to get in. Her benches. The bikes on their chains. Customers who came because they knew the black door. Where else near the Docks did Zhao’s name keep the crews off? Where else had a ceiling that high? In a city where nothing was ever for rent and everything was for sale?

She went upstairs. He was at his drawing table by the window.

“They’ve sold the building.”

He looked up. At the letter. At her face. And there it was. Something under the smile, like a sticky valve under a clean idle.

“Raiden.”

“Yes. I know.”

“How do you know?”

He put his pencil down.

“Because it was me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t throw a spanner. She just stood there.

“You bought my building.”

“No.”

He went to the suitcase under the bed, the one he still hadn’t fully unpacked. He came back with a fat brown envelope and held it out.

“I bought YOUR building. Yours. Not mine. Not ours.” He held it out further, because she wasn’t taking it. “It’s in your name. Only yours. Cao Jia. I’m sorry. I know I promised I’d only use it when it was important. This was important.”

“And the Lin name?”

“Not on it anywhere. Not mine. Not my father’s.” He swallowed. “And next door. The old sailmaker’s. That’s in your name too.”

She took the envelope. Two deeds. Stamps. Lawyer words she couldn’t half read. And on the line that said Owner, twice, in black type: CAO JIA.

“We’re married.”

“Yes.”

“So why isn’t your name on it?”

“Because you said you’d never be owned.” He stood very still in front of her with his hands at his sides. “I can’t fix your father. I can’t make the Walled City not be the Walled City, or me not be his son. But nobody can put you out of your own door now. Not a landlord. Not a crew. Not my father.”

“And you?”

“Not me either. Husband or not. If you ever want me gone, you put my suitcases on the step and I’ve got no right to argue.” His voice wobbled. “That’s the point. It’s yours.”

She looked at the deed.

“And,” he went on, a bit differently, “your window doesn’t close. The wall behind the bed is wet. You coughed for a week and I had to watch. So I want to rebuild the top two floors. If you’ll let me. It’s your building. You can say no.”

“You’ve already drawn it.”

“I drew it in September. On a napkin.”

“That was a proposal.”

“It was both.”

“You did it without ASKING me!”

“I know.”

“You KNOW? You know?!”

“If I’d asked, you’d have said no, because of the money.” He didn’t look sorry about that part at all. “So I did it, and now I’m asking about the rest.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went downstairs. Through the workshop, out of the black door, across the street to her van. She got in and shut the door. She turned the radio up loud. The station that only played old songs. She sat with her hands on the wheel and the deed on the seat beside her.

He didn’t follow. He stood in the doorway with his hands in his pockets.

The anchor woman came out of her shop and stood next to him and looked at the van.

“What did you do?”

“I bought her the building.”

A woman on the radio was singing about a boat. You could hear it all the way down the street.

“She’ll be twenty minutes. She did it when her best customer died. Twenty minutes, with the radio.” The anchor woman went back inside. “Don’t knock on the window.”

He didn’t knock on the window.

It was a bit over twenty. Then the radio went off and she got out. Her face was white and dry. She walked back across the street with the deed in her hand and stopped in front of him on the step.

“Fine. Rebuild it.”

He held out his arms. She walked into them and stayed there, face in his shoulder, in full view of the anchor woman’s window.

“Next time you ask first!”

“Next time I’ll ask first.”

“You’re lying.”

“A bit.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunar New Year’s Eve was the last day of January. He had to go to the Walled City.

She watched him get ready in the long mirror at the Meridian. Good shirt. Good coat. He stood there for a long time with his left hand in front of him. Then he took off the washer. He threaded it on a black string. He tied it round his neck and tucked it under his shirt, against his chest.

“It’s just tonight.”

“I know.”

“Baba notices hands. Everybody in my family notices hands.” He did up his top button over it. “I’ll be back after midnight. I’ll bring you dumplings. Ah Sim does the pork ones with the thin skins.”

“I don’t need dumplings.”

“You need dumplings.”

He kissed her at the door. She didn’t hold on to him. She’d decided that in the afternoon.

She went down to the garage and worked. Mrs. Tong was shut. The whole street was shut. Every window had people in it, eating, shouting, setting off crackers. She stripped a carb that didn’t need stripping. She did it twice.

At two in the morning she was under a bike when his feet came across the concrete.

“You’re working.”

“Yes.”

“On New Year’s Eve.”

“It’s a bike. It doesn’t know what day it is.”

“It’s two in the morning, Jia…”

He lay down on the second creeper and pushed himself under next to her. He smelled of incense and his father’s cigarettes. He had a plastic box of dumplings on his chest.

“Stole them. Ah Sim saw. She didn’t stop me.” He opened the lid. “Eliana watched me pack them. Over her laptop. Didn’t say a word.”

“Does she know?”

“Eliana always knows something. You can never tell what.” He fished out a dumpling with his fingers and held it to her mouth. “Eat. Happy New Year, wife.”

She ate it off his fingers. It was still warm. She hadn’t eaten since lunch.

He untied the string from round his neck right there under the bike, by the work light. He put the ring back on his finger. Then he lay there with his shoulder against hers and his hand on her stomach.

“Next year,” he said.

“Don’t.”

“Next year you’ll be at the table.”

“Not yet.”

“I know. I’m just saying it out loud, so it’s in the room.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took three months. She slept at the Meridian and rode down to the garage every morning at seven. The builders worked upstairs. Dust came down through the floor onto her benches and she didn’t complain once, because every time she looked up there was something new.

He was there every day in a hard hat. He didn’t play the fool with the builders. He talked to them in short plain sentences. When the foreman said a thing couldn’t be done, Raiden took him to the wall and showed him how. The foreman went red and did it. They called him Mr. Lin. Not young master. Mr. Lin.

In the third week she heard him with the steel man. Their voices came down through the floor.

“Nobody ever sees the inside of a wall, Mr. Lin.”

“I did. I was up the ladder at six this morning with a tape.” Pleasant. Almost friendly. “The mesh on the north wall is half the gauge on my drawings.”

“It’s fine. It’s the same—”

“It isn’t. Take your lorry and your men and go now. You won’t be paid for any of it. And every firm in the city that hires steel will hear about the north wall by Friday. From me. In detail.”

“You can’t—”

Raiden said the man’s name. Then his wife’s name. Then the street his yard was on. Same pleasant voice.

The steel man stopped talking.

The lorry left at nine. Upstairs, somebody started taking the north wall down.

At one Raiden came downstairs in his hard hat with two cartons from Mrs. Tong’s. He put her greens on the side and asked if the dust was getting in her carburettors.

She looked at him for a while. He looked back, pleasant and blank.

“The steel man.”

“He’ll find work. Somewhere far away.” He split her chopsticks for her. “Eat your noodles.”

He wouldn’t let her go up.

“Not till it’s finished. I want you to see it all at once. Like the tram. You didn’t show me the tram in bits.”

She tried once, in March. He was at the bottom of the stairs with the plastic sheet behind him and his arms folded. She kissed him slowly, both hands on his face, until he’d stopped guarding anything at all. Then she slid one hand through the gap in the sheet behind his back.

He caught her wrist without opening his eyes.

“That’s cheating.”

“Yes.”

He kept hold of her wrist. He kept kissing her, too.

At Mrs. Tong’s in January he’d drawn her a workshop inside an old ship, engines and all. Will you marry me again? In front of everyone? Not yet. In February, a house up a tree. Not yet. In March, a tiny flat on top of a crane with a garage for one bike in the cab. Not yet. That one made her laugh out loud, and Mrs. Tong brought extra beef.

Number seven. He folded it into his wallet behind the others.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the first Saturday in April he took the plastic sheet down.

The new stairs were wide oak with a steel rail. He walked her up them one step at a time. At the top he opened the door and stood back to let her in first.

She stopped dead.

It was the napkin. All of it. The long room the whole length of the building, where her two rooms had been. Five tall windows down the street side in steel frames that actually opened and closed. Wide pale boards. A real kitchen at one end with a long oak table and eight chairs. A big low bed at the other end. His drafting table by the first window. Her bench by the second, with a vice already bolted to it. A long soft sofa in dark green.

The shelf over her bench. The glass prize. The tin of washers. The brake fluid.

Through a door, a bathroom. White tiles. A shower head the size of a plate. And a bath, a real one, deep and long.

He’d even filled the gap by the pipe.

“Now.” His voice had gone quiet and serious, like on the back stairs at the gallery. “Now I show you what it’s really made of. And you tell me if it’s too much.”

He walked her round it, wall by wall. Behind the new plaster on the brick walls, steel mesh set in concrete all the way round. Drive a truck into the building and the outside would come down, but the inside wouldn’t. The windows were three layers of glass that would crack and hold. The front door at the top of the stairs was oak on the outside and steel underneath.

“You’d need a lot of time and a lot of noise to get through that. And the anchor lady would come out with an anchor.”

“She would.”

“She’d WIN.”

He opened a narrow cupboard in the bathroom. It wasn’t a cupboard. It was a stair. Up past the water tank to a hatch. Out onto the roof. Across onto the sailmaker’s roof next door. Down an iron ladder into the back lane where nobody went.

“Another way out. Nobody knows it but us.”

Then he took her downstairs to the tool wall.

Her spanners, smallest to biggest. The thirteen between the twelve and the fourteen. She’d hung every one herself, three years ago.

He reached behind the biggest spanner and pressed something she couldn’t see.

The whole wall swung out. Silent. Every tool still on its hook. Behind it, a grey steel door with a keypad.

“I did this in February, while you were up north at the dyno shop. Sorry. It’s the only thing I’ve done without asking. If you knew it was here, and somebody ever made you tell them, you could say you didn’t.”

He opened it. A little concrete room. A light that came on by itself. A vent that hummed. A bench with a mattress. Water, food, a first-aid box, a radio. A phone on the wall with a line that didn’t go through anybody’s exchange.

“You could sit in there three days.” He looked at the room, not at her. “I hope you never go in it. Not once. I built it so I’d never have to lie awake again like I did in that hospital. Not knowing.”

“What’s the code?”

“Your birthday. Fourteen, oh-two.” He winced. “I know you hate it.”

She looked at the open door. Then at him.

“Show me the rest.”

“What rest?”

“You’ve got the look.”

He laughed. Helpless. “How do you always know?”

“I can hear it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her through a new door into the sailmaker’s. It had been empty for ten years and full of pigeons. No pigeons now. Clean. White. Empty except for one thing under a cover.

He pulled the cover off.

A dyno. A new one. The big steel drum in its pit. Straps. A cooling fan taller than her. A desk along the wall with screens and a sensor on a lead for the exhaust.

“You said they cost a fortune.” He took a folded page out of his pocket. It was the page from May. DYNO. Fortune. Find out how big a fortune. “I found out.”

“It’s too much.”

“Yes. I’m a Lin. I’m rich and I’m married to you. This is what happens. You’ll have to get used to it.”

She walked back across the white room and took his face in both hands. Clean hands this time. She looked at him for so long he started to look worried.

“Thank you.”

She’d never said it to him. Not for the coffee. Not for the soup or the floor. She didn’t say it to anyone. Nobody ever said it to her in the shop, so she never learned how.

“Oh,” he managed. That was all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first bath took twenty minutes to fill. She sat on the edge in his shirt and watched it and didn’t believe it.

Then they both got in, though it wasn’t really big enough. Her back against his chest. His arms round her. His chin on her head. The water up to their necks and the cranes lit up beyond the five tall windows.

She’d had two baths in her life. She lay in this one and felt her shoulders let go. Then her back. Then her hands, which were tight even when she slept. They opened under the water.

“Is it all right?”

She took his hand under the water and put it flat on her stomach and held it there.

He kissed the side of her neck. Then lower.

“There’s a drain in the floor,” he murmured against her jaw. “I put it in for this.”

She laughed and turned round in the water to get at his mouth. Half the bath went over the side onto the new white tiles.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, wrapped in towels on the green sofa, she said, “You built it anyway.”

“Built what?”

“The napkin. All of it. Without the wedding.”

“I built the house. We’ve had the wedding. The other question’s still open.” He kissed her temple and reached for a pencil. “Different things.”

The dyno’s instruction manual was on the floor. He turned it over and drew the long room on the back, fast, from above. Two little circles on the sofa. A scale bar.

Will you marry me again? With all of them there? (You’d have a bath.)

“Not yet.”

He folded it into his wallet with the other seven. He hadn’t even waited for the end of the month.

chapters.title: The Meanest Engineer in the City
chapters.desc: April 2022. At a charity gala full of people who know his father, a racing driver with kitchen-scissor hair catches him looking at a crack. By the end of the night she knows he’s married, and Jinx has a new client who pays in gearboxes.
chapters.epigraph: “She could build a bike faster than you could crash it. I’d bet money. I’d bet your money.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
“Seven hundred people. A dinner. An auction. Speeches.” Raiden was lying on the green sofa with his feet in her lap, reciting it like a dentist’s appointment. “I’ll be an idiot from seven till eleven. Then I’ll come home and you can tell me what was wrong with everyone.”

“I’ll come.”

He turned his head on the cushion.

“You don’t have to.”

“I know.”

“It’s the children’s hospital gala. There’ll be people from the Walled City there. Not my family. People who know my father.” He sat up a bit. “People who’ll see you with me and go home and talk.”

“Let them.”

“Jia. They’ll see the ring.”

“Then they see a ring.”

He didn’t say anything for a moment. Then he pulled her down on top of him and kissed her for so long that the rice burned.

“The RICE—”

“Leave it.”

“It’s on FIRE, Raiden.”

“It’s a small fire.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The gala was on the eighth of April, a Friday, in the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel.

She bought the dress herself. A shop in the Coastal High-Rise. The woman behind the counter looked at her tattoos and her shoulders and went into the back. She came out with the only dress in the shop that would fit. Plain. Black. Well cut. It cost more than a carb rebuild.

She did her nails at her own bench, black, with the bottle held in the vice. She came up the stairs holding her hands out in front of her like they were radioactive.

“Don’t touch me. They’re still wet.”

“Come here.”

“They’re WET.”

“I know. Come here.”

He took her wrists and blew on her nails. One hand. Then the other. Slowly, very seriously, like a man cooling soup.

“You look ridiculous.”

“I’m a husband. This is my job now.”

She went to change. She came out of the bathroom in the dress and the jacket and the boots. He was at the top of the stairs in his dark suit and a new silver waistcoat with a pattern like gears. He’d designed it himself and had it made by a tailor in the old town.

He didn’t say anything at all. He went red. All the way to the roots of his hair.

Raiden Lin, blushing. She wanted a photo.

“Say something.”

“I can’t. I’m a Lin. We’re well brought up. Everything I want to say is something I can’t say in a taxi.”

He said some of it in the taxi anyway. In her ear. All the way across the harbour.

Somewhere on the harbour bridge he thought she was looking out of the window. He slid the washer off his finger and into his waistcoat pocket.

She saw. She didn’t say anything. Her ring was on its chain, under the dress, where nobody could see it either. So what was she going to say?

✦ ✦ ✦

The ballroom was gold and white and full. The bit near the door went quiet when they came in.

Heads turned. They looked at her. They looked at him. They looked at his hand on the small of her back. And this time they didn’t look away.

So she looked back.

She’d learned at the shop how to look at a man until he looked away first. She did it now, to the whole bit of the room by the door, one at a time. A man in a grey suit. A woman in pearls. A bald man who’d been staring at her tattoos. They all looked away.

“Oh,” Raiden breathed, delighted. “Oh, do that again.”

“No.”

“Please. Do the bald one again. He’s a judge.”

Then he let go of her back at the edge of the room and threw himself in, arms out, like jumping into the sea.

In thirty seconds he was the silliest person there.

“Uncle! Your tie! That tie is a crime against silk, Uncle. A CRIME.”

“Young man, this tie—”

“Is a crime!”

He hugged an old man who clearly didn’t know him. He got the name of the hospital wrong. He knocked over a little gold chair and apologised to the man on the next one for ten minutes. Then he stopped in front of one of the twelve white marble columns and stared up at it with his mouth open.

“No. No, no, no. This is terrible. Who did this? The feng shui is a disaster. It’s fighting the harbour. Can’t you feel it in your teeth? This whole room’s unlucky. I’m going to lose money at the auction, I can feel it coming up through the floor…”

People laughed. People always laughed. A woman in green patted his arm.

Jinx stood by the wall and didn’t laugh.

Beside her, somebody did. A real one. Short and loud, like a cough.

✦ ✦ ✦

A woman was leaning on the wall next to her. Tall, thin, wiry. Short dark hair that looked like she’d cut it herself with kitchen scissors. A red dress she very obviously hated. Flat shoes. An old burn scar on the back of her right hand, shiny, the exact shape of an exhaust pipe.

Jinx knew who she was. Anybody who’d ever been near a track knew. Serafina Song. The one who raced. Team AURELIA, the black car with gold on the bonnet, in the Asian GT series. The one whose sister was a jeweller and whose family had more money than the harbour.

“Is he yours?”

Jinx looked at Raiden under the column, telling a man in a dinner jacket his whole life would go wrong if he didn’t move his table.

“Yes.”

“He’s very good. I’ve never seen anybody do it that well. My mother would believe him, and my mother believes nothing.” Serafina drank her champagne. “Why does he do it?”

Jinx didn’t answer.

Serafina looked her over sideways. The jacket. The tattoos. The black nails. The grease in the creases of her knuckles that never came out whatever she used.

“You’re a mechanic.”

“Engineer.”

“What kind?”

“Bikes.”

“I hate my mechanics.” She said it with real feeling. “They’re too careful. Everything takes three days. Everything needs a part from Germany. I ask them to try something and they look at each other and go, Miss Song, the regulations.” She finished her glass. “I want somebody who’ll just build the thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden had come back along the wall without either of them noticing. He was on Jinx’s other side with his full glass and his silly face on. His eyes weren’t silly. They went over Serafina the way they went over a building. The scar. The shoulders. The flat shoes. The weight on the balls of her feet.

“You want my wife.”

Jinx turned her head and looked at him.

He put his hand in his waistcoat pocket. He took out the washer. He put it back on his finger, right there, in the middle of the Harbour Hotel ballroom, and she watched him do it.

“Well. My wife. Don’t tell my father. I’ve asked her seven times for a proper wedding. Eight if you count the bath.”

“The BATH?”

“Long story. Very wet.” He smiled at Serafina with every tooth he had. “But she’s the meanest engineer in the city. She built a bike near the Docks with an intake you could hang in a gallery.”

“Raiden.”

“And she stopped it in two metres from a hundred and ninety, and it didn’t drop a bolt. She could build a bike faster than you could crash it. I’d bet money. I’d bet your money.”

Serafina looked at him.

“I don’t crash.”

“Everybody crashes. That’s why you need a mean engineer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina didn’t laugh at that. She tipped her head. She looked up at the column he’d been shouting at. Then back at him.

“You said it was fighting the harbour.”

“Terrible feng shui.”

“That’s not what you were looking at.” She pointed with her empty glass at the top of the column, where the gold met the marble. “There’s a crack. There. You stared at it for ages before you started shouting. I watch tyre walls for a living. I know what somebody looking at a crack looks like.”

Raiden’s smile stayed exactly where it was. It just stopped being a smile.

“It’s cosmetic.” His voice had gone flat and plain. “The marble’s only cladding. The real column’s concrete, inside, and it’s fine. They put the gold on with the wrong glue in 1987. It’s been pulling at the stone ever since.”

“So it’s going to fall?”

“The gold is. One day. On somebody’s head. It won’t bring anything down.” He looked at her. “Don’t sit under it.”

Serafina stared at him. Then she laughed again. The loud short one.

“Oh, you’re AWFUL. You’re absolutely awful. You’re the cleverest man in this room and you’ve spent an hour telling everyone their tables are unlucky!”

She held out her hand. Not to him. To Jinx.

“Serafina.”

“Jinx.”

Serafina’s hand was hard and dry, with calluses in the same places as hers.

“I want a bike.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the taxi home he was quiet. He kept turning the washer on his finger with his thumb.

“You put it back on.”

“She’s a racing driver. She doesn’t know anyone.”

“Her family know everybody. Everybody, Raiden.”

“…Ah.” He stopped turning the ring. “Well. Too late now.”

“Yes.”

“Are you angry?”

“No.”

The taxi went over the bridge. The clock on the dashboard flicked over to the next day. She leaned over and put her mouth against his ear.

“Happy birthday.”

He turned and looked at her like she’d given him a car. She hadn’t given him anything. He went stupid anyway, all the way home. Tomorrow he’d be at his father’s table all day. Tonight he was hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina came to the garage on the Tuesday. She rode a tired old Japanese bike that coughed at the end of the street and died outside the black door.

She got off it and looked up at the sign. TAI HING ROPE & CANVAS. She looked at the anchor woman, who’d come out to look at her. Then she walked in and stopped and looked at the workshop the way Raiden had on the first day. Slowly. All the way to the back.

“Oh. Oh, I see.”

Jinx was on the floor by the sidecar.

She’d started it in January. A big old bike with a frame she’d built for it, and a chair beside it. Long, low, boat-shaped steel, with a seat and a little screen and a board that folded out over the knees. For him. So he could come with her when she went north to a show, or a race, or anywhere further than the tram could get him. So he could sit beside her, at the same speed, and draw.

He didn’t know. It lived under a sheet when he was home.

“Who’s that for?”

“Nobody.”

Serafina looked at the board that folded out over the knees. At the little tray for pencils. She didn’t say anything. Jinx liked her for it.

“What’s it missing?”

“Gearbox. It needs a reverse. You can’t push an outfit that heavy backwards out of a parking space on your own.”

“And?”

“The one in Germany takes four months.”

Serafina thought about it.

“I’ve got one.”

“What?”

“Small, sequential, with a reverse. Out of a little race car somebody built in Japan in the nineties. Tiny thing, for hill climbs. I bought the whole car for parts two years ago and never used it. It’s in a crate in my garage.” She shrugged. “It might fit. If you made it fit.”

“I’d make it fit.”

“I know you would. That’s why I’m here.”

“I’ll pay you for it.”

“No. You’ll build me a bike.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She built it over the summer.

Four months, between the customers and the sidecar and the dyno. She’d stopped calling the dyno too much and started calling it mine. She built Serafina’s bike for Serafina’s body and Serafina’s riding. She spent two Saturdays watching her at Granny Shum’s street races. Granny Shum ran them from a folding chair in a car park. Legal? Not for years. Light. Stiff. Sharp. A frame that told you everything the road was doing through your knees. Nothing on it that didn’t need to be there.

She painted it dark gold, the colour on the bonnet of Serafina’s race car. She didn’t put a carp on the tank. The carp was hers.

Serafina came for it in August. She sat on it in the workshop without starting it. Then she started it. Then she rode it once round the block, fast, and came back, and pulled her helmet off. Her face was wet.

“I can’t pay you for this.”

“You did. The gearbox.”

“That’s not… a gearbox isn’t… this is—”

“You paid me in a gearbox. I paid you in a bike. We’re even.”

Serafina wiped her face with the back of her scarred hand and laughed, wet and furious.

“A bike isn’t money! You can’t call this even. I’m going to say you owe me for that gearbox for the rest of your life. And one day I’m going to turn up at that door and ask you for something, and you’re going to say yes.”

“Maybe.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The gearbox fitted the sidecar in the end. It took a whole new mount, an adaptor plate, and a linkage for the reverse to a lever by her left knee. Three weeks.

On the first Sunday in September she pulled the sheet off and wheeled it out into the street. Raiden came down the stairs with a cup of tea and stopped dead on the step.

He looked at the long steel chair. The seat. The little screen. The board over the knees. The tray for pencils.

He put the tea down on the step, very slowly.

“It’s yours. Get in.”

He got in. He didn’t say anything. He sat with his knees up and his hands on the edges of the chair and his face turned up to her. She put the spare helmet on him, the right way round, and did up the strap.

They went north on the expressway at a hundred and ten, side by side, in the slow lane. Wind in his face. Board out over his knees. He drew the whole way. The bridges. The river. The flyovers. Her, from below, with the sky behind her. He drew until he ran out of pages, and then he drew on his arm.

When they stopped for petrol he climbed out and stood on the forecourt with pencil all up his left arm to the elbow.

“You built me a seat.”

“You can’t ride.”

“You built me a seat next to you.” His voice had stopped working properly. “Jia. You built me a seat NEXT to you.”

“Get back in. We’re blocking the pump.”

He didn’t get back in. He held out his arms. She walked into them on the forecourt, in front of a man filling a lorry with diesel, who stared.

“What are you looking at?” she demanded, into Raiden’s shoulder.

“Nothing, miss.” The lorry driver went very quickly back to his diesel.

chapters.title: Raiden Is Proud of Her for an Entire Week
chapters.desc: October 2022. Her black bike wins Best in Show up north, and her husband tells a petrol station, a toll booth and an entire bus. He tells everyone except his own family. Then he tells Zhao, and Zhao already knows.
chapters.epigraph: “I’d like everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
“Enter.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because then they’ll look at it.”

It was August. He was on the green sofa with his feet over the arm and a sketchbook on his chest. She was at her bench by the second window, filing a bracket that didn’t need filing.

The Northern Custom Show. Every October, in an old aircraft hangar two hours north. She’d gone for six years. She’d walked round it in her old jacket with her hands in her pockets, looked at every bike the big shops had built with their sponsors and their teams of six, gone home, and built something better on her own.

Entered? Never. Not once.

“They’ll look at it and see what I saw on the shipyard road.” He didn’t look up from the sketchbook. “Then they’ll know. And you’ll know they know.”

“That’s worse.”

“That’s the point.” He turned a page. “I’ll fill the form in. You won’t have to touch it. Jinx, the garage, nothing else.”

She filed. He waited. He was good at waiting now. Married a year in September and he’d learned that much.

“Put the carp.”

“Hm?”

“On the form. Where it says the name of the bike.” She blew the filings off. “Put Carp.”

He got up off the sofa. He came across the long room, kissed the back of her neck once over the collar of her overalls, and went to get his laptop.

The back of her neck stayed hot for an hour. Ridiculous.

✦ ✦ ✦

They went up on the Friday night in the van, with the black bike on a borrowed trailer and Raiden drawing the motorway by the light of the dashboard.

The hangar was enormous and freezing and full of men.

Four hundred bikes. Banners. Music from somewhere. Coffee, two-stroke, tyre polish. Men in leather, men in branded shirts, and a few women, not many, who watched her wheel the black bike in and nodded.

Her square of grey carpet was at the far end by the doors. A big chrome cruiser on one side. On the other, a matte green racer with five men round it in matching jackets.

She polished nothing. She put up no sign. She stood the bike on its stand with the front wheel turned a little, how it liked to stand, and stepped back.

One of the jackets laughed. The one with the beard.

Raiden put his hand on the small of her back.

“That one,” he murmured. “I’m going to remember his face.”

“Don’t.”

“Too late. Already filed.”

Her hands were stiff with cold. He noticed before she did. He took both of them and shoved them into his coat pockets with his own, and stood there in front of her like that, chest to chest, in the middle of the hangar.

“People are looking.”

“Let them. It’s a bike show. They’ve never seen a wife before.”

“Shh!”

“Nobody here knows my father.” He grinned down at her. “I could shout it.”

“You could walk home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The judges came round after lunch on the Saturday.

Three of them. A woman from one of the magazines. A young man with a clipboard from a big shop in the south. And an old man who’d built bikes up north for forty years. She’d known his face since she was ten, from the magazines on her father’s office floor.

The jackets talked at them for ten minutes. The old man nodded and moved on.

Then he got to the black bike.

He walked round it. Once. He didn’t say a word. Then he crouched by the engine with one hand on his knee, slow, like his knees hurt, and looked at the intake.

And stayed there.

He put his thumb on the third runner, where she’d filed the mouth by hand. He stopped on the lip. The exact spot Raiden had drawn, the morning after the shipyard road.

Raiden made a noise in his throat. She kicked his ankle.

“Who made this?”

“Me.”

“The whole thing?”

“Frame. Swingarm. Intake. The tank’s out of a scrap one. The engine’s old. I rebuilt it.”

“On your own?”

“Yes.”

The old man looked at her. Then back at the runner.

“Forty-one years I’ve been doing this.” He got up with a grunt. “I’ve never seen anyone match runners that well by hand. What do you call it?”

“Carp.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It won.

They read it out at the end of the day, from a little stage, into a microphone that whistled. Best in Show. Carp. Built by Jinx. Garage near the Iron Docks.

Nobody clapped.

Who was Jinx? Nobody in the hangar knew. Then the women at the far end started. Then the old man. Then everyone else, slowly, still working out if they were allowed.

She stood by the bike and couldn’t move.

Raiden whooped.

An actual whoop. A boy on a roller-coaster. It went straight up into the roof and four hundred heads turned round. Then he grabbed her round the waist and lifted her off the floor and swung her. Her boots flew out. One nearly took the mirror off the chrome cruiser.

“PUT ME DOWN—”

“No!”

“Raiden, I swear—”

“You WON. You won, you won, Jia, you WON—”

She was laughing. When had that started? Halfway round, with her arms locked round his neck and her face in his hair, she was laughing out loud in an aircraft hangar and couldn’t stop.

He put her down. He didn’t let go. He took her face in both hands and kissed her in front of the whole hangar. Somebody whistled. The beard said something and his friends laughed.

Raiden didn’t stop. After a second she didn’t care. She grabbed his waistcoat and kissed him back until the women at the far end started clapping again.

On the way out she stopped at the matte green racer. The beard was packing up.

“Your rear brake line’s touching the exhaust. It’ll boil on the first long hill.”

He stared at her. She walked on.

Raiden had stopped too, trophy under his arm. He picked one of the team’s cards off their stand and read it. Then he smiled at the beard with his silliest face.

“Coastal High-Rise. Tower Four. Ground floor.” He tucked the card into his pocket. “I know the man who signs the fire certificate for that tower. We have lunch sometimes. I might have lunch with him on Tuesday.”

The beard stopped smiling.

Raiden caught her up at the door.

“Will you?”

“Haven’t decided.” He swung the trophy. “I’ll let him think about it for a bit.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was proud of her for an entire week.

He told the man at the petrol station. He told the woman in the toll booth, who hadn’t asked. He told the anchor woman.

“About time.”

He told Mrs. Tong. She gave them free noodles and cut the picture out of somebody’s newspaper and stuck it on the wall behind the counter. Next to her late husband. Next to the crooked photo from the registry steps.

“Three now. Good wall.”

He told the desk man at the Meridian.

“The lady with the bicycle?”

“The lady with the bicycle!”

The desk man shook his hand.

He told the firm in the south on a video call. He told the foreman who’d built the top floors, who rang back two days later because his brother-in-law wanted a bike. He told Big Fok at the shipyard road.

“I know. Everyone knows. She’s going to be impossible now.”

And then the tram got a puncture, and Raiden got on a bus.

Raiden. On a bus. She was on it too, so she saw the whole thing. Before the next stop he’d told the driver, a schoolboy, and an old lady with a shopping trolley. The old lady asked to see the picture on his phone.
