“Very nice.” She squinted at him. “Is she single?”

“No! No, she’s my w—” He stopped dead. “She’s mine. She’s mine. I’ve asked her for a wedding fifteen times.”

“And?”

Jinx leaned forward from the seat behind.

“Not yet.”

The old lady twisted round and looked at her for a long, rude time.

“Say yes. Look at him. He’s told the whole bus.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t tell his family.

She noticed on the Wednesday. They were eating noodles at the long table and his phone buzzed by his bowl.

Elowen.

He read it and smiled. Then he started typing. Fast. A lot. His face was lit up like the hangar.

Then he stopped. He looked at it.

And he deleted it. One letter at a time. She watched every single letter go.

He typed something short, sent it, and put the phone face down.

“What did she say?”

“Am I coming on Sunday. It’s Baba’s birthday dinner.”

“What did you start to say?”

He looked at her.

“I started to say, my wife won Best in Show with a bike she built with her own two hands, and the old man from the magazines got down on the floor and touched the intake.” He picked up his chopsticks. “And then I remembered the terms. So I said, yes, what time.”

She sat there.

Her terms. Nobody from the Walled City. She’d made the first version of that rule in June 2021, arms folded, in his empty flat. She’d signed the napkin in September. And he’d kept it every day since, so well she’d thought it was easy for him.

Was it? He went to Sunday lunch with his ring on a string under his shirt. He came home and cooked for her. He never said one word about it.

She’d thought that meant he didn’t mind.

“I’m so proud of you.” He wasn’t looking at her. He was looking at his noodles. “I want everyone to know. I’d like a plane to write it in the sky. I’ve looked into it. It’s very expensive and the wind spoils the letters.”

“Raiden…”

“I’d like my sisters to know. That’s all. That’s all it is.”

What was she supposed to say? The rule was hers. She wasn’t ready to break it. And she’d just watched him delete the best thing anyone had ever written about her, letter by letter, so that he wouldn’t break it either.

The noodles went cold. She felt sick.

He took her greens. She let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Friday he went to the flower shop.

He was delivering a shelf. Old shipyard timber, for the glasses on Elowen’s kitchen windowsill. He strapped it to the board on the tram and went across the city at twenty kilometres an hour.

Zhao was there. He usually was, on Fridays. In the chair behind the counter that Elowen didn’t let him sit in, with a newspaper.

Elowen was in the back, on the phone to a supplier, being cold and precise about tulips.

Raiden put the shelf on the counter.

Zhao looked at it over the paper. Then at Raiden.

The plan was easy. Put the shelf down. Say something silly. Leave. Raiden had done it a thousand times.

But the sun was coming in across the tulips, across the floor he’d built with a steel room under it, and Zhao’s flat black eyes were on him, and his mouth just went.

“She won Best in Show.”

Zhao looked at him for four seconds.

“Hm. I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“How do you know?”

Zhao turned a page.

“Big Fok. The anchor woman. The boy.” That was Xiao Pan. Another page. “Mrs. Tong’s wall.” Another. “The bus.”

“You know about the BUS?”

Page.

“How long have you known? About her?”

Zhao folded the paper and put it on his knee.

“Since the hospital. The jacket.”

Raiden stared at him. The green jacket on the hospital chair. The big hand lifting it off before Elowen turned round. He’d seen it happen and told himself he hadn’t.

“And you never told Elowen.”

Zhao’s eyes went down. To Raiden’s collar. To where the black string went in under his shirt.

“Or about that.”

Raiden’s hand flew up to his chest. Too late. Far too late.

“How—”

“Mrs. Tong’s wall.”

“That’s a PHOTO, it’s tiny, it’s crooked, you can’t even—”

Zhao looked toward the back of the shop, where his wife was telling a tulip man exactly what she thought of him in a voice that could cut glass.

“Not mine to tell.”

He picked up the paper again.

Raiden’s eyes stung. He let them. He put his hand flat on the counter, beside the shelf. Zhao looked at it. Then, without lowering the paper, he put his own hand on top of it. Once. Heavy. Gone.

“Tell her well done,” said the newspaper. “From me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her that night in the bath.

“Two words. Well done. He’s said about nine words to me in two years, and two of them were for you.”

She lay back against his chest in the hot water. Said nothing.

“He knows. About this.” He lifted his left hand out of the water. The washer shone. “He’s known for a year and he’s never told her. Not his to tell, he says.”

“It isn’t.”

“I know.” He kissed her shoulder. “I’m not asking. I promise I’m not asking. I just wanted you to know somebody in my family knows. And thinks well done. And kept it because you asked.”

He’d drawn her all week. At the bike. By the stage. Up in the air, boots kicking. Boots. Arms. Shoulders. The back of her head. The carp. Every time he got to her face, he tore it out and folded it small. She’d found the little squares in the bin.

She turned her head on his wet shoulder and looked up at him.

“Raiden.”

“Mm.”

“I’m proud of you too.”

He went stiff in the water.

“For what?”

“Keeping it. My rule.” Her voice came out rough. “It costs you. I didn’t know till Wednesday.”

He didn’t say anything. He wrapped both arms round her, under the water, and pushed his face into her wet hair. They stayed until the water went cold and she started complaining. He didn’t let go even then.

“You’re shivering.”

“You’re squashing me.”

“Husband’s privilege.”

“That’s not a thing.”

“It’s in the terms. Number five.”

“There IS no number five!”

“I’ll draw one,” he said into her hair.

The trophy went on the shelf over her bench. Between the glass prize and the tin of washers.

chapters.title: Memes at 2 A.M.
chapters.desc: December 2022. Her husband can’t sleep, so he sends her memes from the next pillow. She works out why before he does. A farm in the borderland, a freezer, eleven hours, and a light she puts in for him.
chapters.epigraph: “You built me a freezer with the light on.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
Her phone buzzed on the floor by the bed. She opened one eye. Two in the morning. The cranes were lit up in all five windows.

A cat. A grey cat squashed into a cardboard box much too small for it, spilling over every side, face completely calm. me fitting into my responsibilities

From IDIOT. IDIOT was lying right next to her. She could feel his shoulder against hers under the duvet. His phone was lighting his face up blue.

Buzz. A tower in some other city, every window a slightly different shape. architect: i have a vision. the vision:

Buzz. A dog in a hard hat.

Buzz. A staircase that went up into the ceiling and stopped. me when i start a sentence

She picked her phone up off the floor.

Jinx: im next to you

He read it. She watched him read it, eighteen inches away.

IDIOT: I know!! didn’t want to wake you

Jinx: you woke me

IDIOT: sorry

IDIOT: [a goat standing on a fridge]

Who did this? Who sent memes to a woman with her elbow in his ribs? She rolled over and looked at him.

“Raiden.”

“Mm?”

“It’s two in the morning.”

“It is! Look at this one, though, it’s a pigeon in a—”

“I can see it. You SENT it to me.”

“It’s better on mine. Bigger screen.”

“Raiden.”

He sent it anyway.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lay and watched him.

He looked fine. Mostly. Hair everywhere. A bit pale in the blue light. But his eyes were going back and forth over the screen too fast. His jaw was tight.

A lorry went past in the street. Its lights swung across the ceiling. His shoulder went hard against hers. Then soft again.

Another lorry. Hard. Soft.

Oh.

He’d done this last year. Same week. She hadn’t put it together then. They’d only just moved in together over the garage, two rooms and the window that didn’t close. But the week after Christmas, which nobody at the Docks bothered with, he hadn’t slept. She’d find him at three, at four. At the drawing table. At the window. Once downstairs with every light on, checking the bolts on the black door.

Couldn’t sleep. Too much coffee. He never drank coffee after lunch. She’d let it go.

And the drawings that week. She’d found a stack of them. Not buildings. Doors. Doors with locks. Doors with bolts. Doors with light coming under them. Stairs going up and up.

She’d thought it was work. Was it? It had never once been work.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the phone out of his hands. He let her. He lay there with his hands still up where it had been, in the dark. Then he put them on his chest. She put his phone face down on the floor beside hers.

“What happened in December?”

Nothing.

“Last year. This week. You didn’t sleep. You checked the door. You drew doors. Hundreds.” She looked at his face in the orange light from the street. “Now it’s every night since Christmas. So. What happened?”

A lorry went past. He waited for it to be gone.

“I hadn’t noticed.” He laughed. It wasn’t a laugh. “That it’s the same week. That’s ridiculous. Fifteen years. You’d think I’d notice.”

“Fifteen years since what?”

He turned his head on the pillow.

“The freezer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“I was nine. At the farm.”

She didn’t move.

“It was winter. The week before New Year. There was fighting on the far side of the river. You could hear it at night. Like somebody hammering a few streets over.”

“Who was fighting?”

“I never knew. Nobody told me anything. Ever.” He was looking at the ceiling. “One night there were trucks on the river road. It went right past the farm gate. They were driving with their lights off. You could hear them coming a long way off. Lots.”

“And your uncle—”

“Not really my uncle. Auntie’s husband. He came into my room and picked me up out of bed. Carried me to the kitchen. There was a chest freezer in the corner. Big old white one.”

Her hand found the duvet and closed on it.

“He took the food out. Put it on the floor. Put a blanket in. Put me on the blanket.”

“Was it on?”

“No. He’d pulled the plug. It was just cold. Frost on the sides.” His voice had gone flat. Not his voice at all. “He said don’t make a sound. Whatever you hear. Don’t come out till I open it. And he shut the lid.”

The cranes hummed outside.

“How long?”

“Eleven hours.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“I could hear them. The trucks. They slowed down at the gate. I could hear the engines through the side of the freezer. Men’s voices. Dogs. Then the trucks went on. Then more came. All night.”

“Who did you think they were?”

“For me.” He said it simply. “I’d heard the women in the village. That my father was an important man in the city. That people wanted things from him. So every truck that slowed down, I thought, that’s the one. That one stops. Opens the gate. Comes in the kitchen. Opens the lid.”

She couldn’t breathe properly.

“So I counted.”

“Counted…?”

“To keep quiet. One, two, three, in my head. Every number. When I got to a thousand I dug my fingernail into my palm. In the dark. To keep my place.” He opened his left hand on his chest and looked at it. “Forty marks. I got to forty thousand. I had them on my hand for a week.”

“Raiden…”

“And in the morning he opened the lid. It was light. The trucks were gone. They’d just gone past. All of them. Nobody came in. Nobody had been coming for me at all.”

He was quiet for a bit.

“There was a tin of peaches on the gatepost. On its own, in the frost. Somebody had left it. I never found out who.” His mouth moved. “I went out in my blanket and ate the whole tin standing up. With my fingers.”

✦ ✦ ✦

What were you supposed to say to that? She didn’t know a single right thing. She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and left it there.

It was going like an engine on the dyno.

“Every December.” He put his hand over hers. “The last week. I don’t sleep. I thought I was just bad at sleeping sometimes. And I check the doors. And I draw doors.” A breath. “I didn’t know that either. Until you said.”

She thought about the doors. Hundreds of them. Light coming under every one. Then she thought about the room behind her tool wall.

He’d shown her in April. A light that comes on by itself. A vent. A phone on the wall, on a line that doesn’t go through anybody. You could sit in there three days. Elowen’s shop, with something under the tulips. Every safe room he’d ever drawn, for anyone. Every single one of them a box you could hide in.

With a light. And air. And a phone. And a way out.

“Oh,” she said.

He turned his head.

“Raiden. You built me a freezer with the light on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His chest stopped moving under her hand. Then it went.

He turned over onto his side, away from her, and pushed his face into the pillow, and his shoulders started to shake.

He hardly made a sound. Of course he didn’t. He’d learned that in a box when he was nine. Whatever you hear. His whole back was shaking and the sounds that got out were tiny and terrible, through his teeth, through the pillow.

Her father never cried. The men at the shop never cried. She’d never once heard what it sounded like when somebody did it properly, all the way up from the bottom. It sounded like this. She hated it.

She pressed herself against his back. She got her arm round his chest from behind and put her face in the back of his neck. And she held him the way she held a bike that wanted to go over. All of her. Everything she had.

“I’ve got you.”

She’d never said that to anyone either.

His cold feet were against her shins. She trapped them between her calves without thinking. He made a wet noise that might have been a laugh.

“Your feet are ice.”

“Shut up.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It went on a long time. Lorries. Lights across the ceiling. Down in the street somebody went past singing a New Year song, badly, four days early. She held on.

The shaking slowed. His breathing went ragged, then long, then almost even. His hand came up and held hers on his chest.

“Sorry.” His voice was wrecked.

“Don’t.”

“I’ve never—I haven’t—not since—”

“I know.”

“I’m so tired, Jia. I’m SO tired. I can’t sleep. Every time a truck—”

She thought about it. Words? Useless. She’d never been any good with them.

“Then I’ll count.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went still against her. So she counted.

Out loud, low, against the back of his neck. One. Two. Three. Slowly, with nowhere to get to. The way she counted turns on a bolt by feel, waiting for it to seat.

“You don’t have to…” he whispered, at twenty-three.

“Twenty-four. Twenty-five.”

At a hundred and twelve a lorry went past. His whole back went rigid.

“A hundred and thirteen.” She didn’t stop. “A hundred and fourteen.”

He went soft again.

At four hundred his hand went loose on hers. At nine hundred his breathing changed. Somewhere past eleven hundred she lost her place and started again from a thousand. Did it matter? It wasn’t for getting anywhere.

“…you skipped,” he mumbled.

“I didn’t.”

“You did. You went back.”

“Go to sleep, husband.”

He made a sound, half asleep, that was definitely a laugh.

She got to four thousand and six. By then he’d been asleep for an hour, heavy, on his side, with her arm round him. She lay in the dark and listened to him breathe. Lorries. Cranes. She didn’t sleep at all.

She didn’t mind.

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept until eleven. She went down at seven and opened the black door and worked. At ten there were no coffees on the bench.

She looked at the empty spot by the vice. She looked at it again ten minutes later. It was stupid how much she wanted them. Four coffees she never finished. Stupid.

At half past eleven he came down in his shorts and a jumper. Hair flat on one side. Eyes still puffy. Four coffees in a cardboard tray, from Mrs. Tong’s, because of course.

She pushed herself out from under the black bike on the creeper.

“You’re late.”

“I’m late.” He put the tray on the bench. “Did you eat?”

“Coffee.”

“That’s not food.”

“There wasn’t any coffee.”

“That’s WORSE.” He stood there looking wrecked about it. “I’ll make congee.”

“After.”

“After what?”

“After whatever you came down to say.”

He looked at her. “You counted to four thousand.”

“And six.”

He didn’t say anything else. He lay down on the other creeper, in his shorts, on the cold concrete, and pushed himself under the bike beside her. Where they’d lain the very first time. Shoulder to shoulder, under the sump, in the orange work light.

There was oil on her cheekbone. He wiped it off with his thumb. Then he looked at his thumb and wiped it on his jumper.

“I love you.”

He’d said it a hundred times. At Mrs. Tong’s. On the registry steps. On napkins. In the bath. Never like this, flat on his back on a cold floor, like he’d carried it all the way down the stairs and it was heavy.

She looked at the underside of the engine.

“I know.”

He laughed through his nose and put his hand on hers on the concrete, palm to palm. Then he turned his head on the creeper and she turned hers, and he kissed her. Slow. Tired. He tasted of sleep and Mrs. Tong’s terrible coffee.

When he pulled back she’d forgotten what she was about to say.

“What?”

“Nothing.” She shut her eyes. “Drink your coffee.”

“They’re all yours.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At two she went across to Mrs. Tong’s.

“Peaches.”

Mrs. Tong looked up from the pot. “What?”

“A tin. Of peaches.”

“In DECEMBER?”

“Yes.”

“Who eats peaches in December? Is somebody sick?” The ladle came up. “Is HE sick? He didn’t come for the coffee at ten. He always comes at ten.”

“He’s not sick.”

“Then what?”

Jinx stood at the counter. How did you say it? He was in a freezer when he was nine and somebody left him peaches. She couldn’t. Not to Mrs. Tong. Not to anyone.

“He likes them.”

Mrs. Tong looked at her over the steam. And kept looking. Then she put the ladle down and took her coat off the hook.

“I haven’t got any. I’ll go to the cash-and-carry.” She was already doing the buttons. “Two buses. In this wind. At my age. For peaches!”

“I’ll go.”

“You don’t know which aisle. Sit.” She pointed at the table by the fridge. “Mind the soup. If it boils, it’s your fault.”

The men off the ships watched Jinx mind the soup for forty minutes. Nobody said anything. One of them gave her his newspaper.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then she swung the tool wall out, opened the steel door, and stood in the little concrete room with the light that came on by itself. She went out to the van and got her drill.

He came down at six with the shopping. She was still in there. She’d put up a shelf over the bench, at the height of somebody lying down. On it was a lamp. A proper one, warm and yellow, with a shade and a switch on the cord. You could turn it on and off with your own hand without getting up. Beside it, the tin of peaches.

He stood in the doorway with the shopping bags hanging off his fingers.

She didn’t turn round.

“In case.”

He put the bags down on the workshop floor. A cabbage rolled out. He didn’t pick it up. He came into the room and put his arms round her from behind and put his face in her neck.

The room was tiny. The lamp was warm. He didn’t say anything. She put her hands over his on her stomach.

“Your cabbage is under the lathe.”

“Leave it.” His voice was muffled in her neck. “It’s a cabbage. It’ll live.”

chapters.title: Ten, Walking Home Alone
chapters.desc: January 2023. How a boy of ten copied a road map onto his arm, crossed a border under the ice in a fish truck, and knocked on his father’s door six days later. Then, at two in the morning, she rides to the Walled City for the first time to see that door.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody was coming. So I went to them.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
“There was a goose.”

“A goose.”

“A big grey one. At the farm.” He had his chin on her shoulder. The bath was going lukewarm and neither of them was getting out. “It used to wait for me outside the outhouse. Every morning. Like a bouncer.”

“Did you win?”

“Nobody won against that goose.” He sounded offended on its behalf. “It died of old age. I was there. I cried.”

She laughed into the bathwater and got some up her nose.

After the freezer, he talked about the farm more. Bits. At odd times. Stirring a pot. On the crate while she was under a bike. Auntie’s geese. The brick kiln. The white water tower he’d climbed at seven and been smacked for.

And every time, he stopped at the same place. The tin of peaches on the gatepost. Then he’d say, and then I came home, at ten, and jump straight to the Walled City. The long table. Ah Sim. His sisters.

How, though? He never said how.

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked on a Saturday in January.

They were next door in the dyno room, late. A customer’s big old twin was strapped down on the rolling road. She ran it, changed the jets, ran it again. He sat on the desk with his feet on a chair, watching the line on the screen climb and dip.

The fan and the engine together were deafening.

She shut it off. The drum went on turning by itself. Slower. Slower.

“How did you come home?”

He looked up.

“You always say and then I came home, at ten. You never say how.” She wiped her hands. “Did your father send for you?”

He took a while.

“No. I walked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat down on the edge of the dyno pit.

He didn’t get off the desk. He sat with his hands hanging between his knees.

“After the freezer I stopped waiting.”

“Waiting for what?”

“Somebody to come. My father. Someone from him. Every time a car came down the river road, I ran to the gate. Every time. Nine years.” He shrugged. “Nobody came. Then I lay in the freezer all night thinking somebody had finally come, and it was the wrong people, and they didn’t come either.”

“So…”

“So I thought, fine. Nobody’s coming.” He looked at her. “Nobody was coming. So I went to them.”

“You were NINE!”

“Ten by the time I went. I waited for my birthday. I don’t know why. I think I thought you had to be ten.” He almost smiled. “There was a road map on the kitchen wall. Uncle used it for the trucks. River road. Border town. The main road south. The city at the bottom, tiny.”

“And?”

“I copied it. Onto my arm. In biro.” He turned his left arm over on his knee, like it might still be there. “Every night for a month. Washed it off, drew it again. Till I could see it with my eyes shut.”

She thought of him at her kitchen table in August 2021, after the roof of the noodle factory, drawing every street under the flyover until two in the morning. She’d asked what he was doing. Making a map. Of every way out.

Oh. Of course. Of course that was where it came from.

“And then I went.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“When?”

“First of May. At night. I had a bag of rice cakes, a bottle of water and forty in coins.” He counted it off on his fingers. “Which wasn’t enough for anything.”

“How far?”

“Three days to the border town. I walked the river road in the day. A farmer let me ride on his cart for a bit. First night I slept in a culvert under the road. Second night, a barn. There was a dog. It didn’t bark.” He looked fond. “Good dog.”

“And when trucks came?”

“Off the road. Flat in the ditch. I was very good at that by then.”

Her stomach turned over. She didn’t say so.

“How did you get across?”

“I didn’t. Not properly.” He looked at his hands. “There were fish trucks every morning. From the river. Big boxes on the back full of ice with the fish in. The men at the crossing never looked in the fish. Who puts their hand in a box of ice and fish at six in the morning?”

She stared at him.

“No…”

“Yes.”

“You got IN—”

“Under the top layer. With a sack over me.” He nearly laughed. “With the fish.”

“Raiden!”

“It was only an hour! There were cracks in the box, it wasn’t dark. And I knew it was going to stop.” He said it simply. “That was the difference. In the freezer I didn’t know anything. In the fish truck I had a map on my arm.”

“You could have died.”

“I nearly did. A bit.” He turned his hands over. His long clever hands, checking they were still there. “When I got out I couldn’t feel them for an hour.”

“Did anyone see you?”

“The driver. He saw me climb out. He didn’t say a word. He just took his coat off and gave it to me. And drove me to the main road.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Then what?”

“Two buses. I didn’t have enough for the second one. The driver let me on anyway.” He ticked them off. “Then a lorry driver going south. He bought me noodles and asked me nothing at all. He had an orange shirt. He dropped me at a service station on the edge of the city. I slept in the toilets.”

“And then you walked.”

“Through the whole city. From the north side. It took a day.” He looked up at the ceiling of the dyno room. “I’d never seen it. Not since I was a baby.”

“But you had the map.”

“On the map it was a dot! And then I was standing in the dot, and it was the biggest thing I’d ever seen in my LIFE.”

She could see it. A skinny boy in a coat down to his ankles, mouth open.

“I’d never seen a building taller than the water tower. I walked past the Coastal High-Rise and thought I was dreaming. I stood under a bridge for an hour just looking at how it stayed up.”

“An hour?”

“Maybe two…”

Of course he did. Of course.

“How did you find the Walled City?”

“I asked an old man at a noodle stall. He looked at me for ages. Then he pointed.” Raiden’s voice changed. “Down a lane. Up some steps. And there was a red door with brass on it. I’d never seen it in my life and I knew it. So I knocked.”

“How long had it been?”

“Six days.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The drum had stopped. So had the fan. Somewhere in the lane a cat was crying.

“Who opened it?”

“My father.”

He was looking at the floor.

“It was eleven at night. He opened it himself. There were always people to open doors. I don’t know why it was him.” He swallowed. “He looked down at me. On the step. Fish man’s coat. Map on my arm. Empty bag.”

“Did he know you?”

“He hadn’t seen me since I was three days old.” A breath. “And he knew me. I watched it happen on his face.”

“What did he say?”

“Nothing. For ages. Then, you shouldn’t be here. Then, they’ll take you. That’s why you were there.”

“And you said?”

“I said, nobody came. In the freezer. Nobody came, so I came.”

He looked up at her then.

“And he sat down. On the step. Lin Jian sat down on his own front step like his legs had gone. Put his face in his hands. Then he put his arms round me.”

His voice cracked straight down the middle.

“He didn’t send me back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got up off the edge of the pit. She went and stood in front of him, between his knees, and put her hands on his face.

He let her. His eyes were wet and bright.

“And then you decided to be stupid.”

He laughed. It surprised him. She felt it under her palms.

“That night. Yes.” He leaned his face into her hands. “In a room at the top of the house that had been mine for ten years, that I’d never been in. I lay there thinking, he didn’t send me back. But he wanted to. He said I’d be taken.”

“So?”

“So I had to be somebody nobody would bother taking.” He shrugged in her hands. “In the morning I came down to breakfast as the stupidest boy in the Walled City. And I’ve been him ever since.”

“You weren’t stupid.”

“No. I was ten, and I’d crossed a border in a box of fish with a map on my arm.” His mouth twisted. “I was the least stupid boy in the Walled City. That’s why I had to hide it.”

She stood there holding his face.

A boy in a fish man’s coat on a red step. A big grey man sitting down on that step with his face in his hands. And her own father at his desk under the yellow lamp, writing in his book, who’d never once come looking for her. Four years. Not once.

And Lin Jian. The man in the dark coat. She’d been afraid of him since she was nine, since the black car came down the lane under the flyover and every man in the shop stood up.

He’d opened his own door.

“Show me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Show you what?”

“The door.” She let go of his face. “Show me the door.”

He went rigid under her hands.

“The Walled City?”

“Not inside. I’m not ready for inside.” Her heart was going. “But I want to see the door you knocked on. Stand where you stood.”

“It’s two in the morning.”

“Good. Nobody’ll be there.”

He stared at her. Then he slid off the desk so fast the chair went over.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood in the workshop doorway in his coat, done up wrong. She did the buttons again. Then she zipped his jacket over the coat right up to his chin, so his nose disappeared into the collar.

“I can’t breathe.”

“You can breathe.”

“I can’t SEE.”

“You don’t need to see. You need to sit.”

She put the spare helmet on him. The right way round. She did up the strap. He stood there with his face squashed and his eyes going soft at her over the chin bar.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything!”

“You were going to.”

They went in the sidecar.

The city was empty. Across the harbour bridge with the lights on the water and nothing else on the road. He sat in the chair with the board folded down, not drawing. Just looking up. At every building going past. The way a ten-year-old must have looked up at them, walking through.

She went slowly. She went the long way. Past the Coastal High-Rise. Under the bridge he’d stood under for an hour. She didn’t say why.

He knew why. He didn’t say anything either. His gloved hand came across and gripped her knee, and stayed there.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Walled City was dark and old and steep. A hill of lanes and stairs and walls, houses piled on houses, lamps on brackets.

She’d never been. Not once. She’d been told at nine not to go there. She’d built her whole life around not going there.

And here she was. Riding up its lanes at two in the morning, with Lin Jian’s son in her sidecar.

“Here,” he said, at the bottom of some steps.

She cut the engine. The quiet was enormous.

They went up together. A narrow lane at the top between high grey walls. A lamp. And a door.

Red. Old faded red, nearly brown, with brass studs. A brass lion’s head for a knocker. A brass plate beside it with nothing written on it at all. Two stone steps. A drain.

“That’s it.” He’d stopped at the bottom. “That’s the step he sat on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went up the two steps.

She stood on the top one. Where a ten-year-old in a fish man’s coat had stood at eleven at night and knocked. She looked at the lion. She didn’t touch it.

She put her hand flat on the red wood instead.

Cold. That was all. It was a door. She’d been afraid of it since she was nine. Not this door. The idea of it. The black car, the man in the dark coat, her father’s hands flat on his desk for an hour after.

And it was a door. With a drain next to it. And somewhere behind it, asleep, a big grey man who’d sat down on this step and cried.

Behind her, Raiden’s hand moved. She heard it. The little scrape of his thumb on his ring finger.

She turned round.

He was taking it off. The washer. His thumb was already pushing it over the knuckle. Habit. Of course it was habit. Every Sunday for sixteen months, at this door, he’d done exactly that.

“Leave it.”

He froze.

“He’s asleep, Jia. It’s fine, it’s just—”

“Leave it on.”

He looked at her. He pushed the ring back down. Slowly. All the way.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she came down the steps, he was crying.

Not like after the freezer. He was standing in the lane under the lamp with his hands in his pockets and his face wet. He wasn’t doing anything about it.

“I’d like you to come in.”

“Raiden—”

“One day. I’d like to bring you up those steps and open that door and say this is Jia. This is my wife. To all of them.” He took a breath. “I’d like it more than anything in the world. I’m not asking. You said not yet. I signed. I’m telling you what I’d like. That’s all.”

“I know.”

She looked past his shoulder at the red door. Then back at him.

“One day.”

He shut his eyes.

Seventeen napkins asking for a wedding. Seventeen times not yet. She’d never once said one day. She heard it come out of her mouth. She didn’t take it back.

He opened his eyes.

No joke. He didn’t make a single joke. He took her face in his hands, there in the lane with his father’s door at her back, and kissed her. Careful first. Like she might change her mind. Then not careful at all. Her back hit the old grey wall opposite the red door. Her hands were inside his coat, fists in his jumper. Somewhere a dog barked. A window went yellow high up, and went dark again.

“We’ll wake him,” she said into his mouth.

“He sleeps like a rock.” He kissed her again. Then he pulled back, breathing hard. “Let’s go home. Let’s go home now, or I’m going to do something very disrespectful against my father’s wall.”

“You already did.”

“Something MORE disrespectful.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Halfway down the steps he stopped and got his sketchbook out.

He drew the door. It took him two minutes. The red door, the lion, the two steps, the lamp. And on the top step, a figure standing with her hand flat on the wood. Not her face. Her back. The shaved side of her head. Her hand.

He drew one more line at the bottom and held it up to her under the lamp.

1:50. Will you marry me again? In front of them? (I know. Not yet. I had to.)

“Not yet.”

“I know.” He folded it into his wallet. “Eighteen.”

“You’re counting.”

“I’m an architect. I count everything.”

But she held his hand all the way down the steps to the sidecar. And then all the way across the harbour bridge, reaching across with her left hand and riding with her right.

It was a terrible idea. She did it anyway.

chapters.title: A Commission From the Syndicate
chapters.desc: June 2023. She finds drawings on his table for a house on the Peak, with a steel room inside it, and the client’s initials in the corner. They have their first real fight as husband and wife, and they don’t finish it. Then he asks her to a wedding.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody looks at me. That’s the whole point.” “I looked.” — Raiden Lin and Jinx
chapters.content:
The drawings were on his table when she came up.

He wasn’t. He’d run out of oil halfway through dinner and gone to the corner shop in his slippers. The rice was on. The window by his drafting table was open, and the warm air off the street was lifting the corners of five big sheets. A ruler held them down. A mug. Two of her washers.

She didn’t mean to look. Honestly. She went to shut the window. The top sheet lifted. She put her hand flat on it to stop it going.

And looked.

A house. A big old one, three storeys on a slope, with a garden going down in terraces. Across the top, a few lines that could only be the harbour from very high up. The Peak.

She’d been up there once, delivering a bike to a collector who’d made her use the service entrance. She knew who lived up there.

Every room was drawn in. A long drawing room. Stairs. A kitchen. A library in the middle of the second floor. And a room that wasn’t on the plan at all.

You’d only see it if you knew how he drew. She knew how he drew. The walls round the library were too thick. A few centimetres, all four sides. On the next sheet, the section, there was a gap between the library ceiling and the bedroom floor above. A metre of nothing. And inside it, in his tiny capitals: SEE SHEET 5. DO NOT ISSUE.

She lifted the mug.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sheet five was a room.

Inside the library walls. Behind the bookcases. A steel box, drawn in section, every layer of the walls marked. Steel plate. Something she didn’t know the name of. Concrete. Steel again. A door that was part of a bookcase, hinges drawn in detail, a locking bar, one word: rated. Air from the roof through filters. Its own power. A water tank. A line out.

Like the room behind her tool wall. Except hers was a box to sit in for three days. This one was for somebody people would come for with a lot more than a truck.

The title box. Bottom corner. Where the client’s name went. C.S.

Her hand went cold on the paper.

Everybody in the city knew those letters. At the Docks they said them under their breath or not at all. Chen Si. Head of the Syndicate. The man the Walled City answered to. And the crews in the Slums answered to the Walled City. And her father’s buyers answered to the crews.

The very top of the whole heap she’d climbed out from under. Sitting on the Peak. And her husband was drawing him a room nobody could get into.

Behind her, the rice boiled over.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stairs with the oil and stopped in the doorway.

She hadn’t moved. Sheet five under her hand. Rice hissing all over the stove. Whatever her face was doing.

He looked at her. At the table. He put the bottle on the floor. Slowly.

“Ah.”

He went past her and turned the rice off.

“I was going to tell you,” he said to the stove.

“When?”

“When it was finished.”

“Like the building.”

“Yes.” He turned round. “It’s the old Song house. Aurelia’s family. She grew up there. Her father’s going to lose it this year. When it goes to auction, she’ll buy it back. And Chen Si wants it safe before she ever walks through the door.”

“So he asked you.”

“Zhao told him about Elowen’s floor. Under the tulips.” Raiden put his hands in his pockets. “He came to the firm. Waited in reception for an hour, reading a magazine about kitchens.”

“Chen Si. In RECEPTION.”

“Very politely. Then he said he’d like a room his wife could go into if anyone ever came for her. And he’d like her never to know it was there unless she needed it.” He looked at her. “And could I do that. And I said yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Do you know what he is?”

“Yes.”

“Do you know who my father’s buyers answer to? And who THEY answer to?” Her voice was going up. She couldn’t stop it. “He’s the top. The top of everything I got out of. Everything I’ve kept away from that black door for five years. And you’re drawing him a ROOM—”

“I know.”

“You said you made places safe for your family!”

“Aurelia’s Elowen’s best friend. Chen Si’s Zhao’s brother. Not by blood. Block C, when they were boys. Zhao would die for him. Zhao would die for her.” He breathed. “In my family, that’s family.”

“And who keeps YOU safe?”

That stopped him.

“You’ve drawn the inside of Chen Si’s house.” She picked up the mug. Cold tea slopped over her fingers. “Every wall. Where he hides when they come. On your table. By an open window. Under a MUG.”

“Jia…”

“Anyone who wants that man only has to get to you first. You’re the key. And you left it by the window!”

“Nobody knows. Nobody looks at me. That’s the whole point. That’s why I’m—”

“I looked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He shut his mouth.

She put the mug down too hard. Tea went all over sheet four.

“I looked. On the shipyard road. Half a second and I knew you weren’t a fool. Serafina knew in an hour. Anyone who really looks knows.” She swallowed. “Nobody important’s bothered yet. One day somebody will. Somebody who wants that room. And then they come to the black door. Then they come to you.”

She was shaking. Her whole body. Her fists were shut and she couldn’t make anything stop.

What was this? Why was she shaking?

“I’m frightened.”

She’d never said that out loud in her life. Not once. Not under the flyover. Not anywhere.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came across the room.

She put her hand up flat on his chest. He stopped. His heart was going under her palm as fast as hers.

“Don’t. Don’t do the face. Don’t make a joke.”

“I’m not going to make a joke.”

He wasn’t. She’d never seen his face like that. Not on the gallery stairs. Not at his father’s door.

“I love it.”

She stared at him.

“I’m not going to lie to you. Not about this. I love that room.” He put his hand over hers. “A box nobody can open, inside a library, and nobody knows it’s there. Not the builders. Not the guests. Not Aurelia, till the night she needs it.”

“Raiden—”

“And somewhere in this city a florist went under her own tulips and shut a bolt and lived, because of a floor I drew.” His voice cracked. “I spent eleven hours in a box that wasn’t safe. That’s why I’m good at this. I’m not going to stop. I can’t.”

“I’m not asking you to stop!”

“Then what are you asking?”

She didn’t know.

That was the worst part. She stood there with her hand on his chest and didn’t know, and it made her angrier than anything. So she grabbed a fistful of his shirt and pulled.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came.

He kissed her like he was angry too. Hard. Both hands in her hair. She’d never felt that from him. She kissed him back exactly the same. She walked him backwards across the long room without meaning to, and then they were on the stairs, banging into the wall, one step at a time.

“You left it by the window,” she said into his mouth, on the fifth stair.

“I know.”

“Raiden.”

“I’ll get a safe. A proper one. In the steel room.” He kissed her jaw. “I’ll never leave them out again. I’ll draw it all in my head and only put it on paper in a locked room with the light on. Is that what you want?”

“I want you not to be the key.”

“I can’t not be the key. I’m the key to everything I’ve ever drawn. That’s what drawing it MEANS.” They’d reached the bottom. The workshop, dark, only the street light under the roll-up door. “But I can be a key nobody finds. I’m good at that. I’ve been doing it since I was ten.”

“I found you.”

“You weren’t looking. You nearly ran me over.”

She shoved him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He hit her bench.

The long one under the windows, with the vice on the end. It rattled. A tray of screws went over. He sat back against the edge and she stood between his knees.

“I’m still angry.”

“So am I.”

“What are YOU angry about?”

“That you’re right. You’re always right.” He put his hands on her waist. “You looked at sheet five for two minutes and saw the one thing I’ve been not thinking about for three months. And you’re frightened. I hate that. I did that.” His thumbs pressed in. “I’d rather you threw a spanner at me.”

“I still might.”

“Can I tell you something you won’t like?”

“No.”

“You’re the key too. To me.” He looked up at her. “Anyone who wanted me would only have to get to you. You’ve known since the hospital. That’s half of why you made the terms. Not just because you won’t be owned. Because you know what being my wife makes you.”

She didn’t answer. He was right. She hated it.

“So we’re both keys. We’re both frightened. And we’re both rubbish at saying so.”

“I hate you.”

“No, you don’t.” He stood up off the bench, lifted her, turned, and sat her on it. Screws crunched under her. “Here’s a rule. Nobody goes upstairs till the fight’s finished.”

“Then we’ll be down here all night.”

“That’s the rule,” he said, and kissed her before she could find anything wrong with it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t finish the fight.

They tried. In the gaps.

“I’ll get the safe.”

“You’ll forget.”

“I never forget anything. I remember the colour of the lorry driver’s shirt in 2008.”

“…What colour?”

“Orange.”

She laughed. She didn’t want to. Her head went back against the window and his mouth went to her throat and she laughed anyway, furious.

He got the knot of her overall sleeves undone at her waist. She got two of his shirt buttons and lost patience and pulled. A button pinged off into the dark.

“That was a good shirt.”

“It was a stupid shirt.”

“It was a stupid GOOD shirt—”

She bit his shoulder to shut him up. He made a noise she’d remember for weeks.

“You’ll tell me when you go up there.”

“Every time.”

“Before. Not after.”

He stopped. He lifted his head. In the gold stripe of street light his face was dead serious.

“Before.”

Then the vice handle. He caught it with his elbow and swore. She laughed again. Then she stopped laughing. He had one hand flat on the window behind her head so it wouldn’t hit the glass. He didn’t go slow. Slow was the last thing she wanted. The bench creaked under both of them. He tried to be careful. She hooked her heels behind his back and pulled him in. He gave up on careful and said her name into her neck like a swear word.

It was rough and angry and close. Then it wasn’t angry. It was just close. His forehead on hers in the dark. Her hands spread on his back, holding him there. The stripe of street light across the concrete. Neither of them talking at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she sat on the bench in his torn shirt. He stood between her knees with his face in her neck.

“We didn’t finish.”

“We’ll finish tomorrow.” His voice was muffled. “Or we won’t, and it’ll just get smaller.”

“That’s not how fights work.”

“It’s how ours work. We’re married. I’ve read about it.”

“Where?”

“A magazine. In a reception. About kitchens.”

She hit him. Not hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

He bought the safe that week.

A big grey one bolted to the floor of the steel room. On the third day, without her asking, he took her hand and wrote the code on the back of it in pencil.

Her birthday. Backwards.

She looked at the four numbers on her skin all afternoon. She didn’t wash it off till the next morning.

He never left a drawing out again. He drew the Peak house at the firm in the south, in a room with no windows. And every day he went up to the Peak, before he went, her phone buzzed.

IDIOT: Going up. Back by six.

And at six:

IDIOT: back

She never answered the first one. She always answered the second.

Jinx: Good.

She never deleted them. By Christmas there were forty on her phone, in pairs. Some nights, under a bike where nobody could see, she scrolled through them with her thumb.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Saturday in June he cooked fish.

He took the bones out of hers without looking. Then he kept looking at her across the long table. Then at his plate. Then at her.

She knew that look. The napkin look. But there was no napkin. There wasn’t a pencil anywhere near him.

“Say it.”

He put his chopsticks down.

“Elowen’s getting married.”

“She’s already married.”

“Properly. Again.” He rubbed his face. “She and Zhao did it at a registry in 2020. On a Tuesday. In about four minutes, with Chen Si as a witness and nobody else. Aurelia’s been furious about it for three years.”

“Like us.”

“We had Mrs. Tong. Much better witness. She cried.” He tried to smile and it didn’t work. “So Aurelia’s organising a real one. The flower shop. September. Every Lin. Every friend. My father.” He looked at his hands. “Everybody.”

She didn’t say anything.

“I’d like you to come.”

There it was.

“Not the Walled City,” he said fast. “The flower shop. In the old town. You’ve ridden past it. It’s a shop, Jia. Tulips. A floor I drew. Not the red door. Not inside. A room with flowers and my sisters and some chairs.”

“Raiden.”

“I’m asking. I’ve never asked, not for this. I’ve kept your terms for nearly two years. I’ll keep them longer if you say no. I’ll go on my own and come home and tell you what was wrong with everyone.” He swallowed. “But I’m asking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at him across the table.

The red door. Her hand on it, cold. One day. Zhao behind his newspaper saying well done. A woman she’d never met, who’d gone under her own tulips and shut a bolt and lived. Evangeline, the silent sister, the one he talked about in a voice that went strange.

The message he’d deleted one letter at a time. How tired she was of being that.

Both of them keys. Both of them frightened.

“What do I wear?”

He didn’t move. He sat there with the fish going cold and looked at her. She watched it reach him. Slowly. A building coming up out of fog.

“Whatever you want.” His voice had gone. “The jacket. Your overalls. I don’t care. Jia. You’ll come?”

“I said what do I wear.”

He got up so fast his chair went over.

He came round the table and pulled her out of hers and held her so hard her feet left the floor. Thank you. Into her hair. Over and over. Thank you. Thank you.

She stood in his arms and let him. September. Three months.

She was going to need a better dress.

chapters.title: Jinx Meets the Lin Family Properly
chapters.desc: September 2023. Elowen’s wedding in the flower shop: thirty people standing, a father in his funeral suit, four sisters. “Jinx, my wife, she built Xiao Pan’s bike, don’t touch her tools.” Two years of secret marriage, out in one sentence, and one silent sister who nods.
chapters.epigraph: “You were the little girl under the bench. With the carburettor. I’ve always wondered what happened to you.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
“Don’t tilt it.”

“I’m not tilting it.”

“You’re tilting it, Jia, there’s a corner coming, the corner’s coming—”

“I can see the corner.”

“There are FOUR TIERS back there.”

It was nine on Saturday morning and she was driving a cake across the city at the speed of a funeral.

Elara’s cake. Elara was on a day shift and couldn’t swap, so Raiden had volunteered the van. Raiden had volunteered Jinx’s van. He’d come down the steps with the box in his arms like a man carrying a bomb, and now he was twisted round in the passenger seat with one hand flat on the lid, taking photos.

“Cake in the van,” he narrated. Click. “Cake surviving a pothole.” Click. “Cake judging me.”

“Who are you sending those to?”

“Elara. She said one an hour. I’m doing one a minute.” He took one of his own face with the cake behind it. “She’ll love it.”

“She’ll block you.”

He laughed. His knee was going up and down. It had been going up and down since five.

She parked in the lane behind the flower shop. He carried the cake in through the back door. She didn’t go in.

She sat in the van with the engine running and her hands on the wheel and looked at the back door of Elowen’s. A plain door. A drain. A bin.

He came out ten minutes later with sugar on his jacket and a pink petal stuck to his thumb.

“It’s under the arch. It’s perfect. I nearly died.” He leaned in through her window. “You could come in. Just for a look. There’s nobody in there yet but Elowen and the dogs.”

“Tonight.”

“Tonight.” He kissed her through the window. “Tonight.”

He ate the petal off his thumb on the way back to the van. Then he took a photo of himself doing it.

Raiden: it fell off

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d bought the dress in August and not worn it. Dark red. The same shop in the Coastal High-Rise, the same woman, who’d looked at her shoulders and gone into the back without being asked. It fitted like her own skin. Jinx had tried it on once in front of the long bathroom mirror, looked for a while, and hung it up. A month. She hadn’t looked at it once.

At six she put it on. Then the boots. Then the old black leather jacket with the burn on the cuff.

He was on the edge of the bed in his silver waistcoat, the gear one, doing up his shoes. He looked up.

“The old one.”

“It’s the one I came to the hospital in.”

He stood up. He came and tucked the loose bit of her hair back behind her ear, the bit that never stayed, and left his hand there against her cheek.

“Perfect. You look like you might fix something.”

“I might.”

“Please don’t fix anything at my sister’s wedding.”

His tie was crooked. She grabbed it and yanked it straight. His head went forward.

“Ow.”

“Better.”

There was a black string round his neck. It went in under his collar. She could see the shape of the washer through his shirt.

Neither of them said anything about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They took a taxi. Her hands were shaking and she didn’t trust them on the bars. He held one the whole way and didn’t talk. That was how she knew he was frightened too. Raiden, not talking. In a taxi. For twenty minutes.

ELOWEN’S, on a corner in the old town. A big window full of flowers. She’d ridden past it a hundred times, slowly, and never stopped.

The door was open. Inside, an arch of old dark shipyard timber with the bolt holes still in it. Thousands of tiny lights strung across the ceiling, off. White roses in buckets down both sides. Tulips. People.

Thirty people, standing.

She stopped on the step. He stopped with her. He didn’t pull. He just waited.

She put her hand inside her collar and found the chain. She undid the clasp. It took three tries. Her fingers were useless. She slid the washer off it, the thick one she’d cut on her own lathe two years ago, and put it on her left hand. Over the knuckle. It went where it was meant to go and stopped.

He was staring at her hand.

“Jia… Rings catch in—”

“No engines tonight.”

He made a noise. A cracked, broken little noise, there on the step. Then he hooked his finger in the black string round his neck and pulled it out of his collar and snapped it. Just snapped it. The washer dropped into his palm. He put it on his finger. His hand shook so badly it took two goes. Then he put his arm round her waist and walked her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Everyone!”

The silly party voice. Thirty heads turned round.

“Jinx, my wife, she built Xiao Pan’s bike, don’t touch her tools.”

Nobody made a sound.

She stood in the doorway in his arm with thirty people looking at her. So she looked back. The gala trick. One at a time, until they looked away.

Most did. Not all.

A big grey man by the cooler, in an old black suit too tight across the back, hands clasped in front of him. He didn’t look away. He went completely still. He was looking at her left hand. She knew who he was. She’d known since she was nine.

She kept looking. He kept looking. Ten seconds. Fifteen. Then Lin Jian turned round and walked out of the shop past them, onto the step, and stood there with his back to the room.

“Oh no,” Raiden breathed. “Oh no, no. Baba—”

“Leave him.” Elowen, from somewhere by the arch. Cool as ice.

A woman in gold at the counter. Beautiful, hair up. She looked Jinx over from her boots to her hair and back down, slowly, the way Jinx looked at a frame she was thinking of buying. Then she smiled. Interested.

And at the back of the shop, a woman alone, by the wall, in pale blue. Tall and still, with a face like something carved and long black hair in a knot.

She didn’t look away either. She looked at nobody else. Straight down the whole length of the shop, past the buckets and the tulips and thirty people, at Jinx. No expression at all.

They nodded at the same moment. Once. Evangeline. The paper twin. The one he talked about in the voice that went strange.

You too, the nod said. You’re the other one in this room who’s watching the door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao was by the arch in black, with a pink sugar flower in his lapel. He looked at her for four seconds.

“Hm.”

“Hm.”

Raiden turned a laugh into a cough so badly that Zhao looked at him for four more.

✦ ✦ ✦

She ended up backed into the corner by the cooler. The big glass fridge where the roses were kept cold. People kept being brought to her one at a time. Raiden was beside her, glowing like a lamp. He’d stopped trying to stop himself.

“This is my wife.”

An old man from a tea shop.

“This is my WIFE.”

A detective in a plain coat who said nothing and looked at her hands.

“Have you met my wife?”

Two dogs in ribbons, who sniffed her boots and lay down on them.

“Raiden.”

“Sorry. Sorry! I’ve been saving it up. Two years. It’s coming out all at once.”

A young woman in a hoodie with a laptop against her chest walked straight up to her.

“I’m Eliana, I’m the youngest, I’ve known about you since February 2022, you’re on a spreadsheet.”

She walked off. Jinx stared after her. February 2022? Five months after the registry. How?

“Don’t,” said Raiden faintly. “Don’t ask. Nobody ever asks.”

A small fierce woman stuck her hand out. A hospital lanyard still round her neck over her dress.

“Elara. I’m a surgeon.” Her eyes dropped to Jinx’s hands. The shiny old marks on the backs. “Are those burns from an exhaust? You should use silicone gel.”

Jinx opened her mouth. Elara wasn’t there any more. She’d seen a tall man in glasses come in off the street and forgotten Jinx existed.

“Was that your cake?” Jinx asked the empty air.

“That’s Elara. Always.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then the crowd shifted, and Elowen was there. Green dress. Pearls. Calm and sharp. Raiden’s eyes in a woman’s face, exactly his and nothing like his at all.

Raiden opened his mouth. Elowen looked at him once. He shut it and went to find a drink.

“Your wife.”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“Two years. Next week.”

Elowen’s face didn’t move. Nobody’s face in this family moved unless it wanted to. Jinx was starting to get that.

“Two years.” Elowen’s voice was perfectly level. “He came to Sunday lunch every week. He brought me a shelf. I used to lie awake at night thinking he was lonely.”

“He wanted to tell you. I made him not.” Jinx didn’t look down. “My terms. I wrote them on a napkin.”

“Why?”

“I grew up in a chop shop under the flyover. My father’s buyers bought from your father’s people. When I was nine your father’s car came down our lane and every man in the shop stood up.” She held Elowen’s eyes. “He kept it because I asked. He never broke it once.”

Elowen said nothing. She turned her head and looked across the shop at Zhao by the arch. He felt it. His shoulders moved.

“Zhendong knew.” It wasn’t a question.

“Since the hospital. He took my jacket off the chair before you turned round.” Jinx hesitated. “And there’s a photo on the wall at the noodle shop. From the registry.”

Elowen shut her eyes.

When she opened them there was something in them Jinx knew. She’d seen it in her own mirror every time Raiden bought her something she hadn’t asked for. Fury. Love. The fury losing.

“I’m going to kill him.” Very calm. “After the wedding.” She looked back at Jinx. “Thank you for Xiao Pan’s bike. He cried the first time he rode it. He made me promise not to tell you.”

“I know. I saw.”

Elowen reached out and straightened the collar of the old jacket where it had turned under at the back.

“It suits you. Don’t let Aurelia buy you a new one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lin Jian was still on the step. She went out. She didn’t know why. Her legs went.

She stood beside him. He didn’t look round. Big. Grey. Heavy. Hands in his pockets. A paper cup of tea he wasn’t drinking. She waited to be frightened. She’d been frightened of him for nineteen years.

“You were the little girl under the bench.”

She turned her head.

“At Old Cao’s. Under the flyover.” He was looking at the street. “I went there once. About a debt. 2005, maybe 2006. There was a little girl under the bench in the office with a carburettor in pieces on a newspaper. A screwdriver bigger than her hand.”

“I…”

“While I talked to her father, she put it back together. All of it. Ten minutes. I watched her.” He was quiet. “I’ve always wondered what happened to you.”

She couldn’t move.

“I asked your father, when I left. Who’s the child? He said mine. I said, she’ll be better than all of us.” A breath. “He laughed. I didn’t.”

Her father, after the black car left. His hands flat on the desk for an hour. Not saying anything. She’d thought it was fear. Nineteen years she’d thought that. Was it? She’d never asked.

“My son has a wife.”

“Yes.”

“For two years.”

“Next week.”

“He didn’t tell me.”

“I told him not to.”

He took that. She watched him take it. His jaw worked.

“Does he eat? He never ate when he came home. Ten years old and like a stick. The cook used to chase him round the kitchen.”

“He cooks.”

Lin Jian turned and looked at her.

“Every night. Soup. Fish. Dumplings. He makes his own noodles with a wine bottle. He takes the bones out of my fish. He washes my overalls.” She stopped. “He eats my greens.”

The big grey man looked at her. Then he laughed.

A huge rusty sound, like it hadn’t been used in years. It went right down the street. An old woman across the road opened her window to look. He laughed with his head back on the step of his daughter’s shop, then stopped and wiped his eyes with his thumb.

“Ah Sim taught him. He used to sit on her kitchen step. Every day. The only person in that house he’d sit with.” He shook his head. “I didn’t know he’d kept it.”

“He kept everything.”

“Yes. He would.”

Inside, someone was calling for him. Nine o’clock. He turned to go in. At the door he stopped.

“Come on Sunday. For dinner. Or don’t. The door’s red. He’ll show you.”

“I’ve seen it.”

He looked back over his shoulder.

“He showed me. I stood on the step.”

Something went over his face. Then he nodded. Once. Slowly. Exactly the way Evangeline had. And went in to walk his daughter down the aisle.

✦ ✦ ✦

The wedding took about twenty seconds. An aisle four metres long. Lin Jian walking Elowen down it, stopping halfway, and a question about a lemon tree that Jinx didn’t understand and that had opened Zhao Zhendong’s face like a door. The lights had come on at nine forty-one, all of them at once, gold, and Eliana refused to say why.

Zhao kissed Elowen under them like nobody else was in the shop. Aurelia counted out loud. Raiden whistled through his fingers.

And Lin Jian stepped back and stood beside his son. And Raiden put his arm round his father without even looking. Jinx saw it. Raiden didn’t know she saw.

There was cake. There was champagne in paper cups. Aurelia made a speech about Elowen being wrong about everything for ten years. Elowen made one back. Then their husbands stood up at the same moment, said the same word, mine, and sat down again. Aurelia threw a napkin at hers.

Jinx stood at the back by the wall. Evangeline was next to her. She hadn’t moved since about eleven. They hadn’t said one word to each other. Pale blue and dark red, side by side against the wall, watching the door. Every so often Evangeline’s eyes went to the window. To the roof across the street. And stayed. And came back. Jinx didn’t ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after one, Raiden found her. He put his forehead down on her shoulder and left it there.

“Was it all right? Was it awful? Was it too much?” Into the jacket. “You can tell me. Tell me what was wrong with everyone.”

She thought about it.

“Your father laughed.”

His head came up.

“On the step. I told him you cook. He laughed so loud a woman across the road opened her window.”

He stared at her.

“He doesn’t laugh. He hasn’t laughed since—I don’t know. I don’t REMEMBER him laughing.”

“He laughed.”

His face crumpled. He stood there in front of her in his silver waistcoat under all those little gold lights, trying not to cry and losing.

Beside her, Evangeline turned her head. Looked at her brother. At Jinx. Back at the door.

But the corner of her mouth had moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past two Raiden was carrying both dogs out to Zhao’s car, one under each arm, because they were asleep and Elowen had said so. His father was asleep in a chair by the door with his funeral jacket over his knees. They got a taxi home.

He kissed her at the first red light. Slow, with his hand on her jaw, like he’d been saving it all night in front of thirty people. Then at the second. At the third the driver cleared his throat.

“The lights are green, sir.”

“I know.” He didn’t stop.

“Jia.”

“What?”

“My wife.” He said it to the taxi roof, amazed. “I said it. In front of Baba. Out LOUD.”

“I was there.”

“Thirty people!”

“Go to sleep.”

He fell asleep on her shoulder before the harbour bridge with his mouth open, holding her left hand. His thumb kept going over her ring. Even asleep.

At the black door she paid the driver and got him out and up the stairs. She took his shoes off. She undid the waistcoat. He opened one eye.

“Jia. You came.”

Same as on the stretcher on the Docks road. Exactly the same. Then he was gone again.

She lay down beside him in the dark red dress and the old jacket. She didn’t take any of it off. Not the dress. Not the jacket.

Not the ring.

chapters.title: Her Father Calls After Five Years
chapters.desc: Autumn 2023. A secret car built at night for a friend, and a husband who comes down at two in the morning with soup and asks nothing. Then, in November, a phone call from under the flyover, a photograph of an old camp bed, and a note on the bench.
chapters.epigraph: “Gone to see my father. Don’t come. Back tomorrow.” — a note on the bench, in biro, on the back of an invoice
chapters.content:
“You owe me for the gearbox.”

Serafina, in the black doorway, on the third Saturday in September. Behind her, a quiet man in a dark jacket who looked like nothing at all. That was the problem. Jinx had grown up round men who stood like that, outside her father’s shop.

“No.”

“You haven’t heard what it is.”

“It’s standing in my doorway.” Jinx sat up on the creeper. “Bureau.”

“I can’t tell you that,” said the quiet man.

“I build bikes. Cars are bikes for cowards.”

“I’m not asking you to build a car. I’m asking you to help me build one. Here. Where nobody’s looking.” Serafina put her hands in her pockets. “And he wants out, Jinx.”

Out. Of that. Jinx looked at the man again. Differently.

“One order. No questions. I don’t want to know where, or who’s chasing, or your name.”

“Agreed.”

“And you wash my floor. Every night. Good soap.”

So that was that. She didn’t tell Raiden either. It wasn’t hers to tell.

“Big job on,” she told him. “A customer’s car.”

“A CAR? You? You hate cars.”

“I’m not building it! I’m helping.”

“Cars are bikes for cowards.”

“I know what cars are.”

He let it go. He was good at letting things go when she asked. Better than she was.

Every night after dinner she pulled the roll-up door down. Serafina came. The quiet man came. After the first week a girl turned up with a rucksack, two laptops and a soldering iron. Nobody explained her either.

A grey old Toyota estate with wooden-bead seat covers. Two or three in the morning, every night. Then upstairs, into bed. He’d turn over in his sleep and put his arm round her.

“Mm. You smell of brake cleaner.”

“Go to sleep.”

“Going…”

He never asked.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth Saturday, at two in the morning, he came down. She heard him on the stairs. She looked up from under the bonnet. Serafina froze with the lamp. The girl in the passenger seat stopped soldering. The quiet man was under the car. He didn’t move at all, which was worse.

Raiden stood at the bottom of the stairs in his shorts and a paint-spattered jumper with his sketchbook under one arm. In his other hand, a pot with a lid. He smiled his most cheerful, most useless smile.

“Darling, I’ve brought soup, why is there a man from the Bureau in your garage?”

“I can’t tell you that,” said a voice from under the car.

Raiden stopped.

He put the soup on the bench. He looked at the legs sticking out from under the Toyota. At Serafina with the lamp. At his wife, who had her arms folded and a face that dared him to ask one more thing.

“Right. Right. Lovely.” He sat down on an upturned crate. “I’ll just draw it, shall I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew it for four hours. He didn’t do the voice once. He sat on the crate with the board on his knees and drew while they worked. Serafina kept glancing at him. Jinx didn’t. She didn’t need to. She could hear the pencil.

At six the grey light came in under the roll-up door. He unpinned a sheet and held it up. The car. Dented, beaded, boring. Every chip in the paint. Except he’d drawn the outside like glass, and through the glass you could see all of it. The engine. The brakes. The tank. The girl’s wiring, like a silver web.

At the bottom, in his careful capitals: Nobody’s car, as it really is. R. 2023.

Serafina stared at it. “Nobody’s car.”

“That’s its name, isn’t it? You name all of them. Jinx told me.” He looked at her. “What else would you call it?”

Serafina didn’t say anything. She just looked.

“Nobody. Yes. That’s its name.”

The quiet man had come out from under the car, wiping his hands. Raiden held the drawing out to him.

“Every building I draw has a door in it that nobody knows about. My brother-in-law taught me that. In a flower shop.” He waited until the man took it. “Every car should have one too. This is yours.”

The quiet man looked at the plain grey outside, and everything under it.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me.” Cheerful again already, already turning to the stairs. “Thank my wife. And never bring it back with a hole in it, she’ll kill you, I’ve seen her do it to a carburettor.”

He went back up to bed. The soup was still warm. Ginger and pork. Four bowls. He’d brought four bowls.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning he made her eggs with tomato and didn’t mention it. She stood at the long table watching him slide them onto her plate. Something sat in her chest she didn’t have a word for.

“Thank you.”

“For what?”

He kissed the top of her head and went to his drawing table.

“Raiden.”

“Mm?”

“You didn’t ask.”

“You didn’t want me to.” He sharpened a pencil. “I can ask now if you like. Who’s the man from the Bureau? What’s the car for? Why does Serafina look like she hasn’t slept since August?”

“No.”

“See? Much better not asking.” He blew the shavings off. “Eat your eggs, wife.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The car was finished in October. It went under a cover at the back of the sailmaker’s, next to the dyno. Serafina came once a week to start it and listen to it and leave. Every time, Jinx pulled the door down after her and stood with her hand flat on the cover.

She had a bad feeling. She’d had it since the flower shop. She didn’t know what it was.

People talked. That was what she thought afterwards. Thirty people in a flower shop. Then a restaurant. Then the street. A guitar.

The Lin boy’s wife. A mechanic from the Docks. Built a boy’s bike. Tattoos to the shoulders. Old Cao’s girl, from under the flyover. Lin Jian laughed on the step.

People talked. And somebody listened.

✦ ✦ ✦

The landline rang on a Tuesday in the middle of November. The old black phone by the door. Nobody ever rang it. It was the number from the rope company’s letterhead and nobody had ever changed it. Raiden was in the south at the firm. She was at the bench with a set of carbs in pieces on a rag.

She picked it up.

“Jia.”

She stood with the phone in her hand and didn’t breathe. Five years and eleven days. She hadn’t heard that voice since the night she left. He’d stood in the yard under the flyover with his hands hanging and watched her load the lathe and said you’ll come back. She’d said no. She’d driven away.

It sounded older. Thick. Something heavy on his chest.

“How did you get this number?”

“The paper. Under the bike. Someone brought it to the shop.” A breath. “Best in Show. I saw it.”

She said nothing.

“Jia. I need you to come.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Why?”

He told her. Badly. In pieces. In the silences she could hear the flyover. Trucks. The concrete humming. Her whole childhood was in his silences.

“The old buyers stopped coming. Since the spring. Something at the top.”

“What?”

“I don’t know. Nobody tells me. They stopped coming, and the protection stopped with them.” He breathed. “Then a new crew came. From the other side.”

“Who?”

“A man called Guo.”

“What does Guo want?”

“He bought my debts.”

“What debts?”

A long silence.

“The rent. Since spring. Parts. Money I borrowed in the summer, for the roof.” Another silence. “And some I lost. At cards. In the back of the place on the corner.”

She shut her eyes.

“How much?”

He told her.

More than he’d ever see in his life. Not much for her. She could nearly pay it out of the tin under the bench. She opened her mouth to say so.

“He doesn’t want money.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Then what?”

“Bikes. Twelve. Out of what comes through the yard.”

“Stolen.”

“New numbers. New papers. Good ones, fast ones.” He couldn’t say the rest. She said it for him.

“The kind nobody catches.”

“He knows what they called you. Somebody told him.” Her father’s voice was shaking. “If Jinx builds him twelve bikes, the debt’s gone. And if not—”

“If not what?”

“He’s been here. Every night. Him and his men. They sleep in the office. On your—” He stopped. “On your camp bed. I kept it. I never took it down.”

Her whole body went cold. Toes first.

“Please… Jia. Just come and talk to him. Once. I’m sixty-one. They’ll take the shop. They’ll—” His voice broke. She had never once heard it break. “Please. You’re the only one he wants.”

“No.”

She put the phone down.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stood there. Then she went back to the bench and picked up a carburettor and looked at it. What had she been doing to it? She couldn’t remember.

Her mobile buzzed. A number she didn’t know. No words. A photo.

The office at the shop. She’d have known it anywhere. The little square window with the wire in the glass. Her father’s desk. The yellow lamp.

And under the window, the camp bed. Hers. Green canvas, rusty frame, the burn on the corner where she’d put a soldering iron down at eleven. Somebody had been sleeping in it. The blanket was thrown back.

On the pillow, a photograph. Pinned to the canvas with a screwdriver driven straight through it.

Raiden. On the step of the flower shop. Silver waistcoat. Laughing. His arm round a woman in an old leather jacket. Her face had been scratched out with something sharp.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember sitting down. She was on the concrete with her back against the bench leg and the phone in her hand. The carburettor in pieces above her on the rag. She couldn’t stop looking. At the screwdriver. Through his laughing face. Into the pillow she’d slept on until she was twenty-two.

Everyone I love is something somebody else can take.

He’d said that. In June 2021. Thirty-first floor, arm in plaster. She’d said I can stand in front of myself.

She’d been so sure. The danger was the Walled City. The Lins. Being his. Keep her side and his side, never go through the red door, and they’d both be fine.

And it was her side. All along. Her father. Her shop. Her camp bed. She’d walked into a flower shop and put a ring on in front of thirty people. And somebody under the flyover had heard. And now there was a screwdriver through her husband’s face.

You’re the key too, he’d said. On the bench in June. Anyone who wanted me would only have to get to you.

She hadn’t believed him. Why hadn’t she believed him?

✦ ✦ ✦

She got up. She put the carburettor back together. Slowly, by feel. Every jet, every screw, the float. Her hands needed something. It was the only way she’d ever known how to think.

She went up and changed. Overalls. Boots. The old jacket. She came down and stood in front of the tool wall.

She left the steel room shut. Nothing in there she needed. She took down the thirteen. A set of picks. Her good screwdrivers in their roll. A torque wrench. She put them in her old bag. The one she’d left the shop with five years ago and never carried since.

Thursday. He’d be in the south all day on Thursday. He always was. She’d go under the flyover. She’d find out what Guo wanted. Give it to him, or not. Come home. And he’d never know there’d been a screwdriver through his face.

Go before they see you. The hospital. The service lift. She’d thought he was ashamed of her. Three weeks she’d hated him for that. And here she was. Doing it. Exactly that.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stairs at seven with the shopping and stopped at the top. She was at the stove. That never happened. Frying eggs. Badly.

“You’re cooking.”

“Eggs.”

He put the bags down. He came and looked into the pan. Burnt at the edges. Raw in the middle.

“Jia. What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Jia.”

“I said nothing.”

“You’re frying eggs.”

“People fry eggs!”

“You don’t.” He looked at her. The crack-in-the-marble look. Of course he could see something. When had she ever hidden anything from him? She’d never even tried. And now she was standing there with her face doing nothing, and he was watching her do it. The gallery stairs. The hospital. Everything he’d done for thirteen years before he met her.

“I burnt them.”

“You did.” He kept looking. He didn’t push.

He took the spatula out of her hand and turned the gas off. He tipped the eggs in the bin. Then he put his arms round her from behind and rested his chin on top of her head.

“I’m here. Whatever it is. When you want. Or never.”

She stood in his arms and didn’t tell him. It was the worst thing she’d ever done.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday he left for the firm at eight. She kissed him at the door. Too long.

“What’s that for?”

“Nothing.”

He looked at her. Then he got in the taxi. He turned round in the back seat and watched her through the rear window all the way up the street.

She went back in. Before. Not after. She’d made him promise that, on the bench. And he’d done it every single time. Going up. Back by six.

She took an invoice off the pile and turned it over and found a biro. Capitals, because her handwriting was terrible. GONE TO SEE MY FATHER. DON’T COME. BACK TOMORROW. J. She put it on the bench under the thirteen’s empty hook.

The anchor woman was on her step across the street when Jinx wheeled the black bike out.

“Where are you going?”

“North.”

“With that bag?” The anchor woman looked at it. She’d seen that bag once before, five years ago, on the day Jinx arrived. “Does he know?”

“Go inside.”

“Hah.” She didn’t go inside.

Jinx rode north toward the flyovers. Exactly the speed limit. The whole way.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home before five. He didn’t know why. He’d sat at his desk drawing a staircase all morning and getting the risers wrong. After lunch he’d put the pencil down and thought, home. Just that.

Roll-up door down. Black bike gone.

“Nine o’clock,” said the anchor woman, from her step. She hadn’t moved all day, by the look of the cold tea beside her. “North. With the old bag.”

“The old bag?”

“The one she came with.” She looked at him. “She told me to go inside.”

“Did you?”

“Hah.”

He let himself in by the side door. Dark. Cold. Tidy. She never left it tidy.

The note.

He read it three times in the grey light. Then he looked up at the tool wall. At the empty hook between the twelve and the fourteen.

He knew. All of it, at once. Her at the stove, burning eggs, her face doing nothing. The kiss at the door. And August 2021, a roof across the road from a shop under the flyover. Her boots over the drop. Something happened when I was seventeen. I’m not telling you that one. Her father in the little square window, writing in his book.

He didn’t sit down. He wasn’t going to ring anyone. Not yet.

He went upstairs to his drawing table. He opened the long flat drawer at the bottom, the one he never opened in front of her. He took out a roll of paper and spread it on the table and weighted the corners with her washers.

The map. He’d started it the night of the roof, at her kitchen table, under the bare bulb. Every street under the flyovers. Every lane, alley, fire escape, gap in a fence.

And then two years of evenings she’d never known about. The city archive had the plans of most of the buildings in the Slums of the Industry. He’d read every one. Walls. Stairs. The drains under the lanes. Which roofs joined, and which didn’t.

He’d never asked her if he could. Why would he? It was her childhood. It was the place that had hurt her. Of course he knew every way into it.

At the end of a lane under the lowest flyover, a long low building. Three roll-up doors. A little square window in the side.

Don’t come. He rolled it up and put it inside his jacket.

“No,” he said to nobody, and went down the stairs two at a time.

chapters.title: The Men Who Own Her Father
chapters.desc: Under the flyover: a polite man in reading glasses, a debt to be paid in stolen bikes, and a dead brother’s motorbike that hasn’t run in nine years. Then her useless husband wanders in through the scrap heap with a bag of dumplings and a floor plan in his jacket.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m terribly sorry. I think I’m lost. Is this the right flyover?” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
Nothing under the flyover had changed. Except her father. Same lane. Same pillars going down into the ground. Same orange lights that never went off, because the sun never got in. Three roll-up doors, all up. CAO MOTOR REPAIR. Bikes on the pavement. The trucks overhead, which you stopped hearing after a day and heard again the second you came back.

He was standing in the middle door. He’d seen her coming down the lane. He stood with his hands hanging at his sides, exactly how he’d stood the night she left. She stopped the bike in front of him. Killed it. Took her helmet off.

He was old. That was all she could think. Five years and he’d got old. Grey hair gone white. Shoulders come forward. Those big hands she remembered on every engine, on her head once when she was small, were spotted now. They shook a little.

His mouth worked.

“Jia.”

“You got old.”

“…Yes.”

“Where is he?”

✦ ✦ ✦
