Guo was in the office. In her father’s chair, at her father’s desk, under the little square window with the wire in the glass.

Thin. Fifties. Grey shirt buttoned to the neck. Reading glasses. Drinking tea out of one of her father’s chipped cups. He looked like an accountant. He looked like the man who came round for the rent on a scooter.

Two men behind him. A big one by the door with a scar through his eyebrow. A small one sitting on her camp bed with his boots on the green canvas, right by the soldering-iron burn.

Guo put the cup down.

“Miss Cao. Or Jinx? Which do you prefer?”

She said nothing.

“Jinx, then.” A nice smile. Really nice. “Sit. Have some tea. Your father’s tea is terrible, but it’s hot.”

“I’ll stand.”

“As you like.” He folded his hands. “I’m so glad you came. Your father thought you wouldn’t.”

“I nearly didn’t.”

“But I told him. A woman who builds a bike for a boy with burnt hands and won’t take his money isn’t going to let her own father lose his shop.” He peered at her over the glasses. “That’s what I heard. That you’re good to people.”

“So?”

“So it’s a weakness, you know. In business.”

She looked at the small man.

“Get OFF that.”

The small man looked at Guo. Guo lifted one finger. The small man got off the bed and went and stood by the wall.

“There. We can be civilised.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Twelve bikes.” Guo smiled. “From what comes through the yard. Built well enough that nobody ever traces them.”

“And then?”

“And then twelve more.” Pleasantly. “I won’t lie to you. There’s money in it, done properly. Nobody’s done it properly under here since you left.”

“He has.”

“Your father?” Guo took the glasses off and polished them on his shirt. “He’s old. His hands shake. The last three he built me were picked up by the police inside a week.” He put the glasses back on. “You were bad luck for the police. That’s what they told me. I’d like some of that luck.”

“I don’t do that any more.”

“I know. You build beautiful bikes for rich men by the Docks. I saw the newspaper. Best in Show.” He reached into his shirt pocket. “And you have a husband. A rich one. With a famous father. I saw that too.”

He put a photograph on the desk between them. Face up. The flower shop step. Raiden laughing in his silver waistcoat. Her face scratched out.

“Such a happy boy. Everybody says so.” Guo tapped it. “Not very bright, they say. But happy.”

She didn’t move. She’d learned that here. In this office. Before she could read. The man who moves first loses.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I won’t build you twelve bikes.”

Guo waited.

“I’ll build you one. Tonight. Something nobody else can.” She held his eyes. “When it’s done, the debt’s gone. My father’s free. You never come in this shop again. And you never say his name.” She put one finger on the photograph. On Raiden’s face. “Or look at this again.”

Dou shifted his weight by the door. Out in the yard somebody dropped a spanner. Guo looked at her over his glasses. On and on. Then he smiled. A different smile. Interested.

“One bike.”

“One.”

“Something nobody else can do.” He got up, slowly. Came round the desk. Went past her, close enough that she smelled tea and soap. “Come with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a bike in the back corner of the yard. Under a tarp. The corner by the wall where the scrap went, where she’d never been allowed as a kid because of the rats.

Guo pulled the tarp off himself. Her stomach dropped. A Kawasaki. A seventies 750 two-stroke triple. Three cylinders side by side. Three chrome pipes out the back like the barrels of a gun. They used to call them widowmakers. Blue, once. Now dust, rust and pigeon droppings. Flat split tyres. A dead leaf in the air box.

“My brother’s.”

His voice had changed.

“He rode it twenty years. Loved it more than his wife. Then he died. Not on it. In a hospital, of something boring.” Guo looked at it. “It’s sat here ever since. Your father said he’d fix it for nothing, as a favour, and put it in the corner and never touched it.”

“Seized?”

“Every mechanic says it’s finished. Pistons rusted into the barrels. I’d need a new engine. There aren’t any. Sell it for parts, they say.”

He put his hand on the tank. Lightly. On the dust.

“Make it run. By six in the morning. If I can start it and ride it once round this yard, the debt’s gone. Your father’s free. You never see me again.” He took his hand off. “If not, you build me twelve. And then twelve more. And I keep the photograph.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She crouched by the engine. She didn’t touch it. Three barrels, fins packed with dirt. Three carburettors, crusted green. Chain rusted solid in a curve like a fossil.

Done properly? A week. Two. Clean workshop. Right parts. The dyno. Nobody watching. She thought about the screwdriver through his face.

“Parts?”

“My brother kept everything. There’s a box. Rings, gaskets, seals, plugs. For a rebuild he never did.”

“I need my father’s tools. The big lamp. Nobody in the yard.”

“You’ll have Dou.” The man with the scar. “By the door. All night. In case you get ideas about leaving.”

Dou nodded at her. Like a waiter.

“Six o’clock, Miss Jinx.” Guo was already walking back to the office. “I’ll bring tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She started in the middle of the afternoon. She dragged the bike out under the big lamp on its flat tyres, rims scraping. Up on a stand. She got her father’s tool chest out of the shop. Red drawers. Every tool still in the drawer it had been in when she was five.

Her father stood in the shop doorway and watched. He didn’t come out.

The heads first. The nuts were rusted and she had to heat every one with the torch and wait. Under the heads, the tops of the pistons. Brown. Fused. She tried them. Nothing.

So she soaked them, and sat on an oil drum in the yard, and waited for the oil to get down into the rust.

Dou stood by the door with his arms folded.

“Won’t go,” he said, after an hour. “Nobody can make that go.”

“Then you’ll get a good night’s sleep!”

“I don’t sleep on jobs.”

“You slept on my bed.”

He shut up. When she tried again, she warmed the first barrel. Not much. Too much and it was ruined. She put a block of wood on the piston and hit it. Once. Hard.

It moved. A millimetre. She felt it in the mallet before she saw it. She sat back on her heels under the lamp and breathed for the first time in an hour.

✦ ✦ ✦

By nine she had all three barrels off. Three pistons on their rods. Rusted. Scored. Ugly. She held each barrel up to the lamp and looked through it. Brown inside. Not cracked.

Not cracked. She could hone them. New rings from the dead brother’s box. Then, if the crank was all right. If the seals were. The ignition. Three carbs. The oil pump.

How many ifs was that? Too many. She put the first barrel in the vice and started honing.

It was always dark under the flyover. It got darker. The orange lights buzzed. Trucks went over. Her father had gone into the office. Through the little square window she could see him at the desk with the lamp on. Not writing. Just sitting. Guo had gone somewhere. So had the small man. Dou stood by the door.

She held the first bore up to the light. Clean. Grey. Cross-hatched, the way it should be. She laid it on a rag. She’d just started the second when she heard a voice in the lane.

✦ ✦ ✦

A cheerful voice. Loud. Lost.

“Hello? Hello! Sorry. Excuse me. I’m terribly sorry. I think I’m lost. Is this the right flyover? There are rather a lot of them. I’ve been under three.”

Her hands stopped on the hone. Dou turned round in the doorway.

And round the end of the scrap heap, from the one direction nobody ever came from, came Raiden.

There was a gap back there. Between the wall and the pillar, behind the heap. She’d squeezed through it every day of her childhood to get to school. She’d thought nobody else alive knew it was there.

Good grey trousers. The clean brown shoes, not clean any more. Hair everywhere. A smear of something on his cheek. A paper bag in one hand that said Mrs. Tong’s.

He stopped in the middle of the yard under the lamp and looked round with his mouth open. Bikes. Pillars. Scrap. A tourist in a cathedral.

“Oh! Oh, THERE you are.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dou had a knife. She saw it come out of his jacket. Short. It turned in his hand. She was on her feet with the hone in her fist.

Raiden looked at Dou. At the knife. He smiled the enormous, stupid, shining smile he wore for rooms full of strangers.

“Oh, hello! I’m so sorry. I’m the husband. I’m lost. Well, not now, I’ve found her, but I WAS lost. I got the bus. Two buses. I’ve never been on two buses.” He held up the bag. “I brought dumplings. She never eats when she’s working. Would you like one? They’re pork.”

Dou looked at him.

The bag. The brown shoes. The waistcoat under the jacket. The face. Jinx watched him look, and watched him decide, the way everyone always decided, in about two seconds.

The useless one. The happy one. Not very bright. The knife went down. Not away. Down.

“How did you get in?”

“Through there?” Raiden pointed vaguely behind him. “There’s a sort of… gap. I think a cat showed me. There was definitely a cat.” He beamed. “Is she in trouble? She left a note. It said don’t come. She always says that. She said it about the dumplings.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden had already counted. Two men in the yard when he came round the heap. One now. The big one with the scar, right hand, knife held low like a man who’d used it before and not often. Weight on his heels. Slow, then.

One door to the lane. One to the office. The gap behind him. A window with wire in the glass, and an old man behind it. Somewhere past the office, a third roll-up door, half down.

And his wife, standing under a lamp with a hone in her fist, black to the elbows, looking at him like she was going to kill him.

She was alive. She was standing up. Everything else was arithmetic. He went on smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo came out of the office drying his hands on a handkerchief. He looked at Raiden under the lamp with his paper bag. Jinx watched him work out who it was. Watched him smile.

“Mr. Lin.”

“Hello! Do I know you? I’m so sorry. I meet so many people. Was it a party? I’m hopeless with faces.”

“We haven’t met.” Guo came close. He looked at Raiden over his glasses the way he’d looked at Jinx in the office. “But I’ve seen your photograph.”

“Oh, the newspaper? That was her, really. I was just holding the trophy.”

Guo laughed. A real laugh. Delighted. He looked from Raiden to Jinx with the hone in her fist, and back. He laughed again. He tucked the handkerchief away.

“Well, well. You came all this way. On two buses. To bring your wife dumplings.” He shook his head. “You’re very welcome, Mr. Lin. Stay as long as you like.” He turned. “Dou. A chair for Mr. Lin. He’s our guest.”

At the office door he looked back at Jinx over his shoulder. Now I’ve got both of you.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden sat on the oil drum. He put the bag on the bench by the vice and took out a carton. Took the lid off. Split the chopsticks. Opened the little packet of chilli oil. Quick and neat, like the very first morning in her garage.

Dou went back to the door with the knife. She looked down at him.

“I said don’t come!” Her voice was shaking. Was it fury? She didn’t even know. “I wrote it. In CAPITALS.”

“I know.” He didn’t look up. The silly smile stayed on, for Dou. His voice didn’t. Low. Just for her. “You also wrote it on the back of an invoice for a clutch you haven’t charged for. You left the thirteen’s hook empty. And you burned eggs on Tuesday.”

“Raiden—”

“Eat something.” He held up the chopsticks. “You’ll need your hands.”

She took them. She didn’t eat.

“How did you find the gap?” A whisper. “I used it to get to school. Nobody knows about that.”

“I do. Two years.” He looked up, finally. One second. His eyes were steady as a level. “It’s on the archive drawings from 1974.”

“The ARCHIVE?”

“There was a drain. They filled it in, the wall settled, the pillar didn’t.” He went back to the carton. “I told you. I made a map of every way out.”

She stood there holding the chopsticks.

“Every way in, too. It’s the same map.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She ate four dumplings standing up. She didn’t taste one. She was shivering. She hadn’t noticed till now. November, under a flyover, in a vest, with her jacket over the drum hours ago. He noticed. Of course he noticed. He took his own jacket off and put it round her shoulders. He did up one button at the front. He didn’t say a word.

“You’ll be cold.”

“I’m never cold. I’m a Lin. We run hot.” He was already shivering. “Hone your thing.”

She put the second barrel back in the vice. He got up off the drum. He went to her father’s red tool chest. Top drawer. The right one, first time. He took out the big rubber torch that had lived in that drawer since before she was born. He switched it on. He came and stood beside her at the vice and held it steady, exactly where she needed it. On the inside of the bore.

She hadn’t told him where. He’d watched her for two and a half years.

“Is it going to run?” Under the trucks.

She looked at the bore in the light.

“I don’t know.”

“All right.” He didn’t move the torch a millimetre. “Then I’ll hold the torch until you do.”

chapters.title: She Builds Her Way Out
chapters.desc: One night, one engine, three cylinders that haven’t moved in years. Her husband holds the torch, her father comes out of the office to point at the wrong jet, and just before six the widowmaker coughs.
chapters.epigraph: “Lie to it. Just this once. We’ll fix it properly after.” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
“Your arm.”

“It’s fine.”

“You’ve had it up for two hours.”

“It’s FINE, Jia. Keep going.”

By midnight she had all three bores honed. They sat in a row on the clean rag, grey and cross-hatched under the torch. She put her hands flat on the bench either side of them and breathed. Then she picked up the first piston.

The old rings were rusted into their grooves. Of course they were. She broke them out with a pick, in brown flakes, and scraped every groove clean with a bit of broken ring. Her father had shown her that when she was six. Three pistons. Two grooves each. An hour.

Raiden didn’t move the torch once. The new rings were in the dead brother’s box, wrapped in oiled paper. The paper had a date on it. 2013. She unwrapped one and it was perfect. Bright. Ten years in a box under a flyover, waiting for a man who died.

She held it up to the light. Something went through her. She didn’t have time for it.

“He was going to do it himself. The brother. He bought all this.”

“And then he got ill.”

“Yes.” She fitted the ring. “And then my father said he’d do it, and put it in the corner.”

“Did your father ever finish anything?”

“Me.” She didn’t look up. “He finished me. Then he stopped.”

Raiden didn’t say anything. The torch didn’t wobble.

✦ ✦ ✦

At one she tested the crankcase. This was the bit that would kill it. On a two-stroke the crankcase was part of the engine. If a seal on the crank had gone, the engine would suck air, run hot, and seize again in a minute. Or never start.

And to change a crank seal on a triple you split the cases. A day’s work. She didn’t have a day. She sealed it up and pumped it full of air and watched the gauge.

It held.

Not perfectly. It dropped. Slowly. She went round with soapy water and the torch, one cylinder at a time. A triple was really three engines sharing a crank.

The left held.

The middle held.

The right one dropped. She sprayed the end seal by the ignition cover, and there it was. A tiny froth. Like someone breathing out. She sat back on her heels.

“That’s bad?”

“It’s a bit bad.”

“How bad is a bit?”

“It might run. It might run for an hour. It might not start.” She wiped her hands. “Or it might start, and seize, and throw a rod through the case. And take my leg off.”

“Ah.”

“I could seal round it. From the outside.” She looked at the froth. “It’s not a fix. It’s a lie. It’ll hold for a day.”

“We only need a morning.”

She looked up at him. Crouched beside her with the torch, in his ruined trousers, grease on his face, pencil on his fingers. Tired. Calm. Completely calm.

“Lie to it. Just this once. We’ll fix it properly after.”

She lied to it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two the barrels went back on. Then the heads. She torqued them down a bit at a time, in a cross, with her own wrench out of her bag.

He held the torch. Dou watched from the door. The trucks went over. In the little square window her father was still at the desk. Still not writing.

Three carburettors next. Crusted green inside. Jets blocked solid. Floats stuck to their pins. She took them apart on a rag and laid out every tiny piece in three rows so nothing got mixed up. Into a tin of cleaner from her father’s shelf.

“What’s that one?”

“A float.”

“What does it do?”

“Floats.”

“Jia.”

“It sits in the fuel and goes up and down and shuts the valve when the bowl’s full.”

“So… it floats.”

“I SAID it floats.”

He nodded seriously. “I’m learning so much.”

While they soaked she straightened up. Her back cracked so loud Dou looked over. She shut her eyes.

When she opened them Raiden had put the torch down on the vice and was standing right in front of her. He took her face in his hands, grease and all. And kissed her. Once. Hard and quick, under the lamp, with Dou watching.

“For luck.”

“Luck isn’t REAL—”

“Don’t tell me luck isn’t real. I know what they call you.”

She looked at him. Then she grabbed him by the collar and pulled him back and kissed him again. Longer. Properly. Dou coughed and looked at the ceiling.

She let go.

“I need the light back.”

He picked up the torch. His ears were red.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was blowing out the second carb’s jets when the office door opened. Her father came out into the yard. Slowly. He stopped at the edge of the lamplight.

He didn’t look at Dou. He looked at the bike, barrels and heads back on. At the bench, the three rows of tiny parts on the rag, laid out exactly how he’d taught her. Smallest at the top. And at Raiden. Holding the torch.

“Who’s this?”

He said it to her. Not to Raiden. Like Raiden was a part on the bench. She didn’t look up from the jet.

“Raiden. My husband.”

Her father went stiff. She felt it from across the bench. His eyes went to Raiden’s hand on the torch. To the steel washer on his finger. Then back to her neck, where the chain was.

“Husband.”

“Two years.”

“You never said.”

“You never rang. Five years.”

“Jia…”

“Don’t.”

Raiden’s torch didn’t move. Not a millimetre. She loved him for it so much it hurt.

“Lin Jian’s son. Before you ask.”

That did it. She watched it go through her father. The black car coming down the lane. The big man in the dark coat. The men standing up. His own hands flat on the desk for an hour afterwards.

“I’ve heard,” said her father slowly. “About him.”

“Everybody has!” Raiden’s party voice. Bright as a bulb. “It’s mostly true. I’m hopeless. I’ve never fixed anything in my life.”

“He hasn’t.” Jinx didn’t look up from the jet.

“I’ve been holding this torch for five hours and I don’t know what any of it does.” He beamed. “How do you do, sir. You’ve got a wonderful tool chest. Every drawer in order. I could tell straight away where she learned it.”

Her father looked at him. Then at the red tool chest. Then he came across the yard. An old man with spotted hands that shook. He stood at the bench beside her and looked down at the three rows.

“Middle jet’s the wrong size.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She stopped.

She picked up the middle jet. Held it to the lamp. Read the tiny number stamped on it.

He was right. One size up. Somebody, sometime, maybe the brother, had put the wrong one in the middle carb. Built like that, the middle cylinder would run rich and foul its plug and cough. And she’d have spent an hour at dawn going mad trying to find out why.

How had he seen that? From the doorway? From across a yard?

“There’s a box. Of jets. Third drawer. At the back. Left side.” He didn’t look at her. He looked at the jet in her fingers. “Tobacco tin.”

She went to the red chest. Third drawer. Back. Left. A tobacco tin with a ship on the lid. The same one. It had been there when she was five. Inside, hundreds of jets in twists of paper, every one labelled in his slow, careful writing. She found the right one and came back.

He’d picked up the float from the third carb. He was turning it in his fingers. The way she turned a bolt.

“This is stuck. Pin’s bent. Straighten it, don’t change it. The new ones are rubbish.” He put it down. “Like I showed you.”

“I know.”

“I know you know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t stay.

He watched her fit the right jet. Then he turned and went back across the yard. At the office door he stopped and looked back. Not at her. At Raiden.

“You’ve been holding that five hours.”

“Five hours and twelve minutes, sir.”

Her father looked at him a while longer. Then he went in and shut the door. Through the little square window she watched him sit down under the lamp and put his face in his hands. She looked down at the carburettor.

Raiden moved the torch an inch, to where she was about to need it. He didn’t say anything.

“Don’t,” she said.

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were going to say something nice about him.”

“I was going to say your nose is running.”

She wiped it on her shoulder. He laughed under his breath. The torch stayed exactly where it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

The carbs went on. Then the ignition. No points on this one. An early electronic box under the tank that nobody under the flyover had ever trusted. She cleaned every connector. She set the timing one cylinder at a time, three times, by the book.

New plugs from the box. Oil in the tank. She bled the pump and watched the oil creep through the little clear lines to each cylinder. Slow. Like something waking up.

The brother’s battery had been dead since 2014. She put the battery off her own bike on it, on leads. Fresh fuel from the can. New tubes in the rotten tyres. They held. Just.

“Can I do anything?”

“You’re doing it.”

“I’m holding a torch.”

“Exactly. Nobody’s ever held one right for me before.” She didn’t look up. “Not once. Not in this yard.”

He went quiet. The torch didn’t move. Then she stood back.

“Is that it?”

“That’s it.”

“Does it look like it’ll run?”

She looked at it. Dust. Rust. Pigeon droppings. Pitted brown chrome. She hadn’t touched the outside at all.

“It looks like it’s been in a corner for nine years.”

“So, yes?”

“So I don’t know, Raiden.”

He nodded, like that was a perfectly good answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Is it morning?”

“Somewhere.”

“How can you tell?”

“Listen.”

Dawn didn’t happen under the flyover. There was no sky to happen in. But the trucks changed. The long night ones gave way to vans and the first buses. The noise went higher and busier. At the end of the lane a woman was rattling up the shutter on a breakfast stall.

Guo came out with a cup of tea. The small man behind him. Dou straightened up by the door. Her father came out last and stood in the office doorway with his hands at his sides. The night she left. Exactly that. Guo looked at the bike. He sipped.

“Well, Miss Jinx.”

She didn’t answer.

Choke on, all three. Fuel on. She waited, counting, while the bowls filled. She turned the key. A red light came on on the dash for the first time since 2014, and Guo’s face moved. Just slightly. She put her boot on the kick-start.

Behind her, she felt Raiden step back. Out of her way. Torch off.

She kicked it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nothing.

A cough. An old man clearing his throat in another room. Nothing.

She kicked again.

Cough. Cough. A puff of blue out of the left pipe. Nothing. Guo drank his tea. She stood with her boot on the kick-start and listened. Not to the engine. To what it had just done. Two coughs. Left pipe only. Left cylinder firing a bit. The other two not.

Flooding. Of course. Choke on too long on a warm morning. The middle and right were wet.

She knocked the choke off the middle and right. She held the throttle wide open, which you weren’t meant to do. She kicked it four times. Hard. Nothing. The old engine turning over and over, pistons moving in new rings.

“Jia…”

“I know.”

She let the throttle go. She kicked once more.

✦ ✦ ✦

It coughed.

And coughed. And caught. Left. Middle. Right, a beat behind. Then all three at once. A sound she’d only ever heard on old videos. High and furious and ringing, a chainsaw full of bees. Blue smoke rolled out of all three pipes. Across the yard. Straight over Guo and his tea.

The whole bike shook on its stand. Like an animal waking up after nine years and remembering what it was. The loudest thing she’d ever heard under the flyover. At the end of the lane the breakfast woman dropped her shutter.

Jinx held the throttle steady, just above idle. Left. Middle. Right. Even. Hot. A bit rough. A bit lean on the right. The lie round the seal holding. Holding. Oil coming through. The smoke thinning. Blue to grey to nearly nothing.

Running.

Five forty in the morning, and it was running.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t turn round. She kept her hand on the throttle and her ears on the engine. She heard Guo put his cup down on the step. Carefully. She heard him come across the yard and stop beside the bike. He said nothing at all.

He stood in the smoke looking at his brother’s motorbike with its three pipes rattling. His face went young. All at once. Like it was 1989 and somebody had just handed him the key. He put his hand on the tank. On the dust. Where his brother’s hand would have gone.

She took her hand off the throttle and stepped back.

“Once round the yard. Gently. The right seal’s held on with sealant. It’ll last a morning. Then you get the cases split and done properly.” She wiped her hands. “Not my father. Someone with a clean workshop.”

Guo looked at her. Then he got on.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rode it once round the yard. Slowly, in first, pipes crackling, smoke going up under the flyover. Past the scrap heap. Past the pillars. Past her father in the doorway and Dou by the door. Once round. Then again.

He stopped in front of her and sat there with the engine running and his hands on the bars. Then he turned it off. The quiet rang in her ears. Trucks. Somewhere, the breakfast woman’s shutter went back up. Guo got off. He stood with one hand on the seat.

“That was very good, Miss Jinx.”

Behind her, she heard Raiden breathe out for what felt like the first time all night.

It was over. Wasn’t it? Standing there in the yard with two-stroke smoke in her hair and her hands black to the wrist. She’d built her way out. Like she’d built her way out of everything her whole life. With her hands.

Then Guo smiled.

“So good that I don’t think I can let you go.”

chapters.title: Raiden Stops Playing Dumb
chapters.desc: Just before six in the morning under the flyover, the deal is broken and a knife comes out. Her useless husband steps in front of her and stops pretending. Then a black car at the end of the lane, and a brother-in-law who owes him one.
chapters.epigraph: “I know every building in this district. I know yours. You added two floors in 2019 on a frame drawn for four. Shall I tell you which beam?” — Raiden Lin
chapters.content:
“We had a deal.”

“We did. And you kept it. Beautifully.” Guo took his hand off the seat of his brother’s bike. “The debt’s gone. I’m a man of my word.”

“Then we’re going!”

“But you see, last night I didn’t know what you were. I thought you were a good mechanic.” He smiled. “Now I know you’re the only person in this city who could do that. In one night. Under a flyover. With an old man’s tools.”

“So?”

“So I’d be a fool to let that go back to the Docks to fix rich men’s bikes. Wouldn’t I?”

Dou had left the door.

He was walking across the yard. Not fast. The knife was out again. The small man was behind him.

“You’ll work for me. Not twelve bikes. As long as I need you. Good wages. Better than the Docks.” Guo looked past her. “And your father keeps his shop. And Mr. Lin keeps his face. His very happy face.”

She didn’t move.

What did she have? The gap behind the scrap heap. The bike. Her thirteen, in the bag on the bench, three metres away. Dou’s knife. The small man. Her father in the doorway. How fast could she—

Raiden stepped in front of her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t do it fast. He did it the way he did everything in a room. Easily. Like he’d just thought of a better place to stand. One step sideways. Now he was between her and Dou. Between her and Guo. His back to her. Hands in the pockets of his ruined grey trousers.

She heard him breathe in.

And then he stopped being stupid.

She felt it go. She was close enough to touch him, and she felt all of it leave. The gallery. The silly smile. The voice. Like an engine changing note when the cam comes on. His shoulders dropped. His head came up. He went completely still.

“Mr. Guo.”

The voice he used for builders. Low. Flat.

Guo blinked.

“I know every building in this district. I know yours.” Raiden didn’t take his hands out of his pockets. “Number forty, Sandpit Lane. Six storeys. Grey tiles. A sign that says Guo Trading, and a gold cat in the window that waves.”

“How—”

“Built in 1981. For four storeys. The drawings are in the city archive. Sheet nine of eleven. I’ve read them.” He tipped his head. “You added two floors in 2019 on a frame drawn for four. Shall I tell you which beam?”

Guo didn’t say anything.

“Third floor. North side. By the stairs. There’s a beam carrying everything above it. A transfer beam. There’s only one.” Even. Pleasant. “And it’s cracked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The yard had gone quiet. Dou had stopped walking. He was looking at Guo. The small man was looking at Dou.

“I walked past last summer. I saw it from the street through the stairwell window. A diagonal crack, about a metre long, from the bottom edge toward the support.” Raiden’s voice didn’t change at all. “That’s shear. That’s a beam telling you it’s had enough.”

“You’re lying.”

“I don’t lie about buildings. I lie about everything else. Never buildings.”

“It’s—”

“It’ll hold a while. A year. Maybe two.” He paused. “Then one day it won’t, and the top three floors come down into the bottom three. With everybody in them.”

He took one hand out of his pocket. His phone was in it.

“I took a photograph. It’s the clearest crack I’ve ever seen. I’ve got the archive drawings. And I’ve got the number of a woman at the Buildings Department who owes me a favour.”

“What favour?”

“I once told her the car park under the new courthouse was about to fall down. It was.” He held the phone up. “One message. She’ll have Sandpit Lane closed by lunchtime. Everybody out. Inspectors in every room. Every drawer opened.”

Every drawer. Guo’s face moved.

Raiden put the phone away.

“I’m not going to send it. Not today. Today you’re going to say the debt’s gone, which you already did. And you’re going to say she’s going home.” He tilted his head the other way. “Then you’re going to go to Sandpit Lane and get your third floor propped before somebody dies in it.”

“And if I—”

“That bit’s free. I’d tell you whatever you did. I don’t like buildings falling on people.”

He turned his head a fraction toward Dou. He didn’t take his eyes off Guo.

“And you. You’ve been sleeping on my wife’s old bed. I know which building you go home to. Fourth floor. At the back. The one with the bad stairwell.” Nothing in his voice at all. “Put that knife away.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo stared at him.

She watched his face. She’d never seen a face work so hard to stay still. He looked at the grease on Raiden’s cheek. The pencil on his fingers. The ruined shoes. He was trying to put it all back together into the happy boy in the waistcoat. The useless one.

And failing. And trying again. And failing.

“You’re Lin Jian’s son.”

“Yes.”

“They say you’re a fool.”

“They do. I worked very hard on it.”

“Your father—”

“My father’s got nothing to do with this. He’s asleep in the Walled City. He doesn’t know I’m here. Nobody in my family knows I’m here.” A beat. “Well. One does.”

At the end of the lane, under the lowest flyover, an engine stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

They all heard it.

Not a lorry. Not a van. Something heavy that idled like a big cat, then stopped. A door opened and shut. Another. Then another, further off, at the far end of the lane.

Footsteps. Not hurrying.

Dou turned round. The small man turned round. Guo didn’t. Guo was still looking at Raiden.

“I rang him from the second bus. Last night, before I came through the gap.” Raiden checked his watch. “I said, I’m going under the Cao flyover. If I don’t ring you by six, come.” He sighed. “It’s five fifty-one. He’s early. He’s always early.”

Zhao Zhendong came into the yard.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in the front. Through the middle door. Past her father in the office doorway, who stepped back to let him by without being asked.

Black coat. Hands in his pockets. Alone.

He didn’t need anybody with him. There were men at both ends of the lane. She’d heard the doors. But he came in on his own and stopped under the lamp in the last of the two-stroke smoke.

He looked round. At the bike. At Dou and the knife. At the small man. At Guo. At Raiden, standing in front of her with his hands in his pockets. At her.

Four seconds each.

It took ages. Nobody moved while he did it. Not even the breakfast woman at the end of the lane, who’d come out to see what the cars were and gone straight back in.

Then he looked at Guo again.

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That was all, for a while.

Zhao looked at Guo. Guo looked back. The colour went out of Guo’s face from the top down. Like oil out of a sump.

Everybody under the flyover knew who that was. Everybody in the city.

“Mr. Zhao…” Guo’s voice had gone thin. “I didn’t know… I wasn’t aware this was—”

“She’s family.”

Flat. The way he said everything.

Guo’s mouth moved. Nothing came out.

“Her father’s shop.” Zhao didn’t look at the shop. “Clean.”

“Yes. Yes, of course. The debt’s gone. I said so. I’m a man of my—”

“Your building.”

Guo stopped.

“Prop it. Today.”

Zhao turned then and looked at Raiden. At Jinx behind him. The corner of his mouth did something. On anybody else it would have been nothing. On Zhao Zhendong it was very nearly a smile.

“That’s the floor paid for. We’re even.”

He walked out the way he’d come. Past her father. Through the middle door. Up the lane. Car doors at both ends. Engines going away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Guo went five minutes later. He didn’t say a word. He wheeled his brother’s bike out by hand. He didn’t want to start it again under the flyover. Not now. Dou and the small man went with him. Dou had put the knife away.

At the corner by the scrap heap, Guo stopped and looked back. Not at Raiden. At her.

“It runs. It really runs.”

“Get the cases split. Properly. Someone with a clean workshop.”

He looked at her a moment longer. Then he went.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden stood in front of her with his back to her in the middle of the empty yard. Trucks went over. At the end of the lane the breakfast shutter went up.

Then she saw his hands.

He’d taken them out of his pockets. They were hanging at his sides. And they were shaking. Badly. The long clever hands that had held a torch without moving from ten at night till dawn were shaking so hard she could see it from behind.

She put her arms round his chest from behind. She put her face between his shoulder blades. She held on.

He made a sound.

“I’ve never done that.”

“I know.”

“In front of anyone. Since I was ten. Never.” His voice was all over the place. “Not at the gallery. Not at the gala. Not for my father. I didn’t know if I could. I didn’t know if there was anybody left under it.”

“There was.”

“I was so frightened, Jia. I’ve been frightened since Tuesday. Since the eggs.” His shaking hands came up over hers on his chest. “Then I read the note. And I thought, she’s done it. She’s done what I did at the hospital.”

“Raiden—”

“She’s gone out the back so they won’t see me.” He laughed, horribly. “And I hated it. I HATED it. I understood why you hated me. All of it. Before I’d finished reading.”

“I’m sorry.”

He turned round in her arms and grabbed her.

He didn’t say anything. He took her face in both shaking hands and kissed her. In the yard, under the lamp, in front of the office window where her father was standing behind the wire glass.

Like he was drowning. He pulled her in so hard her boots left the ground. She tasted salt and two-stroke smoke and chilli oil from the dumplings. She grabbed his collar in her black fists and kissed him back the way she’d wanted to since he came round the scrap heap with a paper bag.

Neither of them stopped until a lorry going over the flyover leaned on its horn. Long. Loud. For no reason at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Foreheads together. Breathing. His face was wet.

“Don’t be sorry. Don’t you dare be sorry.” His voice cracked. “You built a dead man’s bike in one night under a flyover with a seal held on with lies. I’m going to draw your hands on that kick-start till I die.”

“You came through the gap.”

“I know about all the gaps. I told you. I’m the key.” A broken laugh. “You said I left it by the window. I didn’t leave this one by the window. I’ve carried it round for two years. In case you ever went down the lane.”

She stood there with her forehead on his and her hands on his face.

“Take me home.”

“You’re driving.” He sniffed. “I don’t drive. You KNOW I don’t drive.”

She laughed. Out loud, in the yard, under the flyover, with her arms round his neck. He laughed too, helplessly. He lifted her right off the ground and spun her once, like in the hangar up north. Her boots knocked her father’s oil drum over. It rolled all the way across the yard.

Nobody went after it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father was in the office doorway when they went to the bike.

He hadn’t moved. Hands at his sides. He looked at her. At Raiden. At the empty corner where the triple had been.

She stopped in front of him.

What did you say? She didn’t have a single word. Not one.

He didn’t either. His mouth worked, the way it had in the lane.

“The middle jet,” he said at last. Low. “You’d have found it.”

“Eventually.”

“You’d have found it.” He looked at his hands. “You always found it.”

Then he turned round and went into the office and shut the door.

She stood there.

Raiden put his hand on the small of her back. He left it there. He didn’t say a word. He just waited.

After a while she turned round. She put her helmet on him. The right way round. She did up the strap under his chin, and pulled it one notch tighter than it needed to be.

“Ow.”

“Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Tong and the anchor woman were both on the step of the noodle shop when the black bike came down the street. Coats over their nightclothes. Like they’d been there all night.

Had they? Probably. Of course they had.

“WHERE have you BEEN?”

“North.”

“North!” Mrs. Tong looked at Raiden climbing off the back, black to the elbows, trousers ruined, helmet on crooked. “What did you do to him?”

“He held a torch.”

“For how long?”

Raiden, from inside the helmet: “Five hours and twelve minutes.”

The anchor woman looked Jinx up and down. The bag. The hands. The face.

“Hah.”

“Is that a good hah?” Raiden asked her.

“It’s a hah.” She went back inside.

Mrs. Tong had them at the table by the fridge before Jinx had got her gloves off. Congee. Fried dough. Tea so strong it was nearly a solid. The men off the night shift looked at Raiden’s trousers and said nothing.

He fell asleep sitting up halfway through his bowl. Spoon still in his hand.

Jinx took the spoon. She ate the rest of his congee. Mrs. Tong watched her do it.

“He’s your husband,” Mrs. Tong said, low. “Not a dog. You can’t just let him follow you into trouble.”

“I didn’t let him.”

“Did you tell him to stay home?”

“In capitals.”

“And?”

Jinx looked at him. Asleep against the fridge with his mouth open and grease up to his eyebrows. The fridge hummed into his cheek.

“He came anyway.”

Mrs. Tong put another piece of fried dough on Jinx’s plate. Then, after a while, one on his.

“Good,” she said. “Keep him.”

chapters.title: Her Father Says Sorry
chapters.desc: Winter 2023 into 2024. Her father sits on the black step and says sorry, badly. Then the red door opens for her at last, she refuses Lin Jian a favour in his own kitchen, and at New Year she kisses her husband on his father’s roof in front of everyone.
chapters.epigraph: “Nobody has said no to me in my own kitchen since 1987. Sit down. Eat. You’re my daughter-in-law.” — Lin Jian
chapters.content:
“There’s an old man on your step.”

Jinx pushed herself out from under the bike. The anchor woman was in the doorway.

“He’s been there twenty minutes. He won’t knock.”

The second Saturday in December. Cold. Jinx wiped her hands and went to the door.

He was sitting on the step with his back to it, on the cold stone, in an old brown coat she remembered. Looking at the rope shops. The chandlers. Mrs. Tong’s sign. His hands were between his knees.

“You can come in.”

He didn’t get up.

“I’ve never been here.” He was looking at the street. “Five years. I knew where it was the whole time. I used to ride past on the bus. I never got off.”

She didn’t say anything. She sat down on the step beside him.

✦ ✦ ✦

A container ship sounded in the basin. Mrs. Tong came out of her shop, saw them, and went straight back in. Upstairs, through the open window, Raiden was at the stove singing something badly.

“I should have stopped him.”

She went rigid.

“The man. In your room. When you were seventeen.” His hands were tight between his knees. “I heard you. I was in the yard. I heard you shout.”

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t come. I stood in the yard and I didn’t come. Because he was the buyer’s man, and the buyer was the only one still buying from me, and I thought—” He stopped. “I don’t know what I thought. Then you came out with the tyre iron. And his hand.”

“I know what happened.”

“And I told you to say sorry. To HIM.”

She didn’t move.

“I’ve thought about it every night. Ten years. I never said it to anyone.” He breathed. “I’m sorry, Jia. I should have come. With a spanner. Broken his other hand.”

“You were…”

“A coward. Your whole life.” His voice went. “You were never a coward. Not even at five. And I let them give you a name for it, and I was proud. Proud of the wrong thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t forgive him. Not then. How was she meant to? She sat beside him with black hands and a tight chest and didn’t say it’s all right. It wasn’t. She’d never once said a thing to him she didn’t mean.

But she didn’t get up.

“You found the jet.”

He looked at her.

“The middle one. I’d have spent an hour on it. You saw it from the doorway.” She looked at the street. “Nobody else could have.”

He put his face in his hands. She sat there. After a while, without looking, without deciding, she put her hand on his back. On the old brown coat. Between his shoulders. She left it there. Upstairs, Raiden had stopped singing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden cooked a second fish without being asked and laid a third place at the long table. Her father sat down like a man waiting to see a doctor.

He looked round. Five tall windows. The bath through the door. The drafting table. Her bench with its vice. The shelf with the glass prize and the Best in Show and the tin of washers.

“You own this?”

“Yes.”

“The whole building?”

“And next door.” She didn’t look at Raiden. “My husband bought it. In my name.”

Her father looked across the table.

Raiden was taking the bones out of her fish with his chopsticks, without looking. He felt it and glanced up. No silly face. He’d stopped doing the silly face at the long table since the flyover. He just looked back.

“The land under the shop. Who owns it?”

Her father blinked. “I do. My father bought it. In 1969.”

“There’s a developer I know. A decent one, which is rare.” Raiden went back to her fish. “He’s wanted land under the north flyovers for three years. He’ll pay fair. More than fair, if I ask. A flat on the sea side with a balcony. No more rent. No more buyers. No more Guo.”

Her father stared at him.

“If you want. It’s your land. You can say no.”

“Pigeons.”

Raiden looked up.

“I always wanted pigeons. Racing ones. On a roof. My father had them.” Her father looked at his plate. “I never had a roof.”

“The flat’s got a roof.” Raiden picked up his chopsticks again. “I’ll make sure.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The land sold in January. The developer paid twice what it was worth, because Raiden asked. Raiden paid him back the difference in drawings. She only found that out later.

Her father got a flat on the sea side in a low old block with a flat roof. Raiden drew him a pigeon loft. Jinx built it, steel and timber, over three Saturdays. Her father passed her the screws in the right order without being asked.

Twelve pigeons by February. He named them after engines. He rang on Sundays now. Just to say what the pigeons had done. She didn’t say much back. She listened. That was new too.

And she’d started leaving notes. Nobody asked her to. On the back of an invoice, on the bench, under the thirteen’s hook, whenever she went further than Mrs. Tong’s.

DYNO SHOP. BACK AT SIX. J.

He never said a word about them. He kept every single one.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re shaking.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re shaking the pastries.”

The red door. A Saturday in January. Not at two in the morning. Six in the evening. Lamp lit. Lion’s head polished. Raiden on the step beside her with a box of pastries in one hand and her hand in the other.

The washer was on his finger. No string. She looked at it.

“No string.”

“No more string.” He squeezed. “Ever.”

The door opened. Lin Jian. He looked at her on the step in her old black jacket. At their hands.

“You came.”

“I said one day.”

“Yes. He told me.” He stood back. “Come in.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was tall and old. Stairs everywhere. Every sound carried. A long kitchen. A fire at one end. A long table with eleven chairs and no two of them matching.

Elowen and Zhao.

“You’re late,” Elowen told Raiden. “You’re never late.”

“She was shaking the pastries.”

“I was NOT.”

Evangeline, at the end of the table by the fire, in grey, on her own. She didn’t say a word to Jinx all evening. She just sat there and watched her with her face doing nothing at all. Jinx could tell she was pleased anyway.

Elara, late from the hospital, in scrubs under her coat, already talking.

“He’s in theatre, he says sorry—I mean, nobody, nobody says sorry, I’m starving, is that duck?”

Eliana, with a laptop.

“Spreadsheet’s updated.”

“What does that mean?”

“Nothing,” said everybody at once.

And the cook.

Ah Sim was eighty and the size of a child. She came out of the kitchen door with a ladle and looked Jinx up and down, slowly. Then at Raiden. Then at Jinx again.

“He’s fat.”

“He cooks.”

Ah Sim looked at her. Then she pointed the ladle at the chair next to Raiden’s.

“Sit down and eat. You’re too thin too.”

At dinner Raiden peeled her prawns. Every one. Without looking, while he argued with Elowen about a shelf. He put them in her bowl one by one. Lin Jian watched him do it all through the soup. He didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner the others went up to the long room on the second floor to argue about Raiden’s drawings. Jinx stayed in the kitchen. Why? She didn’t know. Ah Sim had handed her a tea towel without asking and she was drying.

Lin Jian came down the stairs and stood in the doorway. Ah Sim looked at him. She put the ladle down and walked out of her own kitchen without a word.

“I need a bike.”

Jinx put the tea towel down.

“Not for me. For a job. In the spring.” He kept his voice low. “Cargo that needs to move fast through a part of the city where vans get stopped.”

“So a bike.”

“A bike that doesn’t look like anything. That carries a case. That nobody can catch.” He looked at her. “Your father used to say nobody could catch yours.”

The black car coming down the lane. Her father’s hands on the desk. Guo. I’d like some of that luck. Twelve bikes. Then twelve more.

“No.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move.

“I don’t build for that. Not for Guo. Not for my father’s buyers. Not for you.” She picked the towel up again. Her hands needed something. “I got out. I’m not going back in because the man asking has a nicer kitchen.”

The fire popped.

“I’ll build you a bike to ride. Any bike. For nothing.” She dried a bowl. “Never one for a job.”

The kitchen was dead quiet. Upstairs Raiden laughed at something. She’d been frightened of this man since she was nine. She stood in his kitchen with a tea towel and found she wasn’t. Not even a little bit. Then Lin Jian laughed.

The huge rusty laugh from the flower shop step. It went straight up the stairs. Upstairs the arguing stopped dead.

“What was THAT?”

“Was that BABA?”

“Nobody has said no to me in my own kitchen since 1987.” He wiped his eyes. “Ah Sim. About a fish.”

He came in. He took a dish off the rack. He took a second towel off the rail. He started drying it beside her. Badly.

“Good… Good, that’s good. He’ll need someone who says no. He’s never had anybody. His sisters let him do whatever he likes because he’s the boy. I sent him away and then let him do whatever he liked because I’d sent him away.” He put the dish down wet. “You say no.”

“All the time.”

“Good.” He picked the dish back up, because she was looking at it. “Then sit at my table any time you like. Sit down. Eat. You’re my daughter-in-law.” He dried the same spot twice. “You were family when you were under that bench with the carburettor. I just didn’t know whose.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell Raiden about the bike. She told him about the dishes. In the taxi home, with his head on her shoulder.

“Your father dried a plate.”

He lifted his head.

“Badly.”

“My father has never dried a plate in his LIFE.”

“He did tonight.”

He laughed so hard the driver looked round.

“What did you SAY to him?”

“Nothing.”

“Jia. The whole house heard him.”

“Nothing.”

He gave up. He put his head back on her shoulder, still laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunar New Year was the tenth of February. They went to the Walled City on the eve.

Everybody did. Every Lin. Aurelia Chen in gold, with her husband. Elara at six in a red dress. And at seven a huge man in a good shirt came up the hill from the car with a kumquat tree on his shoulder.

He stood in the doorway with it. Every Lin in the world looked at him.

“Where do you want the tree?”

Raiden’s mouth fell open.

“Oh my God, she’s found a WARDROBE.”

“RAIDEN.”

He said it three more times before the soup. The wardrobe’s name was Jun Hyuk. He talked to everybody. He talked to Jinx for twenty minutes about the engine in her bike. The intake. How had she matched the runners? By hand? All four? Really?

Evangeline watched him from across the room with no expression at all. Jinx liked him at once.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Mahjong. Four players. Who’s in?”

Lin Jian, after dinner, rubbing his hands.

“Me.” Aurelia, already pulling up a chair.

The table went quiet.

“I’ll play!” Raiden. “I love losing money. It’s my hobby.”

“I’ll play. Somebody has to keep her honest.” Elowen.

Lin Jian looked round the table for a fourth. At Jinx.

“Jia?”

She held up her hands. Black nails. Done at the bench that afternoon with the bottle in the vice.

“Not with these. They’re still wet.”

Raiden put his face in his hands. His shoulders were shaking. Zhao said “Hm,” meaning absolutely not. Chen Si smiled and said he couldn’t possibly play against his wife. Then Lin Jian tried the end of the table.

“Evie?”

Evangeline got up without a word. She sat down. She turned her tiles face down. She beat Aurelia hand after hand. Till two in the morning. Without a word. Jinx watched from the sofa. At some point Aurelia said something about cats.

“There’s a third cat?” Jinx asked, interested.

“There will NEVER be a third cat.”

Behind Aurelia’s chair, Chen Si coughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At midnight even Aurelia left her tiles. Everybody went up on the roof.

A flat roof with a wall round it, and pots of dead geraniums Ah Sim wouldn’t let anybody throw out. The whole Walled City going down the hill below them in lanes and stairs. The harbour. The city across it, waiting.

Twelve o’clock. Everything went up at once. From the harbour. From the Coastal High-Rise. From every roof in the Walled City. Red, gold, white, breaking over the water. The noise coming back off the hill like a war.

She stood at the corner of the wall. He came and stood behind her. He put his arms round her waist and his chin on her shoulder.

“Happy New Year, wife.”

She turned round in his arms. She didn’t say anything. She looked at him with the fireworks going red and gold over his face. And she kissed him.

Not hard. Not like the yard, or the bench. Slow. Both hands on his face. On his father’s roof, in front of his entire family, with the sky breaking open over the harbour.

He went completely still. Then he kissed her back the same way. Slow. Like he’d been waiting years for her to do it in exactly this spot. Behind them somebody whistled. Eliana.

“Finally.” Elowen.

“Hm.”

She didn’t stop.

When she did, he had his forehead against hers and his eyes shut.

“In front of everyone.”

“Yes.”

“On my father’s roof.”

“Yes.”

He opened his eyes. He reached into his jacket. She knew what for. Her breath caught, the way it had at Mrs. Tong’s in September 2021.

His wallet. The soft old brown one. Behind the cards, a fat wad of folded paper. Napkins. Receipts. The back of a dyno manual. A drawing of a red door.

Thirty of them.

He didn’t take one out. He just showed her, in the light of the fireworks. Then he put it back.

“Not tonight. Tonight’s yours. I only wanted you to see I’ve kept them all.”

She looked at him.

“Ask me in March.”

He went white.

chapters.title: She Lets Him In
chapters.desc: March 2024. The thing that happened when she was seventeen, a steel cabinet she’s had since she left, and its code. Then the thirty-first napkin, two creepers under a bike, to scale, and a yes. Then a wedding at Mrs. Tong’s on a Thursday, the one his family can come to, and a bike show up north in their good clothes.
chapters.epigraph: “Oh-three-one-one. The day I left. It’s the code to everything I own that’s mine.” — Jinx
chapters.content:
“I was seventeen.”

He went still behind her in the water. The ninth of March. Two in the morning. The bath going cool, her back against his chest, the cranes lit up through the window.

She hadn’t planned it. She’d thought about it for two and a half years. Since the roof of the noodle factory, boots over the drop. I’m not telling you that one. She’d always thought it would be somewhere hard and bright. The workshop, lights on, standing up. So she could walk away.

It was the bath. And it came out of her like the triple under the flyover. A cough. Another. Then all at once.

✦ ✦ ✦

“I slept in the office. On the camp bed. Under the window.” She was looking at the cranes. “My father slept in the back room. There was a door between. He never locked it. Nobody locked anything.”

“Okay.”

“The buyer’s men came at night sometimes. To look at what was ready. Usually he dealt with them in the yard.” A breath. “One night one of them came in the office.”

His arms didn’t move. But they changed.

“I woke up. He was standing by the bed. He’d been drinking. He said something. I’m not telling you what.” Her voice stayed flat. “He put his hand on the blanket. On my leg.”

Raiden’s arms went to iron.

“There was a tyre iron under the bed. There was always one under the bed. I think I put it there at twelve. When they started calling me Jinx and looking at me different.” She shrugged against him. “I don’t remember putting it there. I just knew it was there.”

“Jia…”

“I broke his hand with it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He breathed out behind her. Long. Shaking.

“Two bones. I heard them. He went out in the yard screaming. And my father came out of the back room.” She stopped. “He’d been awake. He’d heard me shout before. He’d heard. He hadn’t come.”

His heart was going against her back. Hard. Fast. Furious.

“He looked at the man holding his hand. He looked at me in the office door with the tyre iron. And he told me to say sorry.”

“Did you?”

“No.” She looked at the cranes. “I went back in and shut the door. I sat on the camp bed with the tyre iron on my knees till morning.”

“Jia…”

“The next night I put a spanner under my pillow. A thirteen. I slept with it there five years. Every night. Till I’d saved for the van and the lathe and three months’ rent on the black door.”

“The thirteen on the wall—”

“Same one. The one I threw at you.” She almost smiled. “That’s why it’s worn.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything. She’d thought he would. He always talked. She’d thought he’d say something about her father, or the man, the way he had on the roof. He didn’t stop it. I can see it from here.

He didn’t. He held her. Both arms, round her chest and her waist, so tight she could feel every breath he took. Every one of them shook. Then his face was against her shoulder. On the top of the carp. Wet. Not from the bath.

“Thank you.” His voice was wrecked. “For telling me.”

“You never asked.”

“I never will. Not one thing you don’t want to give me. Everything or nothing. For the rest of our lives.” A breath. “But I’m glad you did. God, I’m glad.”

She turned round in the water. Half of it went over the side. She knelt up and took his face in her hands. His eyes were red and his face was wet and he wasn’t doing anything about it.

“There’s more.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him downstairs in towels. Through the dark workshop. Past the tool wall. Past the steel room. To the corner by the lathe, where there was a grey steel cabinet, waist-high, bolted to the floor, with a keypad on the front.

He’d seen it every day for two and a half years. It had been there before him. She’d brought it from under the flyover on the night she left and bolted it down on the very first day. Before the lathe. Before anything.

He’d never asked what was in it. Never touched it.

“Nobody’s opened this but me.”

She typed four numbers. Oh. Three. One. One.

“The day I left. The third of November. It’s the code to everything I own that’s mine. The bank. The phone. This.”

The cabinet opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Not much in it. A tyre iron. Old and black, with a bend near the end where it had hit something hard.

A drawing. Crayon, on the back of a parts invoice from 2002, folded and unfolded so many times it was soft as cloth. A motorbike drawn by a child. Wheels too small. Letters backwards. And the engine in enormous detail. Every fin on every cylinder.

A photograph. A woman in a red dress, from behind, walking away down a lane under a flyover. Blurred. A set of keys on a ring. A padlock. Two doors.

“The shop. I never gave them back. I thought I might need to go back in one day.” She looked at them. “I don’t need them any more.”

He knelt down on the concrete in his towel and looked.

“That’s your mother.”

“I think so. He never said. I found it in his desk when I was ten. I took it.”

He looked at the photo. Then at the crayon bike. Slowly, he started to smile.

“You drew the engine. When you were six. Every fin.”

“I was five.”

“Five.” He touched the edge of the paper. Just the edge. “You drew every fin on every cylinder and got the wheels wrong and didn’t care. Because the engine was what mattered.” He looked up at her. “That’s the best drawing I’ve ever seen.”

“It’s terrible.”

“I’ve seen drawings in a museum that cost more than this building. That’s better.”

“Raiden.”

“It’s the truth.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She shut the cabinet. She stood with her hand flat on its cold top.

“You told me about the freezer. The fish truck. The step. You gave me every door in your life.” She looked at him. “I never gave you one.”

“You don’t have to.”

“That’s the code. Oh-three-one-one. The cabinet. The bank. Everything.” Her voice didn’t wobble. Much. “You can have it. I don’t care what you do with it. I want you to have it.”

He knelt there and looked up at her. And started to laugh. With his face wet.

“Sorry. Sorry. It’s just… the first day under the black bike. Before you’d told me your name.”

“What?”

“I lay there thinking, I can get into any vault in this city and I can’t get into her.” He wiped his face. “I never said it out loud. It was too stupid even for me. And you’ve just handed me the code.”

She held her hand out. He took it. She pulled him up off the floor and into her arms. Both of them in towels in the dark at three in the morning. She kissed him. He kissed her back slowly. Like he had all night.

He did. They both did.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drew it at the long table, under the lamp. In his towel. He didn’t ask. He sat down with his pencil and his ruler and a paper napkin from the drawer. He kept a stack of them now. For exactly this.

She sat across from him and watched. She couldn’t see what it was. She didn’t try. Her heart was going harder than at the kick-start under the flyover.

When he’d finished he didn’t slide it across. He picked it up. He came round the table. He knelt on the floor beside her chair and held it up. Not a house this time.

The black bike, from below. Like lying on the floor looking up at the engine, lit orange by a work light. Two creepers side by side. Two tiny people on their backs with their shoulders touching. Between them on the concrete, one hand palm up. Another one on top.

The scale bar. 1:10.

And under it:

Will you marry me again? In front of them? (The first place I ever asked you anything. 31.)

✦ ✦ ✦

She looked at it so long he started to shake. Kneeling there in his towel holding it up. She thought of the black car coming down the lane. Her father’s hands flat on his desk. Lin. From the Walled City. Don’t ever go there.

She thought of the red door, and her hand on it. Lin Jian drying a dish badly beside her. You say no. Good. Zhao in the yard. She’s family. Elowen straightening her collar. Evangeline nodding, once, down the whole length of a flower shop. Her father on the black step. Proud of the wrong thing.

Thirty napkins in a wallet. Against his chest. Two and a half years.

Ask me when I can say yes without walking into your father’s house.

She’d walked into his father’s house. She’d said no to his father in his own kitchen. And nobody had owned her. Not for a second.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t move.

She watched it go into him. All the way down. The way yes had gone into him at Mrs. Tong’s that first time, with chilli oil on the napkin. The way thirty not yets had, after.

“Say it again. I’m sorry. I’ve had not yet thirty times. I need—say it again.”

“Yes.”

“Yes?”

“YES, Raiden. Yes. Yes. Get up off the floor, you idiot.”

He didn’t get up. He put his face down on her knees and cried.

Like after the freezer. From the very bottom. On his knees on the long room floor with the napkin crushed in his fist. The same sound she’d heard once, in December, in the dark. Only there was nothing sad in it this time.

She put her hands in his hair. She bent over him and pressed her face to the back of his neck and held on.

When he lifted his head his face was a mess. He didn’t care. He stood up and pulled her up out of the chair and kissed her. Not slowly. Napkin still in one fist. The other hand at the knot of her towel.

“I want you. Now.”

“You’ve got a napkin in your hand.”

He put it down on the table. Flat. He smoothed it once. Carefully. Then he came back to her, and she had him by the towel before he’d even straightened up.

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her backwards to the bed with his mouth on hers. The towels went somewhere. It was clumsy. Wet hair everywhere. Her knee caught the bedframe. She swore. He laughed into her neck. Then he wasn’t laughing.

She always took charge. Always. Tonight she didn’t. She lay back and let him, and it nearly killed him. She could see it. His hands shaking on her. His mouth on the carp, the inside of her wrist, the hollow of her throat.

“Yes,” he said against her skin. Over and over. Trying the word out. “Yes. Yes.”

“Stop saying it.”

“Never. I’m saying it till I’m ninety.”

He took his time. Far too much time. She pulled his hair. He didn’t hurry. She said his name in a voice she’d never heard come out of her own mouth. He lifted his head. He looked at her like it was the best thing anybody had ever said to him.

Then nobody said anything at all. Afterwards he lay with his head on her stomach and his arm across her hips.

“Jia.”

“Mm.”

“Small or big?”

“Small.”

“How small?”

“Three people.”

He thought about it. “Elowen. Zhao. And Eliana, because Eliana will find out anyway and never forgive us.”

“Fine.”

“And Baba?”

“Your father will want four hundred people and a lion dance.”

He was quiet. “…He would.”

“He gets the photo.”

“Where?”

She didn’t even think about it.

“Mrs. Tong’s.”

✦ ✦ ✦

CLOSED. WEDDING.

Red marker. The same sign, from the same drawer.

“AGAIN!” Mrs. Tong told the taxi driver, the postman and the man who delivered the cabbages. “Twenty years I never shut this shop. Now twice for the same two!”

The fourth of April. A Thursday. Ten in the morning. Elowen in green, with her hand over her mouth from the moment she walked in. Zhao in black at the back, arms folded, next to the fridge. Eliana in a hoodie, phone up, filming.

“For the spreadsheet.”

Raiden wore the silver waistcoat with the gears. Jinx wore the dark red dress from the flower shop, her boots, and the black leather jacket with the burn on the cuff.

Their table. The one by the fridge, with its back to the wall. Mrs. Tong stood at the end of it with her ladle like a judge.

“Anybody object?”

“Hm.”

That was Zhao.

The ladle swung round at him. He looked at the ceiling.

“Nobody objects.” Mrs. Tong banged the ladle on the table. “Ask her.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was pale. His hands were flat on the table either side of where his bowl usually went. Like the first time. Exactly like the first time.

“Jia.” He swallowed. “Will you marry me again? In front of them?”

“Yes.”

Flat and exact. The way she said everything. He made a sound like he’d been hit. At the back, Zhao put a hand over his eyes.

“And you?” Mrs. Tong jabbed the ladle at Raiden. “Do you?”

“YES!”

A man on the pavement outside stopped and looked in through the glass. He took a ring out of his waistcoat pocket.

Steel. Plain. Aurelia’s goldsmith, Enzo, had made it out of an offcut of stainless from her own bench. From the intake of the black bike. Because she’d said gold was soft and rings got caught in engines.

He put it on her finger. Right next to the washer. She looked at the two of them side by side. The washer she’d cut on her own lathe the week before a registry. And this.

“I’m keeping mine,” he said. “The washer. You measured it by holding my hand. I’m never wearing anything else.”

“Good.”

Then she took them both off, and threaded them onto the chain round her neck. The new one and the old one. They clicked together against her chest.

“Rings catch in engines.”

“I KNOW they catch in engines—”

“I’ve got a clutch tomorrow.”

Elowen laughed out loud behind her hand. Elowen. Out loud. He kissed her against Mrs. Tong’s fridge. Hands in her hair. The fridge shuddered. A magnet fell off.

“I’m still filming!”

“Stop filming.” Elowen.

Zhao looked at the ceiling. Nobody stopped anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then the bike show. The spring one up north. Two hours up the motorway in her van, straight from Mrs. Tong’s, in their good clothes. A box of pastries on the dashboard that Mrs. Tong had handed over crying.

He drew the whole way. She drove with one hand. The other was on his knee most of the time. They walked the hangar for three hours. Her in red with her boots and her jacket. Him in silver with pencil on his fingers.

The old man from the magazines was there. He looked at her dress. At the chain, which had slipped out of her collar while she bent over a gearbox. Two steel rings on it. At Raiden beside her, holding her hand.

“Well.”

“Today!” Raiden, before she could stop him. “This morning. In a noodle shop. She said yes on the thirty-first napkin.”

The old man looked at Jinx.

“Congratulations. Best in show.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Raiden told everyone for a month.

The petrol station. The toll booth. The anchor woman, who said about time. Then she went into her shop. She came out with a brass anchor the size of her hand, gave it to him, and went back in. The desk man at the Meridian. The firm in the south. An entire bus.

Mrs. Tong’s wall got a fourth picture. Her late husband. The crooked registry steps. The black bike from the newspaper. And now the two of them, kissing against her fridge, with a magnet in mid-air. Eliana had sent it. Jinx told nobody at all.

She opened the black door at seven on the Friday. A clutch. Two sets of brakes. A carb rebuild. A phone fight with a collector who wanted his tank painted gold.

And every so often, under a bike, in the dark, she put her hand up to her chest. To the two rings on the chain under her overalls. She held them a second. Let go.

On the Monday he caught her doing it. From the crate, with his sketchbook on his knee. He put the pencil down and watched her across the workshop until she looked up.

“What?”

“You did it again.”

“Did what?”

He smiled, and picked the pencil back up, and didn’t tell her.
